Summary: Overenthusiastic Repeated exception occurrence
Description: The new \\"Repeated exception occurrence\\" pop-up is a potentially good idea, but sadly is currently deeply flawed. For me it regularly cuts in on the first rather than a repeated occurrence.\\n\\ne.g. an Error breakpoint on an original IOException\\n\\n	throw new Error(\\"Failure for \\\\"\\" + expression + \\"\\\\"\\", e);\\n\\nis diagnosed as arepeat, presumably because the not-enabled breakpoint on IOException is incorrectly assumed to have already been reported.\\n\\nSurely the VM should be maintaining a stack of all exceptions objects thrown by more nested execution, so that when the above breakpoint occurs, the stack state is\\n\\nIOException (matching e) - not yet reported\\nnew Error - not yet reported\\n\\nthe new Error therefore causes an unconditional suspend.\\n\\nIff the new Error is rethown then its 'already reported' state may influence the \\"Repeated exception occurrence\\"  dialog.\\n\\nSimilarly iff the IOException is re-thrown the \\"Repeated exception occurrence\\" dialog may kick in.\\n\\nBut the first breakpoint hit on Error and/or IOException should NOT mess the user up with a \\"Repeated exception occurrence\\" dialog for something that is not a repeated occurrence.

Summary: [10,11,12][compiler] NoSuchMethodError at runtime when invoking method on multiple bounded typed lambda argument
Description: While fiddling with some (admittedly a bit esoteric) typing, I think I have found a bug in ecj. It seems that even though the compiler correctly infers a multiple bounded type, and accepts accessing members of any of the types of the multiple bounded type, when the multiple bounded type appears as a lambda argument, only the first of the listed types can have methods invoked during runtime.\\n\\nAs this is a little involved to explain with text only, I have prepared small project which reproduces the problem:\\nhttps://github.com/runeflobakk/broken-method-dispatch (more details in the readme)\\n\\n\\nsrc/main/java contains a small example domain model, where in particular WithMessageRecipients contains a method with the following signature:\\n\\n<CONTACT extends WithName & WithEmailAddress> List<? extends CONTACT> getMessageRecipients();\\n\\n\\nsrc/test/java contains a test which accesses methods on both the WithName and WithEmailAddress interfaces on elements of the list returned from the getMessageRecipients() method. The one using a for loop assigning each element to an inferred var type works fine, but when the elements appears as lambda arguments using a Stream, the invocation fails at runtime with a NoSuchMethodError.\\n\\nThe code both compiles and executes with not problems with the OpenJDK compiler.

Summary: [9] -Xbootclasspath/a should still be supported
Description: Since bug 518866 Java 9+ projects can no longer append to the bootclasspath, although this is still legal in Java 9.\\n\\nPrior to Java 9 this used to work as follows:\\n\\nAbstractJavaLaunchConfigurationDelegate.getBootpathExt() detects the System Library using the property IRuntimeClasspathEntry.STANDARD_CLASSES. Then, all entries with property IRuntimeClasspathEntry.BOOTSTRAP_CLASSES that come after the System Library are detected as *appending* to the bootclasspath.\\n\\nSince bug 518866, however, the System Library is marked as IRuntimeClasspathEntry.MODULE_PATH or IRuntimeClasspathEntry.CLASS_PATH, i.e., IRuntimeClasspathEntry.STANDARD_CLASSES is no longer used.\\n\\nAs a result, configurations that should use -Xbootclasspath/a use plain -Xbootclasspath causing the JVM to throw an error:\\n-Xbootclasspath is no longer a supported option.\\n\\n\\nFor a moment I was blaming bug 522696, but signaling -Xbootclasspath and -Xbootclasspath/p is correct. No change required in that area.

Summary: [17][switch pattern] Integrate pattern switch with null analysis / annotations
Description: Switch patterns open a few new options for null analysis with / without null annotations.\\n\\nHere are a few ideas:\\n\\n//---\\n	void foo(Object o) {\\n		switch (o) {\\n		case Integer i -> consumeInt(i);\\n		case @NonNull String s -> {\\n			if (s != null) {\\n				System.out.println(s.toLowerCase());\\n			}\\n		}\\n		default -> System.out.println(\\"default\\");\\n		}\\n	}\\n	\\n	void consumeInt(@NonNull Integer i) {\\n		\\n	}\\n//---\\n\\n\\"case Integer i\\" should interpret 'i' as @NonNull, thus avoiding the current warning:\\n\\nNull type safety (type annotations): The expression of type 'Integer' needs unchecked conversion to conform to '@NonNull Integer'\\n\\nOne might be tempted to respect \\"case @NonNull String s\\", but at a closer look the annotation cannot have any effect here (similar to \\"instanceof @NonNull String\\"): in the matching case the value is null be definition already, changing the annotation to @Nullable is nonsense. => perhaps we should raise a warning/info about uselessness of such annotations.\\n\\nWith or without the useless annotation inside the \\"case String s\\" block, the null check on 's' should be flagged as unnecessary (isn't). But that's simply a consequence of understanding that declaration as implying @NonNull.\\n\\nI still need to check the exact rules when \\"case Object o1:\\" and \\"default\\" may or may not give a null-hint (relating to presence/absence of a null pattern etc).\\n\\n\\nAlso: what about a switch value known to be @NonNull? vis-a-viz a null pattern etc.

Summary: [17][switch pattern][null] default pattern does not apply to null - use this in analysis
Description: Follow up from bug 575593 comment 2\\n...\\n\\"In the vicinity of bug 575051 I learned that after 'default' the selector is known to be non-null. It would be nice to let our implementation use that fact, but unfortunately we have no distinct flowInfo that models just the default branch. Rather all cases are mingled into the cumulative 'caseInits'. I believe this is owed to legacy switches, but in '->' cases separate flowInfos per branch would make a lot of sense, no? \\"

Summary: Incorrect name "this$1" for synthetic field (the name must be "this$0")
Description: Build ID: I20050527-1300\\n\\nSteps To Reproduce:\\nCode to reproduce problem:\\n----\\npublic class NotInteresting\\n{\\n  public static class MyClass\\n  {\\n    public MyClass()\\n    {\\n    }\\n    \\n    public class MyInnerClass\\n    {\\n    }\\n  }\\n  \\n  public static void main(String[] args) \\n  {\\n    MyClass.MyInnerClass instance = new MyClass().new MyInnerClass();\\n    int a = 0;\\n  }\\n}\\n----\\n\\nWhen you compile this class with the Eclipse Java Builder (I used j2sdk1.4.2_06 and j2sdk1.5.0_10) then the synthetic member (pointer to enclosing instance) in variable\\n  instance\\nis called \\n  this$1\\nWhen you compile this class with javac (I used j2sdk1.4.2_06 and j2sdk1.5.0_10) then this synthetic member \\nis called \\n  this$0\\n \\n \\nThis is a problem with serialization when the Eclipse compiled object is written and the javac compiled object is read (or the other way round).\\n\\n\\n\\nMore information:\\n1. I observed the same behaviour with MyEclipse with Eclipse 3.2.1. \\n2. I could not find where the naming conventions are defined in the java language specification but the following text that I found in the documentation of Java 1.1 (when inner classes were invented) suggests that the Eclipse implementation is wrong because \\"this$...\\" must only be generated for enclosing INSTANCES:\\n\\nThe member attribute Synthetic \\nAs discussed previously, the compiler synthesizes certain hidden fields and methods in order to implement the scoping of names. These fields are private unless noted otherwise, or they are at most of package scope. \\nJava 1.1 compilers are required, when producing bytecodes, to mark any field or member not directly defined in the source code with an attribute named Synthetic. (At present, the length must be zero.) This will allow other compilers to avoid inadvertant source-level references to non-private hidden members, and will allow tools to avoid displaying them unnecessarily. \\n\\n(A corresponding mechanism for declaring a local variable to be Synthetic may also be introduced.) \\n\\nJava 1.1 compilers are strongly encouraged, though not required, to use the following naming conventions when implementing inner classes. Compilers may not use synthetic names of the forms defined here for any other purposes. \\n\\nA synthetic field pointing to the outermost enclosing instance is named this$0. The next-outermost enclosing instance is this$1, and so forth. (At most one such field is necessary in any given inner class.) A synthetic field containing a copy of a constant v is named val$v. These fields are final. \\n\\nAll these synthetic fields are initialized by constructor parameters, which have the same names as the fields they initialize. If one of the parameters is the innermost enclosing instance, it is the first. All such constructor parameters are deemed to be synthetic. If the compiler determines that the synthetic field's value is used only in the code of the constructor, it may omit the field itself, and use only the parameter to implement variable references. \\n\\nA non-private final synthetic method which grants access to a private member or constructor has a name of the form access$N, where N is a decimal numeral. The organization of such access protocols is unspecified. \\n\\nDebuggers and similar tools which are 1.1 compatible must recognize these naming conventions, and organize variable displays and symbol tables accordingly. Note that tools may need to parse these names. Compilers are strongly encouraged to use these conventions, at least by default. \\n\\nImplementations of the Java Virtual Machine may verify and require that the synthetic members specified here are defined and used properly. It is reasonable to exploit the nature of synthetic members by basing optimization techniques on them.

Summary: [compiler][loop] definite unassignment analysis involving do and try statements
Description: I20080530-1730\\n\\nOn the following test case, javac raises an error and Eclipse does not:\\npublic class X {\\n  public static void main(String args[]) {\\n	final int i;\\n	do {\\n	  try {\\n		break;\\n	  } finally {\\n		i = 0; // javac error here\\n	  }\\n	} while (args.length > 0);\\n  }\\n}\\n\\nReading JLS 3 $ 16.2.11 and $ 16.2.15, I believe that i is not definitely unassigned after the try statement because it is not definitely unassigned after the finally block, hence it is not definitely unassigned before the condition, hence it is not definitely unassigned after the condition when true, hence having it definitively unsigned before the try does not imply having it definitely unsigned after the condition, hence it is not definitively unsigned before the finally block, hence an error should be reported.\\nIn other words, I'd consider javac as right in this instance.

Summary: [1.5][compiler] better support for not warning about unnecessary @SuppressWarnings
Description: This is related to bug 210213 and bug 212884, but with one more twist:\\n\\nWe are generating a method that causes a warning (regarding potential null dereference) which we manually analyzed as a false alarm. So we want to \\nsuppress that warning and add @SuppressWarnings(\\"null\\").\\n\\nAs reported in other bugs now we are struggling with warnings about\\nUnusedWarningToken. The problem here is: the warning can either be \\ndisabled via the compiler option OR the class into which the method is \\ngenerated can potentially have a @SuppressWarnings(\\"null\\").\\n\\n  (to be specific: it's our compiler that generates this method at\\n  AST level into a user class - not sure if similar scenarios could be\\n  found with model driven technology)\\n\\nSo currently I found no workable way to say exactly:\\n  Don't report this warning \\n  NOR report if you think there is nothing to warn about.\\n\\nThe closest I could come was just using @SuppressWarnings(\\"all\\").\\n\\nAfter it has been decided that @SuppressWarnings(\\"unused\\") does not\\ncover UnusedWarningToken (for good reasons), I was thinking of one extra \\nwarning token so we can say:\\n	@SuppressWarnings({\\"null\\", \\"suppressWarnings\\"})\\n\\nAside from just adding this new token this would also require to\\nhave method CUD.finalizeProblems handle that irritant similar to \\"all\\"\\n(while \\"all\\" would lose this special semantics, because it already\\ncontains \\"suppressWarnings\\" ;-)\\n\\nI'm wondering if others would consider this kind of reflexive\\nsuppressWarnings useful, too. \\n(In our particular case \\"all\\" is actually tolerable).\\n\\nFurther cross-reference: in bug 127533 comment 9 Philippe concluded\\nthat SuppressWarnings should not disable UnusedWarningToken,\\nbut I think this argument strictly holds only when considering\\n\\"unused\\" as the token to suppress UnusedWarningToken, too.\\nHence my proposal for a new token.

Summary: [compiler] String concat shouldn't always call StringBuilder.toString()
Description: Created attachment 161823\\nTest class\\n\\nThe JLS allows a compiler to optimise String concatenation.\\n\\nHowever, I don't think the JDT compiler goes as far as it could, which could be a bit win where the string is not used.\\n\\nWhen the attached class is compiled using the 3.5.1 compiler, and disassembled (javap -c StringThing), the line:\\n		CharSequence cs = \\"[ERROR]\\" + s;\\nhas been turned into:\\n  CharSequence cs = new StringBuilder(\\"[ERROR]\\").append(s).toString();\\n\\nThis is not optimal, as a StringBuilder is, by design, a CharSequence, and therefore the StringBuilder is being converted to a String unnecessarily.\\n\\nIt seems to me that the point of the CharSequence interface is to be able to defer .toString() until absolutely necessary, which, in the case of logging at a disabled log level, is never.\\n\\nNaturally, the JRocket StringBuilder implementation (http://developers.sun.com/learning/javaoneonline/2007/pdf/TS-2171.pdf) would provide more benefits from this optimisation than the Sun one, but hey, I hear they're getting merged!\\n\\nI also wonder if the ECJ JSP compiler would benefit from this optimisation, as that's a whole lot of string concatenation.

Summary: [inline] Cannot inline method with multiple returns [refactoring]
Description: When a method has multiple return statements, it cannot be inlined. The message\\nrecieved is \\"Can't inline call. Return statement in method declaration\\ninterrupts execution flow.\\", which is a big improvement over previous versions\\nwhere it would just inline it and break your code, but I'd like to try and push\\nit further.\\n\\nAn example case:\\n\\n    public String getString(boolean test) {\\n        if(test) {\\n            return \\"True Value\\";\\n        } else {\\n            System.out.println(\\"It was false\\");\\n            return \\"False Value\\";\\n        }\\n    }\\n    \\n    public String doSomeStuff() {\\n        boolean value = true;\\n        String string = getString(value);\\n        return string;\\n    }    \\n\\nThe getString method cannot be inlined.\\n\\nIn this case, the manually refactored code would be:\\n\\n    public String doSomeStuff() {\\n        boolean value = true;\\n        String string;\\n        if(value) {\\n            string = \\"True Value\\";\\n        } else {\\n            System.out.println(\\"It was false\\");\\n            string = \\"False Value\\";\\n        }\\n        return string;\\n    }\\n\\nThis is done be replacing the \\"return\\" statement with an assignment to the\\nexternal variable, in much the same way as a single return statement refactoring.\\n\\nHowever, a more complex method to inline would be:\\n\\n    public String getString(boolean test) {\\n        if(test) {\\n            return \\"True Value\\";\\n        }\\n        System.out.println(\\"It was false\\");\\n        return \\"False Value\\";\\n    }\\n    \\nInlining this code in the same way would result in the code:\\n\\n    public String doSomeStuff() {\\n        boolean value = true;\\n        String string;\\n        if(value) {\\n            string = \\"True Value\\";\\n        }\\n        System.out.println(\\"It was false\\");\\n        string = \\"False Value\\";\\n        return string;\\n    }\\n\\nWhich would incorrectly be returning \\"False Value\\" every time.\\n\\nI'd like to find a way to determine the difference between the first getString()\\nmethod and the second so that the first may be safely inlined. \\nIt would be nice to have a refactoring that could convert multiple returns to\\nsingle returns, so that it could be combined with the inline refactoring, but I\\ndon't see a way to easily do so without using a GOTO statement.

Summary: [JUnit] A better JUnit and Eclipse integration.
Description: I've been using JUnit with Eclipse for quite a while and the more I use it the\\nmore I feel that it does not match with the rest of Eclipse views. If you are\\nfamiliar with Navigator, Package Explorer, Synchronize and some other views,\\nthen you can remember that each of them allows you to choose Working Set in\\norder to reduce number of visible entries for the current activity. \\n\\nWhen your activity is focused around implementing unit tests, running and\\ndebugging them it will be interesting to have a solid view for all existing test\\ncases within your scope of work (e.g. project, package, class). That bring us to\\nthe hierarchical tree similar to Package Explorer that shows all existing tests,\\nincluding test suites with grouped or even generated test cases (it means that\\nall tests has to be compiled and if there are suite()'s, they has to be executed\\nat this step). Each test should allow quick navigation to the tested code and\\ntest case implementation (or to suite() method). User can select multiple\\npackages, test suites or even concrete test cases for the execution. \\n\\nThat hierarchical view should also show state of the last execution of these\\ntests and also if the code or unit tests itself were modified (so you can't rely\\non the result of last test). Actually it could be bit complicated to track\\ndependencies from the changed class and also mark changed tests that depends on\\nthe changed code. \\n\\nUnit test view should also allow selecting a working set in the same way as it\\nis done for other views.\\n\\nPlease let me know what do you think about it.

We expected that the name of the renamed method would be updated for all references, but Eclipse did not update it in this plugin.\\n\\n\\nReproducible: Always\\n\\nSteps to Reproduce:\\n1. Create three plugins: pluginA, pluginB, pluginC, and make pluginB depend on pluginA and pluginC depend on pluginB. \\n\\n2. Create class A in pluginA:\\n\\n       public class A {\\n           public void m() {   }\\n       }\\n    \\n   Create class B in pluginB:\\n\\n       public class B extends A {\\n           @Override\\n           public void m() {   }\\n       }\\n\\n   Create class C in pluginC:\\n\\n       public class C {\\n           public void someMethod() {\\n               new B().m();\\n           }\\n       }\\n\\n3. Invoke the rename method refactoring on method m in class A and specify any new name for it (e.g. m1).\\n\\n4. Summary: [rename] Refactor rename of class to duplicate name can result in invalid source
Description: [RC1]\\n\\nUsing Refactor Rename to rename a class to have the same name as an existing \\nclass in a different package can result in uncompilable code.\\n\\nConsider three classes; a.X, a.Y and b.Z\\n\\n// a.X\\npackage a;\\nimport b.Z;\\n\\npublic class X {\\n  private Y y;\\n  private Z z;\\n  \\n  void func() {\\n    y.getYValue();\\n    z.getZValue();\\n  }\\n}\\n\\n// a.Y\\npackage a;\\n\\npublic class Y {\\n    public String getYValue() {\\n      return \\"\\";\\n    }\\n}\\n\\n// b.Z\\npackage b;\\n\\npublic class Z {\\n  public String getZValue() {\\n    return \\"\\";\\n  }\\n}\\n\\nNow refactor rename b.Z to b.Y, and class a.X will become\\n\\n// a.X\\npackage a;\\nimport b.Y;\\n\\npublic class X {\\n  private Y y;\\n  private Y z;\\n  \\n  void func() {\\n    y.getYValue();\\n    z.getZValue();\\n  }\\n}\\n\\nThere has been no attempt to distinguish between a.Y and b.Y. I think that what \\nshould probably have happened is that\\n  private Y z;\\nshould have become\\n  private b.Y z;\\n\\nThe most frustrating aspect of this bug is that it is not possible to undo the \\nrefactoring, as the two Y classes are now unseparable in a.X. Not too much of a \\nproblem in this scenario, but when the refactoring hits 100+ classes it's not \\nfunny.\\n\\n[I am not suggesting that two classes of the same name in different packages \\n(both under my control) is a good idea. When I encountered the problem, it was \\nan intermediate step in some refactoring I was doing.]

If i wanted to\\nuse the \\"default\\" junit launch configuration, i would just release the mouse\\nover \\"Junit Test\\". If I wanted to create a \\"new\\" launch configuration, I could\\ndrag the mouse over \\"New Launch Configuration...\\" context menu item in the final\\nstep. To launch recent tests, I would access a \\"Junit History\\" pulldown menu\\ninstead of the \\"Run Configuration\\" menu. Summary: [refactoring] Should make Undo the default when change execution fails
Description: I20060131-1200\\n\\nBug 126154 indicates that fatal exceptions can occur during change execution, against which we cannot do anything (e.g. an application like MS Word locked a file the user wanted to rename), and which we cannot detect upfront (because java.io.File does not reveal them).\\n\\nIn such situations we currently show a scary dialog ('scary' is fine;-) with options Undo and Abort, Abort being the default.\\n\\nI think we should make Undo the default here, since that's what's approriate to try in most cases. Alternatively or additionally, we should put a (partial) undo on  the undo stack if the user choses Abort, such that the undo possibility is not lost.

During this time, the ApplicationWindow runnable context is used to report status while the wizard is being initialized. This is bad, because there already is a Dialog open. This has a few problems. 1) You can cancel the dialog, but the operation would still be running. 2) You can't cancel the operation since it is blocked by a modal dialog. \\n\\nI wanted to fix this by creating a properties page that implements IRunnableContext with a progress monitor itself. Properties pages are not a IRunnableContext, but it was relatively easy to make it so using ProgressMonitorPart. (Except that cancelation is not supported) \\n\\nIt turns out even after I did the work to create a Properties page with a progress monitor, there was no way for me to pass in that IRunnableContext to the Wizard. RefactoringWizard is hard coded to use PlatformUI.getWorkbench().getActiveWorkbenchWindow() as the IRunnableContext when calculating the user input pages. (RefactoringWizard#getStartingPage()) Additionally, I can't override this method since it calls package-private and calls other private methods. \\n\\nMy request is to modify RefactoringWizardOpenOperation and RefactoringWizard to accept a IRunnableContext for execution.

Description: How to reproduce:\\n\\n1. Change filter preferences in package explorer (to make it save the \\npreferences at least once)\\n2. Install a plugin that defines a filter using the extension point \\norg.eclipse.jdt.ui.javaElementFilters\\n3. This new filter will be disabled in the package explorer even if it should \\nbe enabled by default\\n\\nCause:\\nWhen loading the filters in \\norg.eclipse.jdt.ui.actions.CustomFiltersActionGroup line 526, the following \\ncode is executed:\\n\\n  String id= (String)iter.next();\\n  Boolean isEnabled= new Boolean(store.getBoolean(id));\\n  fEnabledFilterIds.put(id, isEnabled);\\n\\nUnfortunately, isEnabled will be set to false for all new filters because \\nstore returns false if it cannot find an entry for the given id.\\nThis problem could be solved by using the following code instead:\\n\\n  String id= (String)iter.next();\\n  if (store.contains(id)){\\n    Boolean isEnabled= new Boolean(store.getBoolean(id));\\n    fEnabledFilterIds.put(id, isEnabled);\\n  }\\n\\n(Note that fEnabledFilterIds already contains all the filters before this code \\nis executed, the only thing that happens here is overriding the entries with \\nthe stored non-default preferences. If the store does not contain an entry for \\nthe given id, we will get the default preferences for that filter which is \\nIMHO the desired behaviour.)\\n\\nI've quickly tested this fix and it seems to work.

Summary: [refactoring] refactoring without modal window
Description: Microsoft Refactor! for Visual Basic 2005 Beta 2 provides refactoring without \\nthe overhead of a modal popup window.  You really have to see the demos to \\nappreciate the developer productivity enhancements these will provide.  All I \\ncan say is seeing is believing...\\n\\n\\nOverview of tool:\\nhttp://msdn.microsoft.com/vbasic/downloads/2005/tools/refactor/\\n\\nShort videos that demo this functionality:\\nhttp://msdn.microsoft.com/VBasic/Downloads/2005/Tools/Refactor/30SecDemo.Aspx\\nhttp://msdn.microsoft.com/VBasic/Downloads/2005/Tools/Refactor/3MinDemo.Aspx\\n\\n=====================================\\n- Clicking a variable in the text editor presents a refactoring dropdown icon, \\nthe Microsoft Smart Tag, that allows the variable to be renamed or moved near \\nits first reference.\\n\\n- Clicking on the refactoring dropdown icon lists the possible refactorings \\nand a short description about what the refactoring does to the code.\\n\\n- Block highlighted code presents a refactoring dropdown icon that lists \\npossible refactorings when clicked.  This icon saves the developer from having \\nto right click the block and select the refactoring menu.\\n\\n- The Extract Method refactoring automatically attempts to give the method a \\nname based on comments that come before the highlighted block.  If the code \\ncomment was \\"Do a big job\\" the method would automatically be named doBigJob. A \\nlarge visual indicator is presented to show where the method is to be \\ninserted.  A popup menu presents keyboard shortcuts that can be used to \\ncontrol the position of the visual indicator.  The up arrow will move the \\nindicator above the previous method, the down arrow will move the indicator \\nbelow the current method, the enter key accepts the location, and the escape \\nkey cancels the refactoring.  The default method name is now highlighted so \\nthat it can be renamed.  \\n\\n- Extract Constant, Extract Local, Extract Field refactorings behaves similar \\nto the Extract Method refactoring.\\n\\n- Clicking on a method name, variable, or parameter highlights the text \\nsimilar to the mark occurances does today and puts into automatic rename \\nrefactoring without a modal window.\\n\\n- Reorder Parameters refactoring requires clicking on the refactoring dropdown \\nicon.  This refactoring behaves similar to the Extract Method refactoring in \\nthat a menu appears showing the keys that can be used during the refactoring.  \\nThis time the left arrow moves the parameter left, the right arrow moves the \\nparameter right, the tab selects the next parameter, the shift-tabe selects \\nthe previous parameter, the enter commits the changes, and the escape cancels \\nthe refactoring.  The parameters are visually rearranged.\\n\\n- Cutting and pasting via the clipboard performs an automatic Extract Method \\nrefactoring.\\n\\n=====================================\\n\\nSupported Refactorings without modal windows:\\nReorder Parameters \\nExtract Method \\nExtract Property \\nCreate Overload \\nSurrounds With \\nEncapsulate field \\nReverse Conditional \\nSimplify expression \\nIntroduce Local \\nIntroduce constant \\nInline Temp \\nReplace Temp with Query \\nSplit Temporary Variable \\nMove initialization to declaration \\nSplit initialization from declaration \\nMove declaration near reference

Summary: "Extract Local Variable" should never replace multiple expressions containing "new"
Description: Initial code:\\n\\nif (x) {\\n    d0.add(new Vector<Integer>());\\n    d1.add(new Vector<Integer>());\\n}\\n\\nSelect first occurrence of \\"new Vector<Integer>()\\" and replace with local variable a0, with the box checked to replace all instances of the expression with the variable:\\n\\nVector<Integer> a0 = new Vector<Integer>();\\nif (x) {\\n  d0.add(a0);\\n  d1.add(a0);\\n}\\n\\nThis is of course never going to be semantically correct.\\n\\nThe refactoring engine can't in general know if the given expression will have side effects like this.  However this is a fairly prominent case to catch as an exception -- if the expression contains a \\"new\\", then the checkbox to replace all instances should be greyed-out.  I almost didn't notice that the refactorer did this, because it has always worked for every expression I tried before.  \\n\\nPerhaps there needs to be a warning displayed in the dialog box if there is a method call in the expression and more than one instance of the expression is being replaced, which says that it is the programmer's responsibility to ensure that the function has no side effects.\\n\\nIn general, I think it would be very valuable for JDT to explicitly know when a method has side effects and when it doesn't.  This may be uncomputable in the general case, but it is certainly possible to prove when a function *doesn't* have side-effects.

Description:
DW (5/16/01 1:57:33 PM)\\n ISession might be a better term for an ILaunch.\\n\\nDW (7/30/01 1:31:42 PM)\\n Currently, a launcher launches a debug session, system process,\\n or connects to an already running program. In the future there could be other\\n launchers that may do things such as start a tracing session, or start\\n profiling session, etc. The term \\"Launch\\" (as a noun, i.e. the result of launching)\\n feels awkward and could be better described as a session.\\n\\n Propose to rename\\n ILaunch to ISession\\n ILaunchManager to ISessionManager\\n ILaunchListener to ISessionListener\\n Launch to Session\\n\\n Change DebugPlugin accessor\\n #getLaunchManager -> #getSessionManager\\n\\nISession would be defined as: [\\n\\npackage org.eclipse.debug.core;\\n\\n/*\\n * (c) Copyright IBM Corp. 2000, 2001.\\n * All Rights Reserved.\\n */\\n\\nimport org.eclipse.debug.core.model.*;\\nimport org.eclipse.core.runtime.IAdaptable;\\n\\n/**\\n * A session is the result of launching a program in debug mode, connecting\\n * to a program that is already running in debug mode, and/or\\n * starting one or more system processes (which may or may not be in debug mode).\\n *

\\n * This interface is not intended to be implemented by clients. Clients\\n * should create instances of this interface by using the implementation\\n * provided by the class Session.\\n *

\\n *

\\n * Note: This class/interface is part of an interim API that is still under development and expected to \\n * change significantly before reaching stability. It is being made available at this early stage to solicit feedback \\n * from pioneering adopters on the understanding that any code that uses this API will almost certainly be broken\\n * (repeatedly) as the API evolves.\\n *

\\n * @see Session\\n */\\npublic interface ISession extends ITerminate, IAdaptable {\\n /**\\n * Returns the debug target associated with this session, or null\\n * if no debug target is associated with this session.\\n *\\n * @return the debug target associated with this session, or null\\n */\\n IDebugTarget getDebugTarget();\\n /**\\n * Returns the object used to create this session - for example the program that\\n * was launched. Cannot return null.\\n * \\n * @return the launched object\\n */\\n Object getElement();\\n /**\\n * Returns the launcher that was used to create this session. Cannot return null.\\n *\\n * @return the launcher\\n */\\n ILauncher getLauncher();\\n /**\\n * Returns the processes associated with this session,\\n * or an empty collection if no processes are associated with\\n * this session.\\n *\\n * @return array of processes\\n */\\n IProcess[] getProcesses();\\n /**\\n * Returns the source locator to use when locating source elements associated\\n * with the debug target of this session, or null\\n * if source mapping is not supported.\\n *\\n * @return the source locator\\n */\\n ISourceLocator getSourceLocator();\\n /**\\n * Returns the mode this session was launched in - one of the mode constants defined by\\n * the session manager.\\n *\\n * @return the launch mode\\n * @see ISessionManager\\n */\\n public String getMode();\\n\\n}\\n\\n\\n]\\n\\n\\nAn ISessionListener would be defined as: [\\n\\npackage org.eclipse.debug.core;\\n\\n/*\\n * (c) Copyright IBM Corp. 2000, 2001.\\n * All Rights Reserved.\\n */\\n\\n/**\\n * A session listener is notified of sessions as they\\n * are added to and removed from the session manager.\\n *

\\n * Clients may implement this interface.\\n *

\\n *

\\n * Note: This class/interface is part of an interim API that is still under development and expected to \\n * change significantly before reaching stability. It is being made available at this early stage to solicit feedback \\n * from pioneering adopters on the understanding that any code that uses this API will almost certainly be broken\\n * (repeatedly) as the API evolves.\\n *

\\n * @see ISession\\n */\\npublic interface ISessionListener {\\n /**\\n * Notifies this listener that the specified session has been removed\\n * from the session manager.\\n *\\n * @param session the deregistered session\\n */\\n void sessionRemoved(ISession session);\\n /**\\n * Notifies this listener that the specified session has been added to\\n * the session manager.\\n * \\n * @param session the registered session\\n */\\n void sessionAdded(ISession session);\\n}\\n\\n\\n]\\n\\n\\nISessionManager would be defined as: [\\n\\npackage org.eclipse.debug.core;\\n\\n/*\\n * (c) Copyright IBM Corp. 2000, 2001.\\n * All Rights Reserved.\\n */\\n \\nimport org.eclipse.debug.core.model.IDebugTarget;\\nimport org.eclipse.debug.core.model.IProcess;\\nimport org.eclipse.core.resources.IProject;\\nimport org.eclipse.core.runtime.CoreException;\\nimport org.eclipse.core.runtime.IAdaptable;\\n\\n/**\\n * The session manager manages the set of registered sessions, maintaining\\n * a collection of active processes and debug targets. Clients interested\\n * in session notification may register with the session manager.\\n *

\\n * For convenience, a default launcher may be associated with a project.\\n * The preference is stored as a persistent property with the project.\\n * The debug UI plug-in uses this preference to help determine which \\n * launcher to invoke when the the run or debug button is pressed, based on\\n * the selection in the workbench. If a launcher cannot be determined,\\n * the user is prompted to choose a launcher.\\n *

\\n *

\\n * Clients are not intended to implement this interface.\\n *

\\n *

\\n * Note: This class/interface is part of an interim API that is still under development and expected to \\n * change significantly before reaching stability. It is being made available at this early stage to solicit feedback \\n * from pioneering adopters on the understanding that any code that uses this API will almost certainly be broken\\n * (repeatedly) as the API evolves.\\n *

\\n * @see ISession\\n * @see ISessionListener\\n */\\npublic interface ISessionManager extends IAdaptable {\\n /**\\n * A session in a normal, non-debug mode(value \\"run\\").\\n */\\n public static final String RUN_MODE= \\"run\\";\\n /**\\n * A session in a special debug mode (value \\"debug\\").\\n */\\n public static final String DEBUG_MODE= \\"debug\\";\\n \\n /**\\n * Adds the given listener to the collection of registered session listeners.\\n * Has no effect if an identical listener is already registerd.\\n *\\n * @param listener the listener to register\\n */\\n void addSessionListener(ISessionListener listener);\\n /**\\n * Removes the specified session and notifies listeners. Has no effect\\n * if an identical session is not already registered.\\n *\\n * @param session the session to remove\\n */\\n void removeSession(ISession session);\\n /**\\n * Returns the session the given process is contained in, or null\\n * no registered session contains the process.\\n *\\n * @param process the process for which to find a session\\n * @return the session containing the process, or null if none\\n */\\n ISession findSession(IProcess process);\\n /**\\n * Returns the session the given debug target is contained\\n * in, or null no registered session contains the debug target.\\n *\\n * @param target the debug target for which to find a session\\n * @return the session containing the debug target, or null if none \\n */\\n ISession findSession(IDebugTarget target);\\n /**\\n * Returns the collection of debug targets currently registered with this\\n * session manager.\\n *\\n * @return an array of debug targets\\n */\\n IDebugTarget[] getDebugTargets();\\n /**\\n * Returns the default launcher for the given project,\\n * or null if no default launcher has been set.\\n * The default launcher is stored as a persistent property\\n * with a project.\\n *\\n * @param project the project for which to retrieve a default launcher\\n * @return the defualt launcher, or null if none \\n * @exception CoreException if an error occurs accessing the\\n * persistent property\\n */\\n ILauncher getDefaultLauncher(IProject project) throws CoreException;\\n \\n /**\\n * Returns the collection of registered launchers that can operate in the\\n * specified mode - run or debug.\\n *\\n * @return an array of launchers\\n */\\n ILauncher[] getLaunchers(String mode);\\n \\n /**\\n * Returns the collection of registered launchers.\\n *\\n * @return an array of launchers\\n */\\n ILauncher[] getLaunchers();\\n /**\\n * Returns the collection of sessions currently registered\\n * with this session manager.\\n * \\n * @return an array of sessions\\n */\\n ISession[] getSessions();\\n /**\\n * Returns the collection of processes currently registered with this\\n * session manager.\\n *\\n * @return an array of processes\\n */\\n IProcess[] getProcesses();\\n /**\\n * Adds the specified session to the session manager.\\n * Has no effect if an identical session is already registered.\\n * \\n * @param session the session to register\\n */\\n void addSession(ISession session);\\n /**\\n * Removes the given listener from the collection of registered session listeners.\\n * Has no effect if an identical listener is not already registerd.\\n *\\n * @param listener the listener to deregister\\n */\\n void removeSessionListener(ISessionListener listener);\\n /**\\n * Sets the default launcher for the given project as a persistent property.\\n *\\n * @param project the project for which to set the preference\\n * @param launcher the launcher preference\\n * @exception CoreException if an error occurs setting the persistent property\\n */\\n void setDefaultLauncher(IProject project, ILauncher launcher) throws CoreException;\\n}\\n\\n]

Summary: Editor opening during debugging (1GK266A)
Description: jkca (9/14/2001 2:39:31 PM)\\r\\n\\r\\nCurrently, our code to open an editor when a Thread suspends does not take \\r\\nmultipage editors\\r\\ninto consideration.\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom a customer.\\r\\nWhat they want to do is to open their editor to the source page when\\r\\na breakpoint is hit.  They want to do this without activating the other pages.  \\r\\nOur infrastructure does\\r\\nnot support this.\\r\\n\\r\\nOur code that opens an editor and sets a marker to indicate the current line \\r\\nnumber does the\\r\\nfollowing calls, taken from DebugView.openEditorAndSetMarker(...):\\r\\n\\r\\n<snip>\\r\\n		if (editor == null) {\\r\\n			if (fEditor != null) {\\r\\n				if (!fEditor.isDirty()) {\\r\\n					page.closeEditor(fEditor, false);\\r\\n				}\\r\\n			}\\r\\n			try {\\r\\n				editor= page.openEditor(input, editorId);\\r\\n				fEditor = editor;\\r\\n				page.activate(this);\\r\\n			} catch (PartInitException e) {\\r\\n				DebugUIUtils.logError(e);\\r\\n			}\\r\\n\\r\\n		} else {\\r\\n			page.bringToTop(editor);\\r\\n		}\\r\\n		\\r\\n		if (editor != null && (lineNumber >= 0 || charStart >= 0)) {\\r\\n			//have an editor and either a lineNumber or a starting \\r\\ncharacter\\r\\n			IMarker marker= getInstructionPointer(lineNumber, \\r\\ncharStart, charEnd, isTopStackFrame);\\r\\n			editor.gotoMarker(marker);\\r\\n		}\\r\\n</snip>\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice that we first call page.openEditor(input, editorId); and then later call \\r\\neditor.gotoMarker(marker);.  We could just call page.openEditor(marker);, as is \\r\\ndone in the\\r\\nTaskList.  This change would put the responsibility of this support on the \\r\\nshoulders of the\\r\\nUI team.\\r\\n\\r\\nTo solve the problem entirely, I believe the IWorkbenchPage API will have to be \\r\\naltered to\\r\\ntake an argument to indicate which page the editor should open on.  Also, we \\r\\nwill have to \\r\\nensure that we do not create/activate all pages in a multipage editor before \\r\\nthey are required.\\r\\n\\r\\nOn the other hand, the IWorkbenchPage API does have the facility to open an \\r\\neditor\\r\\non a given marker.  If the implementation of this was coded correctly, it would \\r\\nbe enough\\r\\nto allow WSA to decide which page they would want to show when their multipage \\r\\neditor\\r\\nis first created.  Similarly, we must not activate the other pages until they \\r\\nare needed.\\r\\n\\r\\nI have been unable to determine if the creation of multipage editors requires \\r\\nthe creation & \\r\\nactivation of all of the pages or just the current page.\\r\\n\\r\\nDS (9/14/01 5:05:59 PM)\\r\\n	\\"We could just call page.openEditor(marker);\\" this can only be done if \\r\\nthe marker\\r\\n	is associated with a resource that is an IFile (@see \\r\\nWorkbenchPage#openEditor(IMarker, boolean).\\r\\n	This does not handle the class file story (in jars).

Description: If the JSP source file name has an underscore in it, breakpoints in the JSP\\nwon't get installed successfully until after the JSP has been executed once.\\n\\nHere are the steps to recreate it:\\n\\n- Create the JSPandServletExample web project\\n- Rename webApplication/Form/FormServletResultPage.jsp to FormServletResult_Page.jsp\\n- From the Project's context menu, select Edit Deployment Descriptor\\n- Go to the Servlets page, select FormServlet and click the Initialization button\\n- Click twice on the result_page value to edit it and change it to\\nForm/FormServletResult_Page.jsp\\n- Save web.xml\\n- Put a breakpoint in the Java code of FormServletResult_Page.\\n- Run the web project and run the form example to completion\\n- The breakpoint remains blue and the debugger doesn't stop at it\\n- Now you can remove and re-set the breakpoint and it will be green and\\nwill stop correctly\\n\\nThis doesn't happen if you run the Form example without adding the\\nunderscore to the JSP file name.

Summary: README: thread termination on JDK 1.3 (1GEYVT8)
Description: DW (6/7/01 3:15:10 PM)\\n	Thread termination is not supported on JDK 1.3.\\n\\n	The debugger implements thread termination by invoking #stop on a\\n	thread with an instance of ThreadDeathException. The debugger\\n	attempts to create an instance of ThreadDeathException on the first\\n	class load event received from the VM. On 1.3, the ThreadDeathException\\n	consrtuctro throws a NullPointerException when invoked before a program\\n	reaches \\"main\\" (not sure why).\\n\\n	Users should beware not to catch NullPointerException or any of its\\n	supertypes until after a program has reached main, as this causes the\\n	attempt to create the ThreadDeathException to suspend, from which the\\n	debugger may not recover.\\n\\nDW (6/15/01 10:42:28 AM)\\n	Added to README.

Summary: README: Terminating VM on Linux (1GEYWL7)

The workaround is\\n	to use \\"terminate and remove\\".\\n\\n	There appears to be a bug in the JDI (target side) implementation or VM.\\n	This only occurrs when a thread in the VM being terminated has a suspended\\n	thread. It appears the VM waits forever for the suspended thread to complete.\\n\\nDW (6/8/01 12:49:34 PM)\\n	It appears that terminating the suspended thread will clean things up\\n	since that also resumes the thread (so it can terminate), which allows the VM	\\n	to exit.\\n\\nDW (6/15/01 10:58:28 AM)\\n	Added to README.

Summary: Quiet suspend/resume events (1GI3TLQ)
Description: We need to add a mechanism to the JDIThread to perform \\"quiet\\" suspends/resumes which do\\nnot update the UI. This functionality would be useful for \\"normal\\" (user initiated) evaluations, \\nscrapbook evaluations, and for conditional breakpoint evaluation. In all three cases, we are \\ndoing \\"artificial\\" suspensions (to perform evaluations) that the user should not know about.\\n\\nIn the case of normal evaluation and conditional breakpoint evaluation, the lack of a quiet\\nsuspension mechanism means that the UI flashes rapidly as the JDIThread is suspended\\nand resumed repeatedly.\\n\\nWhen the user runs a scrapbook page in the Debug Perspective, the debug view shows too much\\nof the underlying implementation of the scrapbook. After the user runs code, the debug view shows\\nthem that the underlying thread is suspended. This is confusing to the user because they're being\\npresented with the option to resume but they have no idea why anything would be suspended.\\n\\nSomething to consider is the fact that if a user-defined breakpoint is hit while evaluating code,\\nwe'll have to have a way to override the quiet-mode of the JDIThread to update the UI\\nappropriately.\\n\\nThis can be accomplished (I've implemented it once minus the \\"something to consider\\") by:\\n1) Add a quiet flag to the JDIThread.\\n2) Add suspendQuiet which sets the quiet flag true and calls an internal suspension method\\n3) Add a check in the internal suspension and old resume methods. If the quiet flag is true, don't \\n	update the UI.\\n4) The old resume method should turn quiet mode off. The old suspend method should turn it on\\n	and call the internal suspension method.\\n5) Add  public method to turn quiet mode off and another to fire an explicit UI update.\\n\\nA) When a conditional breakpoint is hit,	call the suspendQuiet method, and perform the evaluation,\\n	if the evaluation comes back true, tell the thread to notify the UI of suspension. If not, resume\\n	execution.\\nB) When the scrapbook is finished with an evaluation, it should call the suspendQuiet method.\\nC) When a breakpoint without a condition is hit, suspend as usual (call the old suspend method).\\n	Calling the old suspend method turns quiet mode off (see step 4) so the UI will update as usual\\n	for breakpoints hit when the thread is in quiet mode (during conditional breakpoint or scrapbook\\n	evaluation).\\n\\n\\nNOTES:

Summary: Performance: use lineToCodeIndexes() instead of locationsOfLine()
Description: I've been stepping through the breakpoint code, and I've noticed that \\nbreakpoints seem to spend a fair amount of time trying to install themselves.  \\nEver time a class prepare event comes in, the breakpoint scans the class to see \\nif it can place itself.  This is particularly painful for inner classes, since \\nthe breakpoint doesn't know which inner class it belongs to.\\n\\nIn ClassTypeImpl.locationsOfLine(), the JDI method locationsOfLine() is \\nrepeatedly invoked.  Unfortunately, this method reports failure by throwing an \\nexception.  This is very slow (especially on Sun-based VMs).\\n\\nThis code could be optimized by asking if the method has lineToCodeIndexes() \\n(indices(sp)?) for that line.  This method returns null for failure instead of \\nthrowing an exception, so should be mush faster.\\n\\nI'm not very familiar with JDI, though, so I'm not 100% certain that the \\noptimization is valid.  It looks a lot less painful to me, though.\\n\\n(20020215 build)

The\\r\\n          specification is being clarified to state clearly that you cannot \\r\\nhave a simple name in an import statement, nor can you import from the unnamed \\r\\nnamespace. \\r\\n\\r\\n          To summarize, the syntax \\r\\n\\r\\n               import SimpleName;\\r\\n\\r\\n          is no longer legal. Description: MA (20.09.2001 10:38:48)\\n	The upating of referenced projects is currently done in our code. The algorithm\\n	preserves project dependencies added by the user.\\n\\nMA (20.09.2001 10:41:23)\\n	Remark that the API\\n		String[] IJavaProject.getRequiredProjectNames();\\n	would better be\\n		IProject[] IJavaProject.getRequiredProjects();\\n\\n		/**\\n	 * @param jproject The Java project after changing the class path\\n	 * @param prevRequiredProjects The required projects before changing the class path\\n	 */\\n	public static void updateReferencedProjects(IJavaProject jproject, String[] prevRequiredProjects, IProgressMonitor monitor) throws CoreException {\\n		String[] newRequiredProjects= jproject.getRequiredProjectNames();\\n\\n		ArrayList prevEntries= new ArrayList(Arrays.asList(prevRequiredProjects));\\n		ArrayList newEntries= new ArrayList(Arrays.asList(newRequiredProjects));\\n		\\n		IProject proj= jproject.getProject();\\n		IProjectDescription projDesc= proj.getDescription();  \\n		\\n		ArrayList newRefs= new ArrayList();\\n		IProject[] referencedProjects= projDesc.getReferencedProjects();\\n		for (int i= 0; i < referencedProjects.length; i++) {\\n			String curr= referencedProjects[i].getName();\\n			if (newEntries.remove(curr) || !prevEntries.contains(curr)) {\\n				newRefs.add(referencedProjects[i]);\\n			}\\n		}\\n		IWorkspaceRoot root= proj.getWorkspace().getRoot();\\n		for (int i= 0; i < newEntries.size(); i++) {\\n			String curr= (String) newEntries.get(i);\\n			newRefs.add(root.getProject(curr));\\n		}		\\n		projDesc.setReferencedProjects((IProject[]) newRefs.toArray(new IProject[newRefs.size()]));\\n		proj.setDescription(projDesc, monitor);\\n	}	\\n\\n\\nNOTES:

Summary: keeping the project references and required project in synch (1GL0L34)
Description: EG (03.10.2001 11:40:48)\\n	the code to keep the required project on the java build path and the\\n	referenced projects in synch is in the UI.\\n\\n	It should be pushed down to JCORE so that people using the\\n	API get the same behaviour.\\n\\n	It got requested on EC today.\\n\\nHere is the posting:\\n------\\nIt seems that classpath entries between projects must always be coupled\\nwith referenced projects.  That is, if project A has a classpath entry\\npointing to project B, then A must also list B as one of its referenced\\nprojects so the builds will fire in the correct order.  When this is not\\ntrue, multi-project builds run in an unspecified order and A might build\\nbefore B.\\n\\nTherefore the method JavaProject.setRawClasspath() should do this update\\nautomatically. Summary: Cannot use external classes on the class path (1G3QVG4)
Description: It is not possible to add an external class or directory to the class path for a java project.  \\n\\n\\nNOTES:\\n\\nPM (11/1/00 3:32:40 PM)\\n	External contributions must be either a jar or a project (a project only contributes its binary output to other projects referring to it).\\n\\nTC (11/2/00 10:57:20 AM) - this is inconsistent with the specification for CLASSPATH. This is a serious\\nlimitation for anything that tries to run an external program (like the WebSphere Test Environment)\\nwithin the Eclipse tool that needs resources on it's classpath.\\n\\nPM (11/2/00 11:25:58 AM)\\n	If all you are interested in is running, then you should not need to include your resources on your classpath.\\n	This is why the notion of build path vs. runtime path can be slightly different. Currently the classpath is very close\\n	to the build path. We are trying to generalize this for runtime (i.e. rt.jar must not be on the runtime path, but should be\\n	on the build path). \\n\\n	I would say that if you care about resources, then they should either be in a jar (easier to manage anyway) or managed inside \\n	a project.\\n\\n	Once we revisit the classpath->build/run path, then your problem could be solved differently.\\n\\n	Giving control to insert random source folders on the classpath, which are external to a project is raising way more issues than your\\n	simple resource access problem. We would have to be careful with grabbing sources from other projects, i.e. where do you put the \\n	resulting .class files ? So this is why the only external contributions to a project are either jars or other projects.\\n\\n	Note: along the same line, random directories outside your workbench are not managed by core, i.e. a change in there will not be reflected\\n		inside the classpath since no rsc delta will be issued... this is why you want your resources to be in core range.\\n\\n	We have no short-term plan for changing the current classpath implementation, the current API specification just looks wrong to me.\\n	In brief, either you manage your resources in a way that can be handled by the classpath (project or jar), or you investigate the support\\n	you can get from launchers so as to insert one extra runtime classpath entry. \\n\\nTC (11/2/00 11:58:58 AM) - After disussing with PM it has become clearer that we need to be able to specify\\nis additional directories to be added to the runtime path. See PR 1G3SPC3:  ITPJUI:WINNT - Cannot extend runtime path in the UI.\\n\\nPM (11/6/00 12:22:53 PM)\\n	Actually, there is no need for a change in the build path. The requirements are only related to runtime path.\\n\\nDA (6/20/01 5:38:48 PM)\\n	Problem still exust in build 0.125.

Summary: Get rid of source attachment root (1GJON3Q)
Description: MA (07.09.2001 14:19:27)\\n	When setting a source attachment, a root path has to be specified, so that classes can be found.\\n	It would be a big progress if JCore has a way to automatically find an appropriate source file for a class.\\n	Advatages would be:\\n		- Easier UI\\n		- Easiear APIs (especially in relation with variable entries)\\n\\n	Approach i have in mind:\\n		Keep a hashtable of all CU names in an source attachment. Simple name matching should work for most\\n		of the classfiles. If two CUs have the same name, always try to find the longest match of package\\n		and CU location.\\n		If simple name matching leads to too many matches always try to find the longest match of package name\\n		and path in zip.\\n	The mapping algorithm will only be called for the first time a source is searched. Afterwards, the source buffer will\\n	keep the reference.\\n\\n\\nNOTES:

Summary: Unpredictable error catching on overridden methods with less visibility
Description: In one project of mine, Eclipse seemed to compile all code correctly, where \\nSun's JDK 1.3.1_02 compiler caught an error described below.\\n\\nAccording to the Java Language Spec, section 8.4.6.3:\\n\\nThe access modifier (§6.6) of an overriding or hiding method must provide at \\nleast as much access as the overridden or hidden method, or a compile-time \\nerror occurs. \\n\\nIn my case, the error was when a method that was public in the superclass was \\noverridden with default access. I altered the overrides to be public as well, \\nand the command-line errors went away.\\n\\nUnfortunately, when I changed them back to reproduce it later, it caught the \\nerror. Hence its unpredictable nature.\\n\\nA bug like this could cause some serious issues when the JVM tries to access \\nthe subclass that has quietly reduced the visibility of an overridden method.\\n\\nThis was running Eclipse 2.O-pre, build 20011219. I have not tried it on a more \\nrecent build, because it would not duplicate on this one. It might be worth a \\nlook.

Summary: Compiler barfs on c:\\ubizen with invalid unicode
Description: Files that are checked in in our source control system (starteam) have a header\\nwith the local filename in the filecomment. Summary: Inconsistent behavior for the method IType.createField()
Description: Given a class whose source code has the following form:\\n\\npublic abstract class TestClass implements ITestClass {\\n    /* (non-Javadoc)\\n     * @see ITestClass#getName()\\n     */\\n    public String getName() {\\n        return null;\\n    }\\n}\\n\\ninvoking the method\\n\\n    org.eclipse.jdt.core.IType.createField(String contents,\\n                                           IJavaElement sibling,\\n                                           boolean force,\\n                                           IProgressMonitor monitor)\\n\\non the object that represents the above type (passing in \\"null\\" for both the \\nsibling and the progress monitor and \\"false\\" for force) will cause the \\ndefinition of the field to be inserted between the comment and the method. I \\nsuspect that the behavior I'm seeing is due to the non-Javadoc comment not \\nbeing associated with the method.\\n\\nThis behavior seems inconsistent because of the user-level preference \\nto \\"Create non-Javadoc comments for overridden methods\\" on the Java|Code \\nGeneration preference page. It seems that the user interface is implying \\nsupport for that style of coding, while the API does not. I believe that in \\norder to fully support that style, the API needs to recognize such a comment as \\nbeing essentially equivalent to a Javadoc comment.\\n\\nI believe that two fixes are possible. The first would be to explicitly stop \\nsupporting that style of coding. I suspect, however, that while this change \\nwould be easy to implement, it would be a very difficult change to make from a \\npolitical point of view.\\n\\nThe second would be to fix the API so that non-Javadoc comments are associated \\nwith the member (or at least method) that follows them. You might want to place \\nadditional restrictions so that the association is only made if\\n\\n - there are no blank lines between the comment and the member,\\n\\n - there is no Javadoc comment, and/or\\n\\n - the phrase \\"(non-Javadoc)\\" must appear as the first non-white\\n   space in the comment.\\n\\nI am running build 20020214 under Microsoft Windows 2000 (5.00.2195).

Summary: Inconsistent treatment of errors for java resource outside src dir

I think this is the\\ncorrect behaviour. However, when the resource is moved inside the source\\ndirectory then moved back out, the compile errors remain attached. If you close\\nthe project, reopen it, then add another file with a .java extension to the same\\ndirectory, the errors are removed again.\\n\\nHere are steps for reproducing this behaviour:\\n\\n- Create a Java project with a source directory of 'src'.\\n- Create a file \\"Bad.java\\" in the root directory of the project.\\n- Put the letter 'x' in it and save it. (Not sure whether this is necessary.)\\n\\nThe file should appear normal. No errors should be reported. Ok.\\n\\n- Move the file into 'src'.\\n\\nThe file will fail to compile and errors will be reported. Ok.\\n\\n- Move the file back into the root directory.\\n\\nThe errors are still attached. This is inconsistent.\\n\\n- Add a file 'KeepErrors.java' to the root directory.\\n\\nThe errors on 'Bad.java' are still there.\\n\\n- Close and reopen the project.\\n\\nThe errors on 'Bad.java' are still there.\\n\\n- Add a file 'RemoveErrors.java' to the root directory.\\n\\nThe errors on 'Bad.java' are removed.

Add folder that contains a dot (e.g. \\"com.ibm\\") to junit.test (in navigator or packages view)\\n	==> folder com.ibm not visible in packages view\\n\\n	Add resource and/or java file to the folder\\n	==> folder and files not visible in packages view\\n\\n	If the test case is done with a folder without a dot then the folder is visible\\n\\n\\nNOTES:\\nEG (4/29/2001 3:25:49 PM)\\n	some more facts:\\n	1) adding a package name a.b.c in the packages view with the New Package wizard works as expected\\n	2) in a project with source folders you can add com.ibm as an ordinary folder to the project using\\n		the basic New Folder wizard.\\n	3) in a project with source folders adding a new folder a.b.c to a package fragment root shows the\\n		behaviour that DM described above, i.e., the folder isn't visible, it exists and shows up in the\\n		packages view.\\n\\n	It isn't a notification problem, the Java Model doesn't surface these folders.\\n\\n	Notice once the Java Model surfaces these folders we have the problem how to distinguish \\n	a folder \\"a.b.c\\" from a\\b\\c that shows up as a.b.c. We would have to use some escape\\n	mechanism, e.g., a\\.b\\.c\\n\\n	However, before addressing this UI issue we first need to get such folders from the Java model.\\n	See also: 1GCP6M8: ITPJUI:WINNT - Adding a file without dot not visible in package\\n	Moving to JCORE\\n	\\nPM (4/30/2001 10:57:56 AM)\\n	Those were filtered out from package fragment creation code. Handling them will be tricky, given there is no way to distinguish them afterwards\\n	unless going back to the underlying resource.\\n	When not filtering them out, the package becomes visible, but then adding one class in it becomes tricky, given the model tries to recreate the proper\\n	folder structure (a/b/c from a.b.c)... \\n\\n	Then this is causing duplicate elements, because a/b/c and a.b.c are producing elements named 'a.b.c'.\\n	What's the point ? How do we want to handle these ?\\n\\n	Enabling the creation of packages with dot names: org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.PackageFragmentRoot.computeFolderChildren(IContainer, String, Vector)\\n\\n/**\\n * Starting at this folder, create package fragments and add the fragments to the collection\\n * of children.\\n * \\n * @exception JavaModelException  The resource associated with this package fragment does not exist\\n */\\nprotected void computeFolderChildren(IContainer folder, String prefix, Vector vChildren) throws JavaModelException {\\n	IPackageFragment pkg = getPackageFragment(prefix);\\n	vChildren.addElement(pkg);\\n	try {\\n		IPath outputLocationPath = getJavaProject().getOutputLocation();\\n		IResource[] members = folder.members();\\n		for (int i = 0, max = members.length; i < max; i++) {\\n			IResource member = members[i];\\n			if (member.getType() == IResource.FOLDER) {\\n				String newPrefix;\\n				if (prefix.length() == 0) {\\n					newPrefix = member.getName();\\n				} else {\\n					newPrefix = prefix + \\".\\" + member.getName();\\n				}\\n				// eliminate binary output only if nested inside direct subfolders\\n				if (!member.getFullPath().equals(outputLocationPath)) {\\n					computeFolderChildren((IFolder) member, newPrefix, vChildren);\\n				}\\n			}\\n		}\\n	} catch(IllegalArgumentException e){\\n		throw new JavaModelException(e, IJavaModelStatusConstants.ELEMENT_DOES_NOT_EXIST); // could be thrown by ElementTree when path is not found\\n	} catch (CoreException e) {\\n		throw new JavaModelException(e);\\n	}\\n}

Description: While doing performance tracing in OptimizeIt, I noticed that the indexer thread was doing\\nwork in situations where it seems like it shouldn't.  For example, if you do a \\"Team->Synchronize with Stream\\",\\nit re-indexes all java files, even though their content hasn't changed.  I traced this down to\\nDeltaProcessor#updateIndex, which has the following code for dealing with changed java files:\\n\\n			IFile file = (IFile)delta.getResource();\\n			String extension;\\n			switch (delta.getKind()) {\\n				case IResourceDelta.ADDED:\\n				case IResourceDelta.CHANGED:\\n					if (file.isLocal(IResource.DEPTH_ZERO)) indexManager.add(file);\\n					break;\\n				case IResourceDelta.REMOVED:\\n					extension = file.getFileExtension();\\n					indexManager.remove(file.getFullPath().toString(), file.getProject());\\n					break;\\n			}\\n\\nUnder the CHANGED case, it should only be concerned with deltas with the F_CONTENT\\nflag set, otherwise the indexes shouldn't be affected. As it is now, it will re-index files\\nwith sync info changes, session property changes, marker changes, etc, unnecessarily.\\nThis is causing a lot of unnecessary work in the index thread.\\n\\nNOTES:\\n\\nPM (9/6/2001 3:16:59 PM)\\n	Agreed, we should not reindex the world unless the content has changed.\\n\\nJohnA (9/6/2001 10:08:52 AM)\\n	There may be other opportunities to improve the java delta processor performance\\n	in this case.  When doing \\"Synchronize with Stream\\" on a typical java project, 20-30% \\n	of the total time is taken in jdt.internal.core.DeltaProcessor.processResourceDelta.  Most of \\n	that time seems to be taken in creating java elements corresponding to the changed resources.\\n	This could perhaps be improved in cases where the delta does not represent content changes.\\n\\nPM (9/17/2001 1:26:13 PM)\\n	Checking the flags for reconciling with .classpath file and triggering file indexing.

Summary: JavaModel cleanup: IWorkingCopy should extend ICompilationUnit and not the other way around
Description: Build R2.1\\n\\nHistorically, IWorkingCopy gathered all working copy concerns, and compilation \\nunits implement this interface, though only the factory method makes sense for \\nthem; thus their implementation of the working copy features do nothing \\nrelevant to clients. Summary: Need to get JavaModel deltas as user types
Description: Current behavior:\\n\\nThe maximum frequency at which JavaModel deltas are currently sent is whenever\\nthe user saves.  For interactive code modification tools that have to keep their\\nown AST updated in real-time, this isn't the most ideal frequency.\\n\\nI have many reasons to desire finer-grained updates.  One fairly simple example\\nis when a GUI builder (that reverse-engineers Java code) wants to update its GUI\\neditor view in real-time as the developer types Java code.\\n\\nIn this case, the optimum time to receive JavaModel deltas is immediately after\\nthe Java incremental builder runs.  Then the GUI builder's AST and editor can be\\nupdated with the new information and can intelligently respond to syntax errors\\nin the code as it is typed.\\n\\nWhy not just create your own incremental builder to handle this case?\\n\\nBecause incremental builders get resource change notifications, not JavaModel\\nchange notifications, so an incremental builder would in effect have to reinvent\\nthe Java incremental compiler.  This is wasteful in terms of precious processor\\ncycles in between the user's keystrokes, not to mention duplicated coding\\neffort.  Again, it would make much more sense for the JavaModel deltas to be\\nmade available as the user types, removing the need to duplicate all this effort.

Summary: [1.5][dom] provide API to ask for super/subtypes
Description: 3.0\\nin java 1.5 the type domain is infinite even without array types\\nso the traditional type hierarchy is less useful to use (programatically) -\\nthere is possibly an infinite number of subtypes or supertypes for a given type.\\n\\nbut many analyses need that kind of information - refactoring is one but pretty\\nmuch anybody who does anything interesting will be in need of that info.\\nwith generics these things become pretty complicated, e.g.:\\nList<? extends Integer> is a subtype of List<? extends Number> but\\nList<? super Integer>   is a supertype of List<? super Number>.\\n\\nSo we would have 1 place that contains that kind of code. Jdt core seems to be\\nthe natural location for that kind of logic (the type checker need that anyway).\\nSo the request is for API that would allow questions of kind 'isSuperTypeOf'

These warnings trigger an \\"Incomplete build path\\" error and\\nEclipse will not allow the project to be built.  \\nAnd yet, under Preferences / Compiler / Build Path, \\"Incomplete build path\\"\\nis set to \\"Warning\\".\\nVery confusing.\\nIf Project / Clean is run, the warnings remain, but the error goes away and\\neclipse allows the project to be built.\\nThere is no indication that a clean needs to be performed, and I do not\\nunderstand why that causes the error to go away.

Summary: [dom] API to get generic type from parametrized type binding
Description: 20041101\\n\\nIn 1.5 we have now 3 'layers' of type bindings\\n\\na.) For a declaration List<T> what you get is a 'generic type' type binding.\\nbinding.getMethods() would return you, amongst others, 'add(T)'.\\n\\nb.) For a reference List<String> you get a 'parametrized type' type binding.\\nWhen asked for its methods you get methods like 'add(String)'\\n\\nc.) A reference 'List' returns a raw type binding, returning a method 'add(Object)'\\n\\nThe current API of ITypeBinding doesn't make a difference between a. and b.\\nand also doesn't have API to go from b. to a. or even from a. to b.\\n\\nWhat does exist are methods 'getErasure()' to get c. from a. and b. and\\nisRawType() to test for c.\\n\\nIn IMethodBinding there is the same problem\\n- add(T)\\n- add(List)\\n- add(Object)

Summary: [index] PatternSearchJob ignores participant index entries.
Description: A problem I've run into, I think I'm forced to use internal API in order to get\\nour JSP index entries in the IndexManager.indexLocations table.\\n\\n- Java index entries are automatically added to this table when you\\n\\"computeIndexLocation\\", \\n- but since we have to compute our own index locations, our locations don't get\\nadded to this table.\\n\\nI think being in this table is required because PatternSearchJob uses it to know\\nwhich indexes to search (it does a check what the parent container path is for\\nthe index, which will be null if not in indexLocations table):\\n\\npublic Index[] getIndexes(IProgressMonitor progressMonitor) {\\n	// acquire the in-memory indexes on the fly\\n	IPath[] indexLocations = this.participant.selectIndexes(this.pattern, this.scope);\\n	int length = indexLocations.length;\\n	Index[] indexes = new Index[length];\\n	int count = 0;\\n	IndexManager indexManager =\\nJavaModelManager.getJavaModelManager().getIndexManager();\\n	for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) {\\n		if (progressMonitor != null && progressMonitor.isCanceled()) throw new\\nOperationCanceledException();\\n		// may trigger some index recreation work\\n		String indexLocation = indexLocations[i].toOSString();\\n		IPath containerPath = (IPath)\\nindexManager.indexLocations.keyForValue(indexLocation); // will be null here\\nbecause not in indexLocations table of IndexManager\\n		if (containerPath != null) { // sanity check\\n			Index index = indexManager.getIndex(containerPath, indexLocation, true\\n/*reuse index file*/, false /*do not create if none*/);\\n			if (index != null)\\n				indexes[count++] = index; // only consider indexes which are ready\\n		}\\n	}\\n	if (count == length) \\n		this.areIndexesReady = true;\\n	else\\n		System.arraycopy(indexes, 0, indexes=new Index[count], 0, count);\\n	return indexes;\\n}	\\n\\nI can get around this problem by adding to indexLocations in the IndexManager\\nwhen we compute our own index location, but I'm not sure if there are any bad\\nside effects of this.

Summary: Arbitrary dependencies are constantly dropped
Description: We have a workspace with about 50 projects and most of them have interdependencies. We make usage of project inheritance and also the exports. Additionally we make heavy usage of user library definitions.\\n\\nProblem is that Eclipse constantly forgets about some of the dependencies. Sometimes you open a Java file and suddenly some of the imported classes are no longer found. It does neither help to close and open the project again, nor a refresh nor cleaning the project. The only solution is to open the properties of the project and modify the sequence of the dependencies of the classpath.\\n\\nWe have detected such a behaviour for projects without further dependencies to other projects and without user libraries, but user libraries definitely trigger the problem more often. *If* the situation happens it gets really worse, since even if you manage to recover the project, where all(most) other projects depend on, those dependend project suddenly have also lost some of their dependencies internally. Again modifying the dependency order is the only possibility to recover.\\n\\nThis wierd behaviour was first noticed with 3.2M5 and continues until now (3.2RC1).

Summary: (Missing) Transitive dependancy and quickfix failing silently.
Description: Situation ========\\nGiven three plugins A, B and C with C depending on B and B depending on A:\\nA <= B <= C.\\n\\nB defines an interface I whose methods contain a type from A as argument or return type.\\n\\npackage B;\\ninterface I {\\n\\n  public TypeFromA method();\\n\\n}\\n\\nIf now C wants to implement I it has to add A to its dependancies. If that is not done, we cannon import the necessary types from A.\\n\\nProblem ===========\\nWhen A is not in C's dependancies and we have the implementation skeleton of I which we want to complete with the quickfix \\"Add unimplemented methods\\", then the quickfix only adds those methods that contain types of dependant plugins and silently omits others leaving our implementation uncomplete:\\n\\npackage C;\\npublic class AnImpl implements I { // we get an error marker here\\n}\\n\\nThe quickfix does not do anything here. In my case, I needed too long to get the point because I thought it was a bug. I tried 3.2.1 instead of 3.3M3, jdk5 instead of jdk6rc1, cleaned all projects and wrote some demo interfaces to isolate the problem. A simple message for the missing dependancy to A would be nice and time saving. Even better would be an automatic completion of the dependancy to A.\\n\\nA more general question:\\nWhy is C not automatically depending an A when B is depending on A?

Summary: ResourceDeltas are lost when merging deltas
Description: Using the Eclipse 20020214 build.\\n\\nI have a Java project with the following structure:\\nJavaProject\\n - source  (PackageFragmentRoot)\\n   - com.ibm.test (PackageFragment)\\n - folder1 (non Java folder)\\n   - folder2\\n\\nI have a wizard which creates two classes in the com.ibm.test package and two \\nHTML files in folder2.  In the Java Packages view, if folder2 is selected and \\nexpanded when the wizard is invokved, after the files are created folder2 will \\nnot be refreshed correctly to display the two new HTML files.\\n\\nI have traced the problem and it lies in JavaElementDelta.addAffectedChildren\\n().  This is called from insertDeltaTree() which is called from \\nJavaModelManager.mergeDeltas().  In this case there are two JavaElementDeltas \\nbeing merged.  The first delta for the project contains no resource deltas.  \\nThe second delta for the project contains resource deltas representing the two \\nnew HTML files.  When the second delta is processed, addAffectedChildren sees \\nthat there is already a delta for the project so it moves on to process the \\ndelta's children.  The problem is that it needs to merge the resource deltas.

Summary: Java Model Notification needs notification that a java class was physically saved
Description: We need to track changes to java classes in our project, so we use the java\\nmodel notification scheme. The problem is that we need to know not just that the\\nworking copy has been changed, but in addition we need to know that the change\\nhas been committed to the file system. The java model notification scheme\\ndoesn't do this. This is a big problem for us because the change is not really\\nimportant to us until it has been committed to a file. (Because when committed,\\nwe will start a new remote vm for that project after the build has completed,\\nwhich we can wait for). If there was one more notification indicating that the\\njava class working copy changes have been committed we could know this.\\n\\nThe only workaround is painful, we need to listen to both working copy java\\nmodel changes and the system IResource changes, and mark in some hashtable that\\nthe underlying resource is dirty from the working copy notifications, and then\\nwhen we get the save notification from the IResource notification we know it has\\nbeen committed. The big problem with this is there is no way of knowing that\\nworking copy changes have been reverted and not saved so that we can clear this\\ndirty flag. At least none that I can track down.\\n\\nWe wouldn't have to do any of this if we just knew (a) changes have been\\ncommitted and (b) changes have been reverted.\\n\\nThanks, Rich

On the other hand, it could also be turned into an official bit-flag\\nand the boolean isCaseSensitive removed. To have both options seems strange to me.

Summary: Editor closes with memory leak (editor doesn't go away in memory)
Description: Build 200210091450\\n\\nThere is a problem with the text hover which causes the editor to stay in \\nmemory after it has been closed. This keeps everything in memory; the action \\ncontributor, the SWT widgets, the EditorSite, the EditorActionBars (when this \\nwas the last editor of that type) and so on.\\n\\nThe way to reproduce is to bring up a java editor, move the mouse over the \\neditor and let it sit long enough for a hover to be initiated. Then close the \\neditor by using ctrl+F4, or quickly move to the \\"X\\" in the title bar to close \\nit. \\n\\nWhat happens is that the text hover manager doesn't remove itself from the \\nShell (to which it added its mouse listener as widgetDisposed listener).\\n\\nIf you move the mouse off of the editor completely and then do ctrl+F4, \\nmouseExit is entered, which then proceeds to remove itself as a listener on the \\nshell before the editor is closed. And in that case, the editor is GC'd.\\n\\nHere is the chain of objects that cause it stay in memory (retrieved thru JProbe\\n(TM)).\\n\\n- CompilationUnitEditor is referenced by \\nCompilationUnitEditor$AdaptedSourceViewer.this$0\\n\\n- CompilationUnitEditor$AdaptedSourceViewer is referenced by \\nTextViewerHoverManager.fTextViewer\\n\\n- TextViewerHoverManager is referenced by \\nAbstractHoverInformationControlManager$MouseTracker.this$0\\n\\n- AbstractHoverInformationControlManager$MouseTracker is referenced by \\nTypedListener.eventListener\\n\\nThe TypedListener was added as a shell listener against the Shell of the \\nworkspace by AbstractHoverInformationControlManager$MouseTracker.mouseHover(...)\\n\\nThis causes a lot of memory to not be returned, especially for our Visual \\nEditor for Java because we have much more in memory than the straight Java \\nEditor.\\n\\nThere may be other things being hold in memory, but this appears to be what is \\nholding the CompilationUnitEditor in memory.\\n\\nThanks,\\nRich Kulp
