Summary: Occurrences finder should use a job
Description: Build: 3.0 M6\\n\\nI noticed that the background task to find occurrences in the file creates a new\\nthread every time, rather than using jobs.  This is exactly the situation that\\njobs were created for (in fact Erich used this as a demo of the job\\ninfrastructure at a code camp).  Some advantages of changing to jobs:\\n\\n- less overhead (currently a new thread is created per key press, jobs use a\\nthread pool)\\n- better handling of priority (currently running in a thread with same priority\\nas the UI, and thus is competing with UI thread for CPU more than it should)\\n- smarter scheduling. Jobs with \\"DECORATE\\" priority are run based on a check of\\nhow busy the system is.  Thus they do not run immediately if there are other\\nthings going on (they will run eventually, just not as quickly). This smooths\\nover bottlenecks when the system is busy.\\n\\nNote that you can prevent this job from showing in the progress view or making\\nthe progress animation (cigarette) move by making it a system job\\n(Job.setSystem(true)).  Generally jobs that the user didn't explicitly start can\\nbe marked as system jobs.\\n\\nIf there was a reason why jobs were considered and rejected, I'd be curious to\\nknow.  If the infrastructure isn't useful to you then I want to fix it.

Summary: [navigation] Status line loses annotation text when selection changes
Description: build I20060110\\n\\n- open a CU with some compilation error (in my case it was an unused private field)\\n- place the caret some term that has no error, such as a class name\\n  - the highlighting does its thing, and the status line is blank (correct)\\n- place the caret in the range of the error\\n  - the highlighting does its thing, and the status line shows the error (correct)\\n- move the caret somewhere else in the range (either using mouse or keyboard)\\n  - the highlighting is unchanged (correct) but the status line is cleared (incorrect)\\n\\nIt looks like the error display is tied to the highlighting, and is optimized to do nothing when the highlighting is unchanged, but someone else is clearing the status line on every selection.\\n\\nExpectation: the status line shows the error text whenever the caret is within the range of an error (likewise for warnings).

Summary: Jar-Packager outputs MANIFEST.MF using platform encoding
Description: Using Eclipse 20020412.\\n\\nThe Jar-Packager outputs the MANIFEST.MF file encoded using the platform \\nencoding. The JAR file specification specifies that values in name-value pairs \\nare UTF8 encoded.\\n\\nSpecification:\\n  section:                       *header +newline \\n  nonempty-section:      +header +newline \\n  newline:                      CR LF | LF | CR (not followed by LF) \\n  header:                       name : value \\n  name:                         alphanum *headerchar \\n  value:                          SPACE *otherchar newline *continuation \\n  continuation:              SPACE *otherchar newline \\n  alphanum:                  {A-Z} | {a-z} | {0-9} \\n  headerchar:                alphanum | - | _ \\n  otherchar:                  any UTF-8 character except NUL, CR and LF \\n\\nNote that JDK does not read the manifest using UTF8, but rather ISO8859_1.\\n\\nThe unicode character \\u0192 is a nice charcter to test with as it doesn't have \\nthe same value in the default Windows encoding (Cp1252) - 0x83. It also maps to \\nthe default DOS encoding (Cp437 or Cp850) - 0x9f.

Summary: JavaBrowsingPerspective - the packages/types and members view clear selection and then contents when an IStructuredSelection event is fired that isn't an IJavaElement
Description: We have an editor in WebSphere Studio that is able to be opened on a .java \\nsource file.  In this editor the user can select objects.  When this occurs in \\nthe Java Browsing Perspective the packages/types and members views are cleared \\nout of their contents.  It would be nicer if the views weren't clear out.\\n\\nThe reason the views are cleared is codein \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.ui.browsing.JavaBrowsingPart.  This listens to \\nselection and if the selection is an IStructuredSelection ( which our editorpart \\nsignals ) it first de-selects the selected items in the editor and then clears \\nthe editor contents.  If the selection is an IStructuredSelection and the items \\nimplement IAdapter but don't return an IJavaElement then the behavior should be \\nthe same as for a TextSelectionEvent which the Java Editor fires right now as \\nthe user selects text and doesn't reset the viewers' contents to null.

Summary: cut number of root packages from package names from package explorer
Description: A useful package name compression feature would be to cut a user-settable \\nnumber of parts from the beginning of the fully-specified package name in the\\npackage explorer, if the full package name is longer than the specified number \\nof parts to be cut. The cutting would be indicated with a dot (.) at the \\nbeginning of the shown version of the package name.\\n\\nEg. with a number of two, a package name of 'com.mycompany.project.test' would \\nresult in displaying something like '.project.test' ( to show that the full \\nnumber of parts were cut). \\n\\nIn case of the full package name is less than or equal to the number of parts \\nto cut, it would show the original package name, eg. with a setting of 4, \\n'com.company.project.test' would be displayed as 'com.company.project.test', \\n'com.company.something' would be 'com.company.something', \\nbut 'com.company.project.something.ui.test' would be only '.ui.test'.\\n\\nIt would be most useful if this number could be set on a per-folder or at least \\nper-project basis, but even if it would be a single setting for the whole Java \\nPerspective, it would still be useful.\\n\\nRegards,\\n\\nRobert Varga

Summary: Should consider using the new font propogation support
Description: 20021126\\n\\nAs of build 20021203 the eclipse workbench will now support declarative fonts. \\nThis will eliminate the need for the PropogatingFontFieldEditor.\\n\\nThere is a new extension point fontDefinition for defining fonts so that they \\ncan be viewed and managed by the workbench fonts preference page. There is \\nalso a defaultTo attribute which when set keeps the entry for the \\nfontDefinition consistent with the defaultsTo entry if the preference for the \\nfontDefinition is not set.\\n\\nFor example if a font called org.eclipse.myplugin.textfont had a defaultsTo of \\norg.eclipse.jface.textfont the value in the font registry for \\norg.eclipse.myplugin.textfont will be the same as the value for \\norg.eclipse.jface.textfont until the user sets a preference for \\norg.eclipse.myplugin.textfont .\\n\\nsee the org_eclipse_ui.fontDefinition doc for more details

Summary: jardesc does not allow workspace-relative paths [jar creation]

Summary: Types view updates when there's no input
Description: The packages view has bugged me with a misbehaviour since Eclipse 2.0. But using\\nEclipse 3.0 it gets me really crazy. To show you what its all about, lets see a\\nlittle example:\\n\\nHaving a Java project (or a plugin project) and also having two folders. The\\nfirst package contains the production code and the second contains all test\\ncases. So you got an directory structure like:\\n\\nProject\\n |-> src\\n  -> src-test\\n\\nThe src-test folder mirrors the package structure of the src folder. Meaning\\nhaving a class pack.pack2.AClass in the src folder results in having a test case\\npack.pack2.TestAClass.\\n\\nTo play a good game with such a project I've open at least two windows. First\\none to edit the src folder classes and a second to play with the src-test folder.\\n\\nTo select the folder the current window is working on I am using a projects\\nviewer and a package viewer. In the projects viewer I select the source folder I\\nwant to work on. And the packages-viewer then shows up all packages(-fragments)\\nof that source-folder and when I select a single fragment the right types show\\nup in the types-viewer.\\n\\nThat's the way I think it's intended to work. But here is the funny part of the\\nstory... . If you add an new package (which source folder ever) in one of your\\nwindows, the second one (displaying a diffrent source folder) gets crazy and\\nstarts to also show the new package, even if it's in a diffrent source folder.\\n\\nTo get rid of the unwanted package within the view, you have to select a\\ndiffrent sourcefolder in the projects viewer, bring up the packages viewer and\\nthen select back to the right sourcefolder. \\n\\nAnd that gets me really crazy. Normally you only add a package once in several\\nhours but currently I am adding tons of it to port some projects to check out\\nhow M6 is feeling. Summary: Java Browsing selection should be updated when CU is reconciled
Description: Builds > 20040206\\n\\nUp to now the selection in the browsing views was always in sync with the caret\\nlocation in the editor because we reconciled the CU in the UI thread using:\\n\\n    synchronized (unit) {\\n        unit.reconcile(false, null);\\n    }\\n\\nThis caused performance blockers in the UI for large files. We now only set the\\nselection if the CU is consistent. As a result, if the name of a member is\\nchanged in the editor then it will no longer be selected in the Members view.\\n\\nThis can be fixed in three ways:\\n1) the editor offers clients a reconciled listener\\n2) the browsing views setup a thread which reconciles the CU, but this can\\nresult in several reconcile calls since the selection change and the background\\nreconciler aren't in sync\\n3) the browsing views setup a thread that polls whether the CU is reconciled\\n\\nI prefer 1) since the time when the update is done is then in sync with the\\noutline page synchronization.

Perhaps they should be supplied via fragments bound to an \\nappropriate extension point.\\n\\nAlso, the function always includes the default locale even if no dictionaries \\nwere found.  I think this behaviour is misleading and prevents the UI from \\npresenting a more useful \\"no dictionaries available\\" kind of cue, if none were \\ninstalled (as in M7?).\\n\\nLooks good.  I hope this support gets generalized somewhat and moved into \\norg.eclipse.text eventually.

Summary: JavaEditor draws squiggle underline over the string
Description: build I20040519\\n\\nJavaEditor draws squiggle underline over the string (a.k.a red see).\\nThis problem is been caused by SWT. It was introduced when we added italic \\nfont support.\\n\\nHere is the situation:\\nThe application set a font in the StyledText. Internally StyledText will \\ncreate 3 more fonts: boldFont, italicFont, boldItalicFont.\\nIn order to line up normal, bold, italic, and boldItalic segments of text in \\nthe same line StyledText need to compute the max baseline amongs all those \\nfonts. Usually these font have same (or very similar) metrics, but sometimes \\nthey are not (example: default font in Solaris).\\n\\nI believe the code that draws the squiggle is getting the normal font from the \\nStyledText, getting its metrics, compute the baseline (ascent+descent), and \\ndraws the squiggle at y + baseline. Since this baseline can be less than the \\nmaxBaseline it possible that the siggle will be drawn over the text instead of \\nthe real baseline where the strings where drawn.\\n\\nRight now we have two solutions:\\n1) The app code will need to create all the fonts and do the same styledtext \\nis doing.\\n\\n2) We add getBaseline() to StyledText and app code start to using it instead \\nof getting the line metrics.

Summary: IDOMMember.getComments() sometimes returns wrong results.
Description: IDOMMember.getComments() appears to attempt to return the \\"doc comment\\" (that\\nis, the Javadoc comment) for the member. The documentation is vague on this, but\\ntesting seems to suggest this is the intent.\\n\\nHowever, in cases where a member has more than one /** */-style comment, unusual\\nresults occur. For example, for in the following Java:\\n\\n   /**\\n    * a first Javadoc comment\\n    */\\n   // public void foo() {\\n   // }\\n   /**\\n    * a second Javadoc comment\\n    */\\n   public void bar() {}\\n\\ngetComments() returns:\\n\\n   /**\\n    * a first Javadoc comment\\n    */\\n   // public void foo() {\\n   // }\\n   /**\\n    * a second Javadoc comment\\n    */\\n\\nThis is inconsistent with the following example:\\n\\n   // a non-javadoc comment\\n   /**\\n    * The javadoc for this\\n    */\\n   /*\\n    * another non-javadoc\\n    */\\n   public void foo() {}\\n\\nin which case, getComments() returns:\\n\\n   /**\\n    * The javadoc for this\\n    */\\n\\nIn general, getComments() returns everything between the first and last detected\\njavadoc-style comment for an element.\\n\\nThis is inconsistent with the way javadoc itself works. Javadoc uses only the\\nlast javadoc comment immediately preceding the element.\\n\\nThe current behavior is the result of code in the\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.com.jdom.DOMBuilder methods enterAbstractMethod(),\\nenterField() and enterType(). Proposed fixes and JUnit tests will be attached.

This\\ncan be anticipated in the preview, where the code is correct, but a class will\\nappear twice, causing this issue.\\n\\nI know that Creating a linked folder to another place in the repository gives a\\nwarning (\\"Location ..... may overlap another resource. Summary: [formatter] String.length() is not suitable for line wrapping for Asian languages
Description: User-Agent:       Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1; SV1; .NET CLR 2.0.50727; .NET CLR 3.0.04506.648; .NET CLR 3.5.21022; MAXTHON 2.0)\\nBuild Identifier: I20090611-1540\\n\\nThere two problems in code format when source contains Asian characters. \\n\\nThe first is about line breaking, in Chinese, a long line of text is breaked by characters, rather than by words. Because Chinese doesn't use space to separate words, so the word-boundary algorithm is definitely different with english languages. Fortunately, we don't need to break Chinese words, while search engines will need to parse the Chinese text and found all the words, a code formatter don't need to do so. \\n\\nI found that Eclipse can recognize the Chinese punctuations, and use them to break long lines, well, that helps little, that's still a word-based line wrapping, and not suitable for Chinese users. It's important that when do line wrapping on Chinese, the word boundary by space isn't existed, you can break on any character. \\n\\nThe second problem is, when calculate the width of a line of text, a CJK character should be considered as double width. That's very usual in the real world, and all fixed-size fonts are designed in this way.  I guess the JDT code formatter calculates the line width using String.length(), so all Asian characters are of width of 1, and that cause the format result very ugly, and are not aligned especially in mixed language. \\n\\nReproducible: Always\\n\\nSteps to Reproduce:\\n1. Summary: [1.5][dom][javadoc] Need better support for type parameter Javadoc tags
Description: 20041130\\n\\nTo document a type parameter, the normal @param tag is used, but with angle\\nbrackets.\\n\\n/**\\n * @param <X>\\n */\\n<X> void foo() {\\n}\\n\\nThe AST currently just returns a TagElement with a sigle children Name 'X' and\\nis currently not distinguishable from a normal parameter.\\n\\nEither text elements '<' and '>' are inserted or we use a SimpleType node\\ninstead of the SimpleName.\\n\\nThe first suggestion would make the accessing of tag names more complicated.\\nThe drawback of the second suggestion is that it does not include the source\\nranges for the open and closing angle brackets, but users can use the scanner as\\nsoon as they see the SimpleType instead of the SimpleName.\\n\\nThe deluxe solution would be a new node type that includes the bracket and has a\\nsimple name.

Summary: [search] Search for method declarations in workspace, disregarding declaring type
Description: For the new RippleMethodFinder, we need to search for all declarations of a\\ngiven method signature in the workspace. This search should *not* take the\\ndeclaring type into account, only the signature must match.\\n\\nThe current behaviour of search for method declarations of an IMethod in\\nworkspace does not make much sense, since it is exactly the same search as when\\nsearching in the hierarchy of the declaring type. Therefore, I think that search\\nfor method declarations in workspace should be changed to only consider the\\nmethod signature of a given IMethod, and not its declaring type.\\n\\nNote that a string pattern search does not help here, since it only takes\\nstrings as parameter types, but we need the real type reference in the method\\nparameters.

Summary: [perf] Excessive File.isFile calls for clients of JavaModel.getTarget(...)
Description: Build: I20050126-0800\\n\\nBACKGROUND:\\n\\nI am working with the JVE team to improve their editor's performance. One \\nsignificant difference between the Visual Editor open time and the JDT's Java \\neditor open time is I/O -- the former often makes 10-20x more I/O events.\\n\\nPROBLEM:\\n\\nWe're making good progress reducing the Visual Editor's I/O. During my \\ninvestigation, I also found the JDT is contributing to unnecessary I/O events \\n(confirmed with FileMon and traced to File.isFile invocations). \\n\\nI noted that many callers of the JavaModel.getTarget(...) method, such as \\nIJavaProject.getAllPackageFragmentRoots, have subsequent tests of File.isFile\\n(), which is equivalent in cost to File.exists() that the \\nJavaModel.existingExternalFiles cache wishes to avoid. In the scenario I \\nmeasured, added a second cache (existingExternalConfirmedFiles) avoided 78 I/O \\nevents or almost 30% of all the remaining I/O events for the JVE \\"open editor\\" \\ntestcase. During a launch, this correction also saves more I/O calls, although \\nI didn't measure them precisely since that occurs on the JVE's background \\nthread.\\n\\nPROPOSED CORRECTION:\\n\\nI have attached a version of JavaModel adding two convenience methods: isFile \\nand getFile, whose purpose is to cache the previously determined status of the \\ngiven target in the static field existingExternalConfirmedFiles. Also attached \\nare several clients of these APIs. I offer them as suggestions, although \\njudging from the nested if...else...if...else that generally follows the \\ninvocation of JavaModel.getTarget, there may be a more elegant way of \\ncapturing the intent by adding added conditions / flags to this API rather \\nthan the simplistic performance-oriented approach I've taken.

Summary: [reconcile] Optimize operation of Java reconciler when build operation is triggered.
Description: The java reconciler comes into play while the user types code and while the compilation process has not kicked in yet to generate the class file. This works fine when the user is writing code but if he presses CTRL+S (auto-build enabled) or triggers a build manually, two threads - the compiler and the Java reconciler - start to parse, resolve, analyse code and build ASTs together. This process is wasteful as far as the Java reconciler is concerned. If the AST is all that it needs, perhaps the compiler can return it as it is to the reconciler.\\n\\nWe should think of better strategies to remove this redundancy at compile time. Filing this bug initially in JDT/UI to get everyone's opinion. May be moved to JDT/Core if needed.

Summary: Eclipse complains with an “Type already defined” error even when the output folder is different for those classes
Description: Build Identifier: I20110613-1736\\n\\nI have a project where I need to have two different implementations for the same exact same class (i.e., same qualified name). The corresponding class files are generated in different output folders, and I have “run actions” that use either one or the other via a custom class-path.\\n\\nExample “.project” snippet:\\n\\n<classpath>\\n <classpathentry kind=\\"src\\" path=\\"src/package/supersource\\"/ output=\\"src/package/supersource\\" >\\n <classpathentry kind=\\"src\\" path=\\"src\\" excluding=\\"com/dragg/supersource/\\" />\\n <classpathentry kind=\\"output\\" path=\\"output\\" />\\n</classpath>\\n\\nUnfortunately, Eclipse insists on reporting the situation as an error: \\n“The type <DuplicatedType> is already defined” (attached to the second one encountered in the classpath order).\\n\\nThe only reference to the type name is a “ImplementedInterface instance = new DuplicatedType()” constructor call.\\n\\nIMO, this *particular* case is not an error; since the two classes have different output folder, nothing prevents Eclipse from actually compiling everything, and indeed, everything seems to work—both classes are checked for other errors and warnings—except that only the first one in classpath order is actually generated. I believe Eclipse should generate the two .class files (in their separate output folders) and at worst trigger a warning.\\n\\nNow, I understand why Eclipse would complain: it needs to check that call to the constructor I mentioned above, and it has two different alternatives, because it uses everything as the classpath when compiling. Given this particular project setup, the ideal behavior would be to try both, but I don’t think that’s tractable in the general case.  But it would be nice if it were at least possible to specify in the .classpath file “when compiling this folder, exclude *this other* folder from the classpath”.\\n\\n(Explanation for the curious: I’m using GWT, which compiles Java to JavaScript. But some libraries are only available in JavaScript and some are only available in Java. I have quite a bit of code that needs to run the same both as pure Java and as JavaScript, which uses a (small) helper class with different Java implementations for the two cases. GWT allows you to declare a “super-source” folder, and the classes defined there are used to replace classes with the same name when compiling to JavaScript.\\n\\nI could probably work around this by splitting the “duplicate” classes into separate projects and playing a bit with exports, but it would be quite complex, and the class doesn’t make sense outside the project.)\\n\\nReproducible: Always\\n\\nSteps to Reproduce:\\n1. Add two source folders to your project, with different output folders.\\n2. Define the same class (i.e., same qualified name) in both source folders.\\n3. Try to build your project.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Pull back temporary bug compatibility mode with javac (AnnotatedConstruct#getAnnotationMirrors() etc.))
Description: BETA_JAVA8: \\n\\nAs of 8b111, there are a few areas where ECJ and javac differ in that either\\njavac has a clear bug or has not implemented some part of the spec.\\n\\nThis CR is to make eclipse mimic javac behavior to the extent possible without\\nintroducing bugs that would affect program behavior:\\n\\nAt the moment, there are 3 items:\\n\\n1. '_' as an identifier triggers a warning in javac, an error in eclipse.\\n2. Annotations are tolerated on dimensions of a class literal expression\\nsuch as int @T [].class.\\n3. javac does not yet diagnose the illegal scenario of a repeatable annotation\\nbeing used along with repeating container.\\n\\nI propose to make all of these warnings at the moment, leave this CR open and\\nrevert the right behavior before GA. This is so as to minimize surprises. Since\\nin each case, we warn clearly and since these areas are chosen carefully as\\nones not affecting run time behavior, we are good.\\n\\nAs we discover more such areas, we should update the list and republish the\\nfull list as a comment, so up to date issues list can be found by reading\\nthe latest comment rather than having to scan through.

Summary: ITypeBinding#getBinaryName() returns incorrect value for TypeVariable's defined by a generic method
Description: Per http://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se8/html/jls-13.html#jls-13.1:\\n\\n\\"The binary name of a type variable declared by a generic method (§8.4.4) is the binary name of the type declaring the method, followed by $, followed by the descriptor of the method (JVMS §4.3.3), followed by $, followed by the simple name of the type variable.:\\n\\n\\nJLS defines the name of the method as part of the binary name; since it is missing; the API doesn't correctly follow its contract and the generated names are not unique.\\n\\nAlso see https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=107001

Summary: Custom user agent for javadoc http connections
Description: org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaElement.getURLContents(URL, String) does not set a user agent, thus uses the default one set by the JDK. Some CDN providers (CloudFlare is one of them) by default uses a browser integrity check (https://support.cloudflare.com/hc/en-us/articles/200170086-What-does-the-Browser-Integrity-Check-do-) that filters out requests that have 'Java/*' as user agent (and possibly others as well) and responds with an HTTP 403. It would be useful, if the request would set a different user agent, e.g.: 'Eclipse JDT/<version>'.\\n\\nPossible workarounds:\\n1. use -Dhttp.agent=\\"<something other than Java/*>\\"\\n2. get in touch with the site's maintainer that is hosted on the CDN and ask them to turn off/customize this check

Summary: If loading Annotation Processor (.factorypath) fails, error message is useless.
Description: Eclipse loads annotation processors configured via a java project settings: \\"Java Compiler > Annotation Processing\\" section with its own VM (the VM used to start eclipse).\\n\\nPROBLEM:\\nIf loading the AP causes some exception to be thrown, eclipse eats this message. It is not visible anywhere (not in the error log, nor on the terminal if you run eclipse from terminal). Eclipse DOES apply an error marker on the entire project, but this error marker doesn't have the exception trace either, and has a rather uninformative error message.\\n\\nThe full message is:\\n\\nUnable to load annotation processor factory 'fully.qualified.name.of.AnnotationProcessorClass' for project project.with.configured.ap\\n\\non element: The project\\nIn folder: (Blank string)\\nSeverity: Error\\nLocation: the string \\"Annotation processor factory path\\" (as in, that exact string, not the actual path)\\n\\nand that's it. No stack trace or any other hint.\\n\\nGoogling for this message mostly gets you red herrings (not something eclipse can fix short of writing a blog post, but this puts some mild pressure on fixing the issue).\\n\\nHOW TO REPRODUCE:\\n\\nYou are upgrading your projects from JDK8 to, say, JDK11. You run your eclipse on a JRE8, but you've hooked up an OpenJDK11 impl and told eclipse that your own AP project is now OpenJDK11. You compile it, and then apply your freshly compiled annotation processor to some other projects in eclipse (right click project, \\"properties...\\", annotation processing, enable it, and point at the jar just made).\\n\\nThen, this bug occurs: These class files (which are \\"-target 11\\") cannot be loaded by a JDK8. The uninformative error message appears, and the annotation processor is not applied when eclipse builds this project.\\n\\nSeparate from this, the error marker blinks into and out of existence seemingly randomly: When you close such a project (one with the error marker) and re-open it, _ALL_ such markers disappear for _ALL_ projects that have one, even if you close and re-open a project that is NOT a dependency of another project with such markers. The markers remain missing (even though the configured annotation processor did not run, so the lack of marker is itself a bug), until you for example touch the .factorypath file or open the project config, or just change any sourcefile in it, which causes eclipse to attempt to load the AP.\\n\\nGiven that this secondary issue only occurs when there is a problem with the AP, that part is a minor nag and becomes far less relevant once the primary issue (of uninformative error messaging) is taken care of.\\n\\nNB: Whilst writing annotation processors and using them on your own projects is perhaps somewhat rare, if this bug occurs it's a wild goose chase to attempt to figure out what's going on. I find it hard to attempt to apply a severity to 'rarely happens, but if it happens, takes ages to chase down'.\\n\\nsuggested fix: Eclipse should update the message to INCLUDE the stack trace. At the very least, the stack trace of the failed classload should be put in the error log.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Add support for JSR 308 - Type Annotations Specification
Description: This enhancement request is a placeholder to document,\\ntrack progress of, discuss, disseminate information\\non the task to incorporate support for jsr 308.\\n\\nThe JSR 308 webpage is http://groups.csail.mit.edu/pag/jsr308/\\n\\nhttp://types.cs.washington.edu/jsr308/specification/java-annotation-design.pdf\\ncontains the latest specification.\\n\\nSection 5 in this document provides the \\"detailed grammar changes\\" and\\nunder this head lists ~20 products that will need to undergo change.\\n\\nThis grammar delta is with respect to the grammar outlined in chapter 18\\nof JLS3.\\n\\nA few key points here:\\n\\n    - Even with respect to JLS3, this delta is not comprehensive, so we\\ncan't go just by this section. As one example, see that the delta misses\\nout annotations on types in the throws specification for a method.\\n(Reported)\\n\\n    - The JLS3 grammar is substantially different (while being\\nequivalent) from what is used by eclipse. To meet LALR(1) criteria,\\nto perhaps aid with error recovery etc, the grammar used by eclipse\\nhas undergone significant transformations.\\n\\n    - The very first production in section 5, namely, \\n\\n      Type:\\n          [ Annotations] UnannType\\n\\n      works nicely for the JLS3 grammar to ensure that any use of a Type\\n      could be annotated, but is misleadingly simple for the eclipse grammer.\\n      In contexts where use of Type is more permissive than what is legal,\\n      Eclispe grammar directly uses other nonterminals from the\\n      Types subgrammar such as ReferenceType, Name, ClassOrInterfaceType\\n      etc. Some of these non-terminals are used in contexts where it would\\n      be illegal to annotate them, so we can't simply \\"wrap\\" these into\\n      new productions with optional preceding annotations as the delta\\n      spec does with Type.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Compiler should reject explicit this parameter in disallowed contexts
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\n   Top of branch contains syntactic support for explicit this parameter\\nto facilitate attaching receiver annotations. The compiler must perform\\nseveral validations here.\\n\\n    - Only at 1.8 explicit this should be allowed (done)\\n    - Only as a first parameter (done)\\n\\nHere is the relevant part of the spec:\\n\\nOnly the first formal parameter may be named this, and such a \\nparameter is only permitted on an instance method, or on a \\nstatic method or constructor of an inner class. The type of \\nthe this parameter must be the same as the class that contains\\nthe method and should include type arguments if that class has \\nany. In a method in an inner type, the receiver type can be \\nwritten as (for example) either Inner or as Outer.Inner, and \\nin the latter case  annotations on both parts are possible, \\nas in @ReadOnly Outer . @Mutable Inner.\\n\\n[I believe the \\"on the static method of an inner class\\" part\\nis wrong - clarifications have been sought from the EG]

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Type annotations must not be allowed on static member access.
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nJSR308: section 2.1.1 states: \\n\\nStatic member accesses are preceded by a type name, but that type name\\nmay not be annotated:\\n\\n@Illegal Outer . StaticNestedClass // illegal!\\n@Illegal Outer . staticField // illegal!\\n\\nIt further states:\\n\\nA static member access may itself be a type use, in which case the used\\ntype may be annotated by annotating the last component of the static member\\naccess, which is the simple name of the type being used.\\n\\nOuter . @Legal StaticNestedClass x = ...; // legal\\n\\nNote however that support for annotations on nested type names is still\\nin the works (bug 383596)\\n\\nAt the moment, the following program triggers two errors:\\n\\n// --------------------------------------------\\nimport java.lang.annotation.Target;\\npublic class X {\\n	static class Y {};\\n	public static void main(String[] args) {\\n		Object o = (@Marker X.Y) null;\\n	} \\n}\\n@Target(TYPE_USE)\\n@interface Marker {\\n}\\n\\n//----------------------------------------------\\n\\n(1) The annotation @Marker is disallowed for this location\\n(2) TYPE_USE cannot be resolved to a variable\\n\\nThe latter is due to the absence of a JRE that supports TYPE_USE.\\nBut once a good JRE becomes available, (1) would go away too and\\nthe program would start compiling while it should not.

Summary: JavaModel.refreshExternalArchives needs to happen before search is primed
Description: When the search engine is primed (as part of calling JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad(IProgressMonitor)) then it populates the index manager based on the information returned from IndexManager#computeIndexLocation(IPath containerPath).  If the underlying index is a pre-built index but it has been deleted from the file-system, then the index is re-created in the workspace metadata and not in the location specified by the INDEX_LOCATION_ATTRIBUTE_NAME classpath attribute.  This is because search has no concept of the classpath containers - it simply knows a list of project and the corresponding archive files.\\n\\nIn JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad(IProgressMonitor) the call to refresh external archives (which populates the index manager with the correct classpath attribute information) happens after the search occurs.  Since the index has already been built from the search call then it ends up being used.\\n\\nThere are two ways to fix this:\\n\\n1) In JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad(IProgressMonitor), move the call to refresh the archives to happen BEFORE the search engine is primed.\\n\\n2) In IndexManager#computeIndexLocation(IPath containerPath, final URL newIndexURL) added via bug 395897, if the existing URL is different from the new URL then the index needs to be rebuilt after it is removed.\\n\\nI think fix 1 makes more sense as, ideally, you want to know the latest archive state before a search is done.  This approach also ensures that the indexer manager is doing less work

Summary: [1.8][model] Superinterfaces of lambda element's IType are missing type arguments
Description: Created attachment 240672\\nPatch 1\\n\\nSuperinterfaces of lambda element's IType are missing type arguments. The effect of this is that method override computations in JDT UI fail (e.g. in Ctrl+T and to render Javadocs for the lambda IMethod).\\n\\nExample:\\n\\n    Function<List<String>, List<String>> sup = (arg) -> {\\n        return new ArrayList<>(arg);\\n    };\\n\\n    Function<List<String>, List<String>> suppe =\\n                new Function<List<String>, List<String>>() {\\n        @Override\\n        public List<String> apply(List<String> arg) {\\n            return new ArrayList<>(arg);\\n        }\\n    };\\n\\nIType#getSuperInterfaceTypeSignatures() on the IType for the lambda returns \\"QFunction;\\". This signature is missing type arguments.\\n\\nThe corresponding anonymous type always returns the supertype via IType#getSuperclassTypeSignature(). Here, it returns the correctly parameterized signature \\"QFunction<QList<QString;>;QList<QString;>;>;\\".\\n\\nFor the lambda IType, resolved supertypes would be also be better than unresolved ones.\\n\\nThe attached patch fixes this, but I don't really understand the difference between the LambdaExpression and ResolvedLambdaExpression types.

Summary: [1.8][model] JavaElement.JEM_LAMBDA_METHOD should not use '*' and '>' as memento delimiter
Description: JavaElement.JEM_LAMBDA_METHOD should not use '*' and '>' as memento delimiter.\\n\\nI just saw that the fix for bug 425134 had to make adjustments in MementoTests. That's not good. Existing JavaElement handles should stay as stable as possible, see Javadoc of IJavaElement#getHandleIdentifier(). '*' and '>' were already used by existing mementos, and such stored mementos cannot be parsed any more now.\\n\\nI see that most \\"safe\\" ASCII characters are already used as token delimiters or in token data, but these look free:\\n\\n&')`\\n\\nForbidden character groups:\\n- identifier characters\\n- characters used in Signature (at least for parameter type signatures)\\n- , is IMO risky as well (often used by clients to separate data)\\n\\nWe should also have a test for lambda type and lambda method mementos. I don't think these will be stored often (since they are inherently unstable), but they can be used locally (e.g. to put an element on the clipboard, or for hyperlinks in Javadoc hovers).

We need to come up with a strategy for this - whether to use the provided jrt-fs that will be bundled with the JDK9 (even when eclipse itself runs on <= JRE 8) or something else (home-grown?). Without this, it's impossible to use JDK9 in project build path.\\n\\n2. JREContainer should evolve to support the new VM installs. Some of the changes known at this point are, removal of /ext and /endorsed. Instead the new module system will be used for extensions.\\n\\n3. Removal of certain JAR files: rt.jar and tools.jar have been removed. If we are hard-coding dependency anywhere, that should be addressed.

Summary: [1.9] jrt visitor implementation should use package-module lookup
Description: Right now, given a JDK 9, JDT has to look into every module (one by one) to find a type, given its qualified name. Obviously this is not scalable, but will change once the following enhancement is added in Oracle's JDK:\\n\\nhttps://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-8066492

Summary: [1.9] Restructure Java Model for Jimage
Description: The current Java model is proving to be insufficient to represent the Jimage structure. As of now now (head of BETA_JAVA9) the entire Jimage is represented as a PackageFragmentRoot and packages are modeled as PackageFragment.\\nBut there is nothing really to hold the modules except for the package-module cache we maintain internally.\\n\\nIt is also a problem for resources that don't have a package and hence no package-module mapping. I think we need to start thinking about changing models. I propose the following:\\n\\nA new kind of PackageFragmentRoot namely ModulePackageFragmentRoot\\nOptional - A new model Jimage to hold the modules. It will make sense when in future we will be required to load individual Jimage files and might also have a mixed set up of Jars and Jimages.\\n\\nWe also need to discuss what happens when we also have modules as source.

Summary: [1.9] Support JRE 9 in JSR199 implementation
Description: Some of the compiler.tool tests fail when run with JRE 9. The failure happens because the EclipseFileManager and it's components don't yet understand Jimage. This needs to be fixed. We also need to look at another identical version of EclipseFileManager in the jdt.compiler.apt bundle.

Summary: [1.9] JDT tests are incredibly slow with JRE 9
Description: I clocked few samples, like NullTypeAnnotationTest, org.eclipse.jdt.apt.tests.TestAll and I clearly see the test take about four times more with JRE 9. Here are the reasons why it is so:\\n\\n1. First and foremost, JDT has no clue how to load only the bootmodules.jimage and we end up reading everything known to the JVM.\\n\\n2. Several sub components assume that JavaModelManager caches the zip files and don't bother caching information themselves. This caching is not available to Jimages,, though.\\n\\nThe latter needs to be looked at case by case and fixed.\\n\\nBut we also need to take a look at (1). We simply can't afford to load every available class in the JVM. Even if we can't read specific jimage files as of today, we should at least be able to load only specific modules. Ideally we should leave it to the user to choose what modules he/she wants to be loaded. But for that, JDT should provide a configurable method. And this should be provisioned in a way that all JDT components (Java Model, compiler, batch compiler, JSR 199 etc.) could leverage.

Description: master, broken at least back to 4.4.1\\n\\n// compile with JavaSE-1.8:\\npackage p18;\\npublic class Klass<T> {\\n	class MethodInfo { }\\n	void addMethod(MethodInfo mi) { }\\n}\\n\\n// compile with J2SE-1.3, in a project that has the above class on build path:\\npackage p13;\\npublic final class J13 {\\n	p18.Klass c; \\n}\\n\\n\\nResult:\\n\\nError in /J13/src/p13/J13.java: The class file Klass<T> contains a signature '(Lp18/Klass<TT;>.MethodInfo;)V' ill-formed at position 17\\n\\n\\nTo debug, set a breakpoint at SignatureWrapper.computeEnd() line: 84\\nwith condition:\\n    toString().startsWith(\\"(Lp18/Klass<TT;>.MethodInfo;)V\\")\\n\\n\\nAnalysis:\\n\\nThe problem is that SignatureWrapper#computeEnd() assumes that type arguments in angle brackets always introduce the end of a type signature. It that were true, skipAngleContents(..) would work fine. But in this case, a nested type name follows. The compound type name is no longer a subsequence of the generic signature, but it picks multiple non-contiguous subsequences (\\"Klass\\", \\"MethodInfo\\").\\n\\nThis bug cannot be resolved by a simple change in SignatureWrapper#computeEnd(). It will also need fixes in callers of that method. In this case in LookupEnvironment#getTypeFromTypeSignature(..).

Summary: APIs to get FQNs and type signatures of method parameter types
Description: 1. API to get the FQN of the method parameter types:\\n\\nCurrently, IMethod.getParameterTypes() returns a String[] having the type signatures of the method parameters which are of the form {\\"QString;\\",\\"I\\"}.\\n\\nThe new API could be added to IMethod and should return the fully qualified type names of the method parameter types, in the same form as obtained from java.lang.Class.getName().\\n\\nSee also: IType#resolveType.\\n\\n2. API to get the type signatures from a type's FQN:\\n\\nThe API could be added to JavaCore and should convert the passed argument (i.e. the FQN of a type in the form which is obtained from java.lang.Class.getName()) to type signature. The returned value is intended to be passed to IType.getMethod(String name, String[] parameterTypeSignatures) to identify a particular method.\\n\\nThese APIs are required to support JUnit5's overloaded test methods: bug 488566.

Description: Automatic modules are important in the migration path to completely module based systems. Summary: [9] Unable to find correct source file for module-info from JRT
Description: As of build 146, the source bundled with the JDK (i.e. src.zip) is modularized. In other words, there is now a new sub folder for each module, under which the corresponding sources are archived. Since this change, the source mapper is unable to locate the correct source file for module-info.class. Because there are several module-info.class present, the mapper always picks up the first one on the list.\\n\\nIt is working fine for other types, though, because we go through each sub folder and look for sources in them. Even here, presence of multiple files with same name will cause problem.\\n\\nThe fix I have in mind is to have JrtPackageFragmentRoot limit its root path explicitly to its module folder.

Summary: [9][test] Create jclMin*.jar for model tests for compliance 9
Description: JDT Model tests use a minimal version of system libraries, named jclMin1.8*.jar. This is used in test projects instead of the whole system libraries for performance reasons. For e.g. many tests would kick off indexing, which would be unnecessary and affect performance with the whole system library in the build path. With JRE 9, the system libraries as JAR have been replaced by jimage and JMOD files and one needs the jrt-fs to read system classes.\\n\\nAs of now, the tests are making do with the existing jclMin1.8.jar. While this is sufficient for most tests, there could be others that require module related information.

Summary: Elements.getAllMembers returns static methods in superinterfaces
Description: The result of Elements.getAllMembers includes static methods in superinterfaces. For example, if called on this type:\\n\\n  public static class MyMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> {}\\n\\nthe result will include the static `of` methods that were added to the Map interface in Java 9. That's incorrect by spec, and also intuitively. You can't write `MyMap.of()` just because there is an `of()` method in `Map`, so the `of()` method shouldn't be included in the result of `getAllMembers()`. Static methods are inherited from superclasses (you *could* write `MyMap.of()` if `HashMap` had an `of()` method) but not superinterfaces.\\n\\nFor the spec, we have this for Elements.getAllMembers <https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.compiler/javax/lang/model/util/Elements.html#getAllMembers(javax.lang.model.element.TypeElement)>:\\n\\"Returns all members of a type element, whether inherited or declared directly.\\"\\n\\nStatic methods in interfaces are not inherited <https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se11/html/jls-8.html#jls-8.4.8>:\\n\\"A class does not inherit private or static methods from its superinterfaces.\\"

Summary: [16] Redeclaring pattern variables with same name should be rejected
Description: The discussion was here:\\n\\nhttps://mail.openjdk.java.net/pipermail/compiler-dev/2021-January/016204.html\\n\\nAnd the spec says this under 6.3.1.4:\\n----\\nIt is a compile-time error if any of the following conditions hold:\\n\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by a when true, and by c when true.\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by a when false, and by b when true.\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by b when true, and by c when true.\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by a when true, and by c when false.\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by a when false, and by b when false.\\n    A pattern variable is introduced both by b when false, and by c when false.\\n\\n    These final cases are to rule out cases of the introduction of pattern variables that may be supported in future versions of the language.\\n---\\n\\nThe Java 16 compiler also reflects this behavior, rejecting the first 10 cases in the following examples:\\n\\n// Rejected\\nboolean b1 = (o instanceof String a) ? (o instanceof String a) : false;\\nboolean b2 = !(o instanceof String a) ? (o instanceof String a) : false;\\nboolean b3 = (o instanceof String a) ? !(o instanceof String a) : false;\\nboolean b4 = !(o instanceof String a) ? !(o instanceof String a) : false;\\n		\\nboolean b5 = (o instanceof String a) ? true : (o instanceof String a);\\nboolean b6 = !(o instanceof String a) ? true : (o instanceof String a);\\nboolean b7 = (o instanceof String a) ? true : !(o instanceof String a);\\nboolean b8 = !(o instanceof String a) ? true : !(o instanceof String a);\\n\\nboolean b9 = (o instanceof String) ? (o instanceof String a) : (o instanceof String a);\\nboolean b10 = (o instanceof String) ? !(o instanceof String a) : !(o instanceof String a);\\n		\\n// These are allowed\\nboolean b11 = (o instanceof String) ? !(o instanceof String a) : !!(o instanceof String a);\\nboolean b12 = (o instanceof String) ? !(o instanceof String a) : (o instanceof String a);

Summary: [17] null, any pattern and corresponding initialization.
Description: Sec 14.11.1 - null and any pattern\\n\\nIf the value is the null reference, then we determine the first (if any) switch label in the switch block that applies to the value as follows:\\n\\nA switch label that has a null case label element applies. Summary: [18][switch pattern] Resolving A Switch Block
Description: Sec 14.11.1 - Delta pertaining to resolving switch block\\n\\nThis paragraph has been expanded in JEP 420.\\n\\nJEP 420 says,\\nResolving a switch block at type T results in an identical switch block except where every switch label L is replaced with the result of resolving L at type T.\\n\\nResolving a switch label L at type T proceeds by resolving all the default and case labels it uses as follows:\\n\\nIf L uses a default label then the resolved switch label uses a default label.\\n\\nIf L uses a case label then the resolved switch label uses a case label with the case label elements determined as follows:\\n\\nAll constant case label elements appearing in L appear in the resolved switch label.\\n\\nAll default case label elements appearing in L appear in the resolved switch label.\\n\\nIf a null case label element and no pattern case element labels appear in L then a null case label element appears in the resolved switch label.\\n\\nIf no null case label element appears in L then for every pattern case label element p appearing in L, a pattern case element label q appears in the resolved switch label, where q is the result of resolving pattern p at type T.\\n\\nThe definition of resolving a pattern at a type is given in 14.30.2.\\n\\nIf a null case label element appears in L then for every pattern case label element appearing in L that is a type pattern declaring a pattern variable x of type U, a pattern case element q appears in the resolved switch label, where q is an any pattern that declares x of type U.\\n\\nAll pattern case element labels appearing in a switch label that also contains a null case element label are required to be type patterns (14.11.1).\\n\\nThis final rule covers an important aspect of resolving a switch label. If a switch label has both null and type pattern case label elements, then these are resolved to a single pattern case label element that is an any pattern. This ensures that the initialization of the pattern variable declared by the type pattern is always handled by the semantics of pattern matching, even when the value being matched is null.\\n\\n\\nwhile JEP 406 says:\\nA switch block is resolved at type U resulting in a identical switch block except where every pattern case label element p is replaced with a pattern case label element whose pattern is the result of resolving pattern p at type U.\\n\\n\\nFeel free to create child bugs as deemed necessary

Summary: [18] VerifyError when guarded pattern contains an AND_AND expression
Description: Consider this testcase: \\n\\npublic class X4 {\\n    public Object literal = \\"a\\";\\n    public boolean foo() {\\n        String s = switch(literal) {\\n            case ((String a && a.equals(\\"a\\")) && a != null)  -> { \\n                yield \\"a\\";\\n            }\\n            case default -> { \\n                yield \\"b\\";\\n            }\\n        };\\n        if (s.equals(\\"a\\")) {\\n            return true;\\n        }\\n        return false;\\n    }\\n    public static void main(String[] argv) {\\n    	X4 c = new X4();\\n    	System.out.println(c.foo());\\n    }\\n}\\n\\nThis code compiles but produces a VerifyError when run. Summary: [1.8][model] Implement IJavaElements for lambda expression
Description: For many IDE functionalities, we need an IJavaElement for a lambda expression:\\n\\n- CodeSelect should resolve the lambda element when the caret is on the '->'. Currently, there's no easy way to see the contract of the functional interface method that the lambda implements. We should show a Javadoc hover for lambdas.\\n\\n- (Quick) Type Hierarchy should include all implementations of a functional interface (bug 423123); ITypeHierarchyChangedListener should notify of changes.\\n\\n- Reference search matches should show up in a 'lambda' element, not in the element that contains the lambda expression.\\n\\n- The parent of a lambda parameter (ILocalVariable) should be the lambda element, not the enclosing element.\\n\\nAbout the only place where lambdas are not relevant for the UI is in IJavaElement#getChildren(), since we don't intend to show lambdas in the Outline (but we can also filter them out in the UI if that's easier).\\n\\nLambdas share many properties of IType and IMethod, but on the other hand also don't support some of their methods. E.g. IType#create*(*) doesn't make sense, the ISourceManipulation methods can just throw a JME, the type name will be \\"\\" (like for anonymous types) and the name range will be null.\\n\\nThe API of ITypeHierarchy looks like we need at least an IType for a lambda.\\n\\nFor existing Java model clients, the best solution would be to have an IType as well as an IMethod for a lambda expression (rather than a new kind of IJavaElement or only an IType but not an IMethod).\\n\\nIf it reduces the implementation effort, we can also try to treat lambda elements as pseudo-elements like ILocalVariable , ITypeParameter, IAnnotation, which are not part of IJavaElementDeltas, and which are not returned by getChildren().

Summary: compiler.apt.tests framework shouldn't let files interact
Description: The org.eclipse.jdt.compiler.apt.tests framework encourages a general approach of \\"copy a source folder from the plug-in resources to a test project; compile the project; look at the results and/or the language model.\\"\\n\\nOften the folder being copied is shared by all tests in a given test suite.  For instance, all the NegativeTests use the files under resources/negative.  The problem with this is that as files are added to a folder, conflicts occur, such that adding a new file can break an existing test (e.g., by causing a previously unresolved type to be resolved).  Also, it slows down the tests (N^2).\\n\\nThere are some advantages to having the test resources be files, rather than just strings in the test case as is commonly done.  But we need the ability to copy only particular files, rather than all files in a folder.

Summary: ExternalPackageFragmentRoot does not expose its content consistently
Description: We introduced a classpath-uri-scheme in Xtext to refer to EMF-resources. In Xtext's standalone mode, we use a classloader to resolve these URIs, in runtime mode, we rely on the jdt to obtain resources via IJavaProject#getAllPackageFragmentRoots and friends.\\n\\nHowever, sometimes we face the problem, that an ExternalPackageFragmentRoot returns a resource from ExternalPackageFragmentRoot#resource() that does not return valid members from IFolder#findMember, even if they exist (at least in the filesystem). This problem occures, if we create an IJavaProject with contents in a ui-wizard and try to resolve a classpath-uri, when the java tooling is not yet fully initialized.\\n\\nThe workaround, that we came up with, is to fall back to the File-API instead of relying on the Resource-API in these rare cases.\\n\\nThe bug seems to be, that ExternalPackageFragmentRoot should not return from resource() when it cannot return an instance, that works as expected.\\n\\nsee http://dev.eclipse.org/viewcvs/index.cgi/org.eclipse.tmf/org.eclipse.xtext/plugins/org.eclipse.xtext.ui.core/src/org/eclipse/xtext/ui/core/util/JdtClasspathUriResolver.java?root=Modeling_Project&view=markup for a pointer to the code, that fails during javacore initialization

Summary: JavaModelCache not updating after ClasspathContainerInitializers fire - causes WTP to not deploy libraries to Tomcat(others)
Description: If you have a project using classpathcontainer initializers, the JavaModelCache will contain invalid information about that project.  \\n\\nTo recreate:\\n1. Create a Dynamic Web project that uses a classpath initializer - Maven is a good example\\n2. Define a Tomcat server (any version)\\n3. Deploy your application to Tomcat, all is good\\n4. Close the Dynamic Web project\\n5. Open the Dynamic Web project\\n6. Redeploy the project to tomcat\\n<project will fail to run because libraries referenced in the classpath are not present>\\n\\nThis is NOT a WTP bug.  The issue is that when the project opens, JavaElement.openWhenClosed is called.  This grabs all the detail on the project and updates it in JavaModelCache.  The problem is that the classpathcontainerinitializers have not yet fired, thus the projectCache contains packageFragmentRoots for some things, but not for the classpathcontainerinitializers that have not yet fired.\\n\\nThe classpathcontainerinitializers fire later.  But after they fire, the JavaModelCache is never refreshed.  When J2EEflexProjDeployable attempts to gather the libraries for deployment, it excludes the libraries defined with classpathcontainers since it attempts to validate them against packagefragmentroots.\\n\\nDevelopers can work around this issue by manually adjusting their classpath or by closing then reopening eclipse.

Summary: Relative Classpath entries should not be resolved relative to the workspace
Description: The relative classpath changes made as part of 3.5M3 resolve classpath entries relative to the workspace directory.  This is most likely not the desired root for a relative entry.\\n\\nLibrary entries should be resolved relative to the project location.  They will currently only resolve relative to the project if it is contained in the workspace.  For projects residing outside the workspace, the library entries are still resolved relative to the workspace root.\\n\\nExample Workspace Location: /home/myhome/workspace1\\nProject location: /home/myhome/development/project1\\nClasspath Library entry: ../third_party/some.jar.\\nExpected resolution: /home/myhome/development/third_party/some.jar\\nActual resolution: /home/myhome/workspace1/third_party/some.jar\\n\\nVariable entries defined relative to a Classpath Variable can't be resolved at all.  The path of a variable entry has the variable name as the first segment.  The extension of the variable is appended to the variable name to complete the path.  If the extension  begins with a relative reference (../), the canonicalization of the Path for the ClasspathEntry removes the variable name completely from the path.  This prevents the ClasspathEntry from being resolved.\\n\\nExample:  Classpath Variable: EXTERNAL_LOCATION = /home/myhome/development/lib\\nClasspath Variable Extension: ../third_party/some.jar\\nExpected resolution: /home/myhome/development/third_party/some.jar\\n\\nWhen the JavaProject reads this from the .classpath file, it calls ClasspathEntry.elementDecode() to create a ClasspathEntry with a path of EXTERNAL_LOCATION/../third_party/some.jar.  As part of the decode process, ClasspathEntry creates a Path instance.  As part of the Path constructor, the path is canonicalized.  This results in a path of /third_party/some.jar.  Subsequent attempts by the JavaModelManager to resolve the variable entry fail because the ClasspathEntry no longer includes the variable name as the first segment of the path.

Summary: JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad race condition leading to incorrect deltas for external JARs
Description: Build ID: JDT: 3.4.5.v_895_R34x\\n\\nI am a performance analyst for an adopting product. This is a complicated issue that I've been investigating aggressively for many days now. The scenario is simple: (1) open our product with a NEW workspace, (2) disable autobuild, (3) import the project interchange.\\n\\nWe have a plugin that calls JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad after receiving a JDT ElementChangedEvent after the project interchange is imported (basically right after the RefreshJob completes). Inside the method JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad, I see VERY different behavior at this point depending on a number of conditions. \\n\\nOccasionally, though this isn't the main problem, JavaModel.getJavaProjects() will return an empty array, which will skip over most of this method. I find that strange since we're only in this method because of receiving JDT deltas after the import of Java projects (55 in total). \\n\\nThe big problem, though, is that the info object for the java projects might not have been built yet, and therefore, inside \\n\\n   JavaModel.refreshExternalArchives (which calls)\\n    DeltaProcessor.checkExternalArchiveChanges (which calls)\\n     DeltaProcessor.createExternalArchiveDelta\\n\\n(So now we're in createExternalArchiveDelta)\\nThis call:\\n\\n  Long oldTimestamp =(Long) this.state.getExternalLibTimeStamps().get(entryPath);\\n\\nresults in a null, since the DeltaProcessingState.externalTimeStamps field hasn't been populated yet. I find that this field is initially populated by \\n\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaModelManager$PerProjectInfo.rememberExternalLibTimestamps\\n\\nwhich might ultimately be called by the DelayedSnapshotJob or by the main UI thread refreshing markers. If one of those occur before the call to get the JAR timestamp, then we properly detect that no change has occurred in the JAR. If not, we incorrectly detect that the JAR was recently added to the classpath and subsequently send out a delta.\\n\\nAs a fix for this issue, in JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad we need to explicitly call something that will populate the DeltaProcessingState.externalTimeStamps if not yet done for new projects. One such call that I found was javaProject.getPackageFragmentRoots. When inserting this call right below the line \\n\\n  classpath = javaProject.getResolvedClasspath(); (somewhere around line 3347)\\n\\nthen the callstack \\n\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaModelManager$PerProjectInfo.rememberExternalLibTimestamps\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaProject.buildStructure                   \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.Openable.generateInfos                      \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaElement.openWhenClosed                  \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaElement.getElementInfo                   \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaElement.getElementInfo                   \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaElement.getChildren                    \\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaProject.getPackageFragmentRoots          \\norg.eclipse.jdt.core.JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad                         \\n\\nwas executed in-thread, eliminating the race condition and never generating spurious deltas on the external JARs.\\n\\nIf a fix for this is possible on the 3.4 maintenance stream, that would be best.\\n\\nAs additional background, this is important to us because we are using the deltas to create a Java search scope. We do not need all the runtime JARs in this scope, and doing a search with them in the scope adds about 25 MB to our live heap, forever kept in the JavaModelCache(yes, there are lots of runtime JARs that get added).\\n\\nWe can work around the issue (for example by iterating through the projects and calling getPackageFragmentRoots before we ever call JavaCore.initializeAfterLoad), but I wanted to make sure that the root cause would be fixed going forward, hence this bug.

Summary: [Build path] Problems due to automatic adding/removal of dependent libraries in Eclipse 3.5
Description: User-Agent:       Mozilla/5.0 (Windows; U; Windows NT 5.1; de; rv:1.9.0.13) Gecko/2009073022 Firefox/3.0.13 (.NET CLR 3.5.30729)\\nBuild Identifier: I20090611-1540\\n\\nSince Eclipse 3.5, when I add a dependency (like a local jar file), Eclipse will look up its dependencies from its manifest and add them to the build path too (if found in the same folder I guess).\\nThis is currently causing several negative side effects:\\n\\n1. Setting the source file/folder for the automatically added libraries mixes up the sources, with the result that source code lookup will almost never work. This is already covered by issue 281551.\\n2. When having a library A (from folder AA) on the build path and adding library B (from folder BB) to the build path, the library A from folder BB will be added again (if existing there), so the build path shows two identical libraries, just with different paths.\\n(I cannot even imagine what will happen if the two libraries were different versions!)\\n3. It is confusing that the automatically added libs appear in the package explorer, but not in f.e. the build path or user libraries dialogs.\\n\\nSolutions imho:\\na) Remove this \\"feature\\".\\nb) Make it optional for Eclipse to automatically add/remove dependent libraries to/from build path (probably the best solution)\\nc) Redesign this feature to avoid the mentioned problems.\\n\\nSee following related issues:\\n- Issue 281551: Source attachments wrong for automatically added libraries \\n- Issue 283806: New API is needed to attach source code for referenced jars in the Class-Path: entry\\n\\n\\nReproducible: Always\\n\\nSteps to Reproduce:\\nShould be easy to reproduce from the what I told in \\"Details\\". Should you still need sth., let me know.\\n\\nA good example to play with is the GeoTools library (having a deep hierarchy of libs in one folder)\\nhttp://sourceforge.net/projects/geotools/files/GeoTools%202.5%20Releases/2.5.7/geotools-2.5.7-bin.zip/download\\n\\n\\n\\nI'm filing it as a bug (not enhancement), since for me it is a regression that prevents me from seriously working with Eclipse 3.5. Summary: missing story for attributes of referenced JARs in classpath containers
Description: HEAD\\n\\nCreate a user library and add a JAR with a \\"Class-Path:\\" reference. On the resolved build path, the referenced JAR appears, but IClasspathContainer#getClasspathEntries() does not include the referenced JAR, so clients cannot set attributes (source & Javadoc location) for such JARs.\\n\\nI see 3 possible solutions:\\n\\na) create an IClasspathContainerExtension with a method like on IJavaProject:\\nIClasspathEntry[] getReferencedClasspathEntries().\\n\\nSubclasses of ClasspathContainerInitializer would then need to update their \\nrequestClasspathContainerUpdate(..), etc. so that attributes can be stored by the container.\\n\\nb) treat the referenced JARs like entries referenced from \\"lib\\" entries, and store and retrieve their attributes in the .classpath file as <referencedentry>.\\n\\nc) don't resolve referenced JARs in classpath containers (i.e. let the container implementer deal with this)\\n\\n\\n(a) would need even more API and changes in client code for a feature that's probably rarely used and that can already be implemented by container initializers if they really want it.\\n(b) would somehow defeat the whole purpose of classpath containers as containers that keep state and can e.g. use that information in multiple instances of the same container (since the referenced JARs would still have to be configured in every project).\\n(c) would kill two birds with one stone\\n\\nMy current favorite is (c). Other ideas or opinions?

Summary: [common navigator] Project Explorer not fully updating with jar classpath container changes.
Description: I found this problem while attempting to fix what appeared to a problem with the Web App Libraries classpath container defined in WTP.  This container automatically automatically adds all jars residing in the project's WEB-INF/lib folder.  There is also listening code which reacts to when jars are added or removed from this folder so the container is reset any time a user changes these jars.  The problem I was digging into was if one of the existing jars was replaced (exact same name, but different contents), the container did not seem to update.  Initially, I enhanced the listening code to catch the jar replace scenario and ensure the container was replaced (i.e calling JavaCore.setClasspathContainer with a new instance of the container), this did not fix the classpath problems.  I observed the following when replacing jars handled by this container regardless of whether the container updated (i.e. I observed exactly the same behavior with and without my fixes).\\n\\nMy testcase was to have two jars named \\"stuff.jar\\" one contained the class test.A, the other contained test.B.  My Web App contained two classes, called NeedsA and NeedsB which each extended their respective classes in stuff.jar (so only one of these can actually compile at a time).  Then, I simply dropped one of the stuff.jars in the WEB-INF/lib folder, and then replaced it with the other.\\n\\nFirst, the underlying JDT compile model seems to be correct.  E.g. the markers view shows the correct errors or lack thereof and the package explorer's class label decorators also show those errors or lack thereof.\\n\\nSecond, the editor's markers are stale and stay that way.\\n\\nThird, the contents of the classpath container's jar in the PackageExplorer when the container is expanded and the jar is expanded is also stale and stays that way.\\n\\nUnfortunately, there does not seem to be any workaround for the user, aside from removing and readding the container or closing and reopening the project to bring all aspects of the JDT model back in sync.  JDT should treat jars added by containers exactly the same as jars added directly to the classpath (I performed the same sort of test of replacing stuff.jar when it was added directly to the classpath, and that always seemed to work).\\n\\nThis is a major problem because an adopter built on top of WTP using this container has some tooling which generates/updates jars that reside in the WEB-INF/lib folder.

Summary: Migration guide to 3.6 for containers with MANIFEST-referred entries
Description: This relates to bug 305037.\\n\\nIn 3.5, when a JAR file that is part of a container refers to another JAR through the MANIFEST.MF, those dependencies were resolved and included as part of the project's classpath. However, this is no longer the case from 3.6 as discussed in bug 305037. Those containers that need this kind of dependency to be resolved must do it themselves, probably by using IClasspathContainer#getClasspathEntries() or some other ways.

Summary: Breaking change in classpath container API
Description: For Bug 305037, a behavior change was implemented such that JDT will no longer resolve manifest classpath entries in jars returned by a classpath container. The classpath containers are now expected to resolve manifest classpath themselves if that is desirable.\\n\\nThe issue is not so much the design (whether the classpath container or JDT be responsible for manifest classpath resolution), but rather that this change in behavior affects existing container implementations written against Eclipse 3.5. This is not a theoretical problem. We came across this when debugging an issue in our product (Oracle Enterprise Pack for Eclipse). A classpath container that works on Eclipse 3.5 does not work on latest 3.6 builds. \\n\\nThere is also a side issue of impact on users as the result of this change impacting user libraries container. If a user has a workspace on Eclipse 3.5 and they define user libraries, they may intentionally or accidentally come to rely on manifest classpath resolution on those jars. Such a workspace when loaded in Eclipse 3.6 will not build. It will not be obvious to users what happened and what they need to correct (explicitly add jars pulled in via manifest classpath).\\n\\nI would recommend trying to come up with a safer approach to solving the issue described in Bug 305037. If it is important to give more control over manifest classpath resolution to container then I would recommend adding new API that allows containers to opt-in for resolution suppression.

Creating \\nworking copies for each code assist is also expensive.

Summary: The implementation for IType.resolveType(String) is not implemented as noted in the JavaDoc specs
Description: The interface mentions in its documentation (javadoc) that resolveType()\\n\\"Resolves the given type name within the context of this type (depending \\non the type hierarchy and its imports)\\". But when a call is made to resolve\\na type which is neither in its hierarchy nor its imports (implemented by \\nSourceType), the method\\nreturns all the resolved types for the input in the entire classpath. \\nThis behaviour seems to go against the specification mentioned in the\\ndocumentation of the API, where the expected output for such an \\nunresolveable input should have been a null.\\n\\n\\nIt seems that SourceType, asks the SelectionEngine\\nto find the selection, and that in turn asks the CompilationUnitScope to\\nresolve all types inside the CompilationUnitDeclaration. If any resolution\\nfails, then the NameEnvironment of the JavaProject is used for resolution.\\n\\nThis change in semsntics may be to support the Code Assist.  In any case,\\nthe specs or function needs to be updated.

Summary: Batch Code Generation is not supported
Description: We have a code generation framework that uses the JDT APIs to create and delete \\ncompilation unit elements.  We have the framework setup such that we can \\ngenerate changes while the Java editor is open on a file.  In this case, we \\ngenerate into the open file.\\nWhat we have found is that doing multiple delete elements (e.g., fields and \\nmethods) within the CompilationUnit is extremely slow and it gets worse the \\nlarger the class and the more elements that are updated.  Looking into the \\nproblem, it appears that the save(...) on the WorkingCopy performs a reconcile\\n().  This happens on each and every element add, remove, or update.  This is \\nexpensive and slow.  What we would like is a capability to halt the save on the \\nWorkingCopy by the JavaModelOperations while doing a batch set of changes.  \\nAfter the changes are complete, we would then save all WorkingCopies that have \\nbeen modified and at this time the reconcile will take place.  Basically, we \\nwould only have one reconcile() on a particular WorkingCopy during this batch \\ncodegen instead of possible hundreds.

Summary: [content assist][performance] Guessing auto-complete parameters doesn't yield
Description: When auto-completing a method invocation, e.g. \\"foo.ba\\" [CTRL-SPACE], it seems\\nthat after selecting the desired method (for example, \\"foo.bar(int[] numbers)\\"),\\nand hitting ENTER, it can take an enormous amount of time for Eclipse to return\\ncontrol to the user.\\n\\nIt would seem that once you've selected the method, Eclipse performs an\\nexhaustive search of objects that could be inserted as parameters.  Particularly\\nwhen auto-completing inside anonymous inner classes, I've seen this take upwards\\nof 5 minutes between teh time I hit ENTER and the time when it actually returns\\ncontrol.  It seems that during this time, the exhaustive search thread behaves\\nvery badly - the UI will not repaint (at all) for the duration of the search.\\n\\nSo, two suggestions:\\n\\n1. The thread performing this \\"guess\\" needs to yield every now and then!\\n\\n2. Allow the \\"guess\\" to be cancelled, either in the normal fashion (the cancel\\nbutton at bottom right of the UI) or by hitting escape.  Of course, in the\\nabsence of #1, since the thread is apparently hoarding the event dispatcher or\\nsomething like that, this isn't of much value...

Summary: [assist] package proposals could be unqualified
Description: from bug 188876\\n\\npackage proposals are always fully qualified and could be unqualified.\\n\\nIf the following class is existing\\n\\npackage p1.p2.p3;\\npublic class Foo {}\\n\\n1) the completion of\\n\\nimport p1| // complete at |\\n\\npropose the completion strings\\n'p1.*;'\\n'p1.p2.*;'\\n'p1.p2.p3.*;'\\n\\n2) the completion of\\n\\nimport p1.p2| // complete at |\\n\\npropose the completion strings\\n'p1.p2.*;'\\n'p1.p2.p3.*;'\\n\\nwe could propose instead the completion strings\\n'p2.*;'\\n'p2.p3.*;'\\n\\n3) the completion of\\n\\nvoid foo() {\\n  p1| // complete at |\\n}\\n\\npropose the completion strings\\n'p1'\\n'p1.p2'\\n'p1.p2.p3'\\n\\n4) the completion of\\n\\nvoid foo() {\\n  p1.p2| // complete at |\\n}\\n\\npropose the completion strings\\n'p1.p2'\\n'p1.p2.p3'\\n\\nwe could propose instead the completion strings\\n'p2'\\n'p2.p3'\\n\\n\\nThe completion of package has some specificity \\n- package and subpackage are proposed\\n- jdt/text use completion string as label in the proposals list.\\n  jdt/text could use instead CompletionProposal#getDeclaringSignature() outside an import statement but inside an import statement only the completion string contains the on demand character '*'. \\n\\nSo if we want to propose unqualified package (eg 'p2.p3;*;') \\n- jdt/text should display unqualified package as label 'p2.p3.*;'\\nor\\n- jdt/core should add API to identify on demand imports to allow jdt/text to build the fully qualifed label
