Summary: progress feedback when there are pending search tasks (1G7SVW7)
Description: EG (1/19/01 2:28:03 PM) from a mail conversation\\r\\nDB>\\r\\nYour current implementation more or less duplicates the code in sub progress \\r\\nmonitors since you want to split up progress between indexing and match \\r\\nlocator. Using sub progress monitors has the advantage that\\r\\n\\r\\n- the match locator doesn't need to do the 100% adjustment. Adjusting work \\r\\nunits it what the sub progress monitor is designed for.\\r\\n- the indexer could easily report progress for each pending index job that has \\r\\nbeen finished. But it isn't a big deal to add this support\\r\\n  to the current implementation without using sub progress monitors.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe [search now] button is in my opinion only a solution for the search dialog. \\r\\nBut we are using the search engine in many different places and we don't want to\\r\\nadd extra buttons in all these case (in some situations the dialog isn't even \\r\\nunder our control). Additional situations where we use the search engine are\\r\\n\\r\\n- the browse button in the class creation wizard.\\r\\n- the open type action in the menu bar.\\r\\n- determining the main method if someone presses run / debug.\\r\\n- and some I am not aware of <g>.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe search cancel confirmer is a way to handle all these cases in a uniform \\r\\nway. Since the dialog doesn't differ in the various search situations may be it \\r\\nis a better idea to set a default search cancel confirmer to the search engine \\r\\nwhen the Java plugin is loaded. The avoids the additional parameter in the \\r\\ninterface.\\r\\n\\r\\n  \\r\\n\\r\\nPM>\\r\\n\\r\\nI like solution 2 better. I do not clearly see why you need to subprogress \\r\\nmonitor instead of the one you give us, we could simply change the increments \\r\\nsize when performing some indexing in addition to searching. \\r\\n\\r\\nI also thing the name of this cancel confirmer should rather be: \\r\\nISearchCancelConfirmer, indeed it would cancel the search operation. Indexing \\r\\nwould still be running.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut now I find confusing to be able to cancel a cancel operation... you need to \\r\\nread the dialog multiple times so as to be sure you do not perform the wrong \\r\\naction.\\r\\n\\r\\nI would rather like:\\r\\n\\r\\nOn the search progress, there is a [search now] button which is only enabled \\r\\nwhen indexing is running in background.\\r\\nThen the cancel only cancels the search. If the user does nothing, then it \\r\\nautomatically wait until indexes are ready.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nDB>\\r\\n\\r\\nWe are still facing the problem what to do if we perform a search via the \\r\\nsearch engine \\r\\nand there are still pending indexing jobs in the queue. Attached some ideas \\r\\n\\r\\nAssumptions made for the Java UI.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Java indexing in general is fast.\\r\\n- Most of the time the indexes are up to date because indexing is done in \\r\\nbackground. So if\\r\\n  the user saves a file and presses search the saved file should already be \\r\\nindexed.\\r\\n\\r\\nI see two approaches to fix the problem (they are comparable to the ones \\r\\ndescribed in 1G3T0OO):\\r\\n\\r\\n- if there are any pending index jobs we do the search based on the current \\r\\navailable information. To\\r\\n  inform the user about that situation we add a warning to the message line of \\r\\nthe corresponding dialogs\\r\\n  saying that the current index information isn't up to date. This is \\r\\nequivalent to LeapFrog were the all types\\r\\n  dialog issues a warning if a build is required and therefore the types list \\r\\ncan be incomplete. To do so\\r\\n  we need additional API at SearchEngine to figure out if there are pending \\r\\nindex jobs.\\r\\n\\r\\n- we always wait for any pending index jobs before we do the actual search. In \\r\\nthis situation indexing\\r\\n  should be cancelable. 1G3T0OO proposes to introduce a new progress dialog. \\r\\nBut most of the time\\r\\n  a dialog/window containing a progress monitor is already open when the search \\r\\nengine is started \\r\\n  (e.g. the search dialog, a wizard, or the application window). Instead of \\r\\nopening a new progress dialog\\r\\n  I would do the following: when the user presses the cancel button of the \\r\\nalready present progress dialog\\r\\n  we pop up a second dialog asking what cancel exactly means (see screen shot \\r\\nbelow). Since this\\r\\n  situation should not occur very often (see assumptions above) I think we can \\r\\nlive with the second dialog\\r\\n  popping up. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nTo implement solution two we have change several classes:\\r\\n\\r\\n- IJavaSearchResultCollector: should not manage the progress monitor anymore. \\r\\nThis makes it hard to \\r\\n  use sub progress monitors since the IJavaSearchResultCollector doesn't have \\r\\nany API to set a new\\r\\n  progress monitor. Instead the progress monitor should be passed to the search \\r\\nengine directly.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Inside the search engine we use SubProgressMonitors to allow the indexer and \\r\\nthe MatchLocator to report progress\\r\\n  independently.  The code could look something like this\\r\\n\\r\\n IProgressMonitor locatorMonitor= progressMonitor;\\r\\n IProgressMonitor indexMonitor= null;\\r\\n if (pendingJobs) {\\r\\n  progressMonitor.beginTask(\\"Searching...\\", 100);\\r\\n  indexMonitor= new SubProgressMonitor(progressMonitor, 15); // 15% indexing\\r\\n  locatorMonitor= new SubProgressMonitor(progressMonitor, 85); // 85% match \\r\\nlocating\\r\\n\\r\\n  // do the indexing and pass the indexMonitor to the indexer. The indexer \\r\\nitself\\r\\n  // calls beginTask on the passed indexMonitor with the number of waiting jobs.\\r\\n  // After each job is finised the indexer calls pm.worked(1);\\r\\n }\\r\\n\\r\\n // call the match locator with the locatorMonitor instead of retrieving a \\r\\nprogress monitor from\\r\\n // the java search result collector. Since the locator monitor is independent \\r\\nthe locator doesn't\\r\\n // have to do the 100% adjustment it currently does.\\r\\n\\r\\n- we pass another object to the search engine called IIndexerCancelConfirmer \\r\\n(may be someone comes up with\\r\\n  a better name). The indexer uses this object to decide what exactly to do if \\r\\nthe users presses the normal cancel\\r\\n  button.\\r\\n\\r\\n- JobManager.performConcurrentJob(...) changes like this\\r\\n\\r\\n    case WaitUntilReady :\\r\\n     if (progressMonitor == null)\\r\\n      progressMonitor= new NullProgressMonitor();\\r\\n\\r\\n     int awaitingWork;\\r\\n     IJob previousJob= null;\\r\\n     IJob currentJob;\\r\\n     try {\\r\\n      progressMonitor.beginTask(\\"\\", awaitingJobsCount());\\r\\n      while ((awaitingWork= awaitingJobsCount()) > 0) {\\r\\n       if (progress.isCanceled() {\\r\\n        int result= cancelConfirmer.open();\\r\\n        switch (result) {\\r\\n         case IIndexerCancelConfirmer.ABORT:\\r\\n          throw new OperationCancelException();\\r\\n         case IIndexerCancelConfirmer.FORCE:\\r\\n          break;\\r\\n         case IIndexerCancelConfirmer.CONTINUE:\\r\\n          progressMonitor.setCanceled(false);  // reset that cancel has been \\r\\npressed.\\r\\n        }\\r\\n       }\\r\\n       currentJob= availableJob();\\r\\n       if (currentJob != previousJob) {\\r\\n        if (VERBOSE)\\r\\n         System.out.println(\\"-> performing concurrent job : NOT READY - \\r\\nWaitUntilReady - \\" + searchJob);\\r\\n        String descr= currentJob.toString();\\r\\n        if (awaitingWork > 1)\\r\\n         descr += \\" (\\" + (awaitingWork - 1) + \\" more to go)\\";\\r\\n        progress.subTask(descr);\\r\\n        progress.worked(1);\\r\\n        previousJob= currentJob;\\r\\n       }\\r\\n       try {\\r\\n        Thread.currentThread().sleep(50);\\r\\n       } catch (InterruptedException e) {\\r\\n       }\\r\\n      }\\r\\n    } finally {\\r\\n     progressMonitor.subTask(\\"\\");  // clear message line since it isn't done by \\r\\ndone call.\\r\\n     progressMonitor.done();\\r\\n    }\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nAny comments\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nNOTES:\\r\\nEG (1/19/01 2:29:16 PM)\\r\\n	I propose to improve the wording of the dialog, but to go ahead with \\r\\nthe DB\\r\\n	proposal.\\r\\n\\r\\nDB (06.02.2001 16:42:46)\\r\\n	The proposal is still valid under the new desktop where the progress \\r\\nbar of the application window isn't modal.\\r\\n	Reason:\\r\\n		- actions that somehow trigger a java search aren't executed in \\r\\na separate thread (they are no operations) or\\r\\n		  they are triggered from an already modal dialog (search \\r\\ndialog, wizard, ....). So all windows allocated in the \\r\\n		  thread that handles the action are blocked anyway. So there \\r\\nis no way that the user can use the UI. \\r\\n\\r\\n		  If there are application windows allocated for a different \\r\\ndisplay then the java model must be fully thread save \\r\\n		  anyway.\\r\\n\\r\\n	PM, will JCORE implement the proposed changes.

Summary: document change infrastructure - missing functionality (1GH2DWC)
Description: AK (7/18/2001 4:45:27 PM)\\n	i stumbled across this when doing Reorder Parameters.\\n\\n	consider the following text: m(m(1, 2),3) \\n	lets's say you want to swap the parameters. so your desired output is: m(3, m(2, 1))\\n\\n	you create 4 move entries in the change creator (first 'm' has position 1):\\n		. move(5, 1] -> 7 //moves the first parameter of the inner call\\n		. move[7, 1] -> 5 //moves the 2nd parameter of the inner call\\n		. move [3, 6] -> 10 //moves the first parameter of the outer call\\n		. move [10, 1] -> 3 //moves the 2nd parameter of the outer call\\n\\n		this gets splitted into 4 replaces (will not give details here - see code of AbstractTextBufferChange)\\n	\\n		anyways,	the replaces are sorted backwards before execution.\\n		to cut the story short - you end up with: m(3, m(1, 2))\\n		\\n		the reason is: 	the moves are treated in the same way as replaces. they should not be, if they overlap.\\n		there should a hierarchy of moves - or another way to say: 'this move must be done before that move' \\n		in the case above - the inner moves must be done before the outer ones.\\n\\n		this is quite serious and i'm not sure how to nicely work around it.\\n\\nDB (31.07.2001 15:12:06)\\n	The current change infrastructure doesn't support any kind of overlapping manipulation. So this is somehow\\n	by design. What you can do is to create two distinct text changes. The first changing m(1,2) to m(2,1) and a second\\n	one changing m(m(2,1), 3) to m(3, m(2,1)).\\n\\nDB (08.08.2001 14:50:58)\\n	I opt to not fix this PR since creating two document changes fixes the problem, although it is not optimal from a speed\\n	point of view (the document gets read two times).\\n\\n	May be with an improved IBuffer implementation (see 1GEJ61L) the speed trade off isn't a problem anymore.

Today to change the \\nname, they need to by hand do a refactor to rename the instance variable and \\nthe getter method. We would like to have instead on our property sheet the name \\nof the object, and if they change it, we would under the covers go do those two \\nrefactors for them.\\n\\nThese would be great also, along the lines mentioned in the 2.1 plan, that they \\ndon't require saving the file before the change is made. Currently the \\"try\\" template \\ndoes not use printStackTrace() and probably should.

Summary: Resolve end symbol problem in Open Type dialog
Description: Build I20030115\\n\\nHere is the proposal we want to implement (it is pretty much what Randy Hudson \\nproposed):\\n\\nThe user must explicitly disable the adding of the wildcard by using a special \\nend symbol. But instead of using the '.' JDT proposes to use the % character. \\nHere are the reasons:\\n\\n- '.' is used in fully qualified name as a separator. The open type dialog\\n  already supports entering qualified names (e.g. junit.framework.* shows all\\n  types in the framework package). So it will be confusing if we use it as the\\n  end symbol as well.\\n- '$' is used by various Unix tools (grep, ...) to denote the end symbol, but\\n  it is as legal character inside a Java identifier. Some generated classes\\n  inside rt.jar contain a $ character. \\n- so we have to use a character that is not a legal character for Java \\n  identifiers. We tried several operators and we decide to go for the % \\n  since it is easy to recognize and easy to type.\\n\\nI have opened the bug to further track this issue. Please add comments to this \\nbug instead of replying to this post since bugs are easier trackable.

Summary: Refactoring: Undo should manage and display non-fatal problems
Description: In the current code, the way to check that it's still possible to perform an\\nundo of a refactoring action, is to call isValid() on each Changes of the undo,\\nand if at least one answer a fatal error, the undo is no performed.\\nThis is not really flexible, undo should manage warning and non-fatal error too.\\n\\nIn JDT Debug, we have rename participant to update the launch configurations and\\nthe breakpoint when a Java element is renamed.\\nIn the launch configuration case, we currently return a fatal error if the\\nlaunch configuration has been delete, because otherwise the execution of the\\nperform() will fail. But this is no a fatal error, it's just an error. The fact\\nthat we cannot undo this change shouldn't block the user to perform the undo.\\nThis change is not an important one, and things won't stop working because this\\nchange was not undo.\\nAlso, if you modify a launch configuration between a refactoring action and the\\nundo, performing the undo may overwrite these modification. It would be better\\nif we were able to return a warning in case, and let the user decide if he wants\\nto overwrite his modification.\\n\\nTo display those warnings and errors, a dialog like the refactoring preview\\ndialog/page should be perfect.

Summary: JavaBuilder - Missing libraries results in insufficient dependency info (1FWYERT)
Description: While trying to reproduce 1FWSFNS: ITPJCORE:WIN98 - Assertion Failed in javamodel,\\nI did the following:\\n\\n- load RemoteJUnitRunner solution from hydrogen\\n- it builds\\n- result is one error in junit.servletui/HTMLWriter.java\\n  due to missing java.lang.Object\\n- add rt.jar to class path\\n- it rebuilds only HTMLWriter.java, producing HTMLWriter.class\\n- no other .java files are compiled\\n\\nThis is because the compiler aborted early when it detected the missing expected library class.\\nOnly HTMLWriter came back as a result (with proper dependencies).\\nSince the builder doesn't have dependencies for the other units, it can't know to recompile them\\nwhen the missing packages are added.\\n\\nNOTES:\\n\\nPM (6/22/00 2:50:16 PM)\\n	The builder should know it has no build state for the other units.\\n\\nNE (6/22/00 4:32:55 PM)\\n	It does, but it can't necessarily act on this knowledge.\\n	It doesn't know whether the change may fix the problem.\\n	The only alternative is for it to try recompiling every compilation unit with no dependency info\\n	every time there is a change, which would be expensive and may not actually fix the problem.

What appears is that since \\r\\nbuild 101 (when we put in the changes for using incremental deltas from other \\r\\nprojects, as opposed\\r\\n	to my code for binary book-keeping), inter-project dependencies are no \\r\\nlonger sensitive to structural changes in binaries.\\r\\n\\r\\nJW (6/12/01 5:44:15 PM)\\r\\n	How much work is this to bring forward?\\r\\n\\r\\nPM (6/12/01 6:44:15 PM)\\r\\n	I have a naive way to make this work, by changing the code of \\r\\nIncrementalImageBuilder.changedSourceElement(SourceEntry)\\r\\n	in the case of non-source change to mark dependents of the changed \\r\\nbinary for recompile.\\r\\n\\r\\n	This is way too much requesting for recompile... I think the right \\r\\nsolution should be to perform indictments on the binary, but \\r\\n	unfortunately at this point it does not have a builder type or a \\r\\nprincipal structure...\\r\\n\\r\\n	I was looking at a simple way to queue those binary changes for \\r\\nconsiderating them along when the updateState is performed, but\\r\\n	could not figure how to do this easily again. Are we stuck with saying \\r\\nthe bug is there, or can you think of a way to solve this one ?\\r\\n\\r\\nPM (6/13/2001 3:44:30 PM)\\r\\n	NE assesses the bug is real, and there is no easy work-around.\\r\\n	\\r\\n	The naive fix would provide the same behavior as pre101 change. NE \\r\\nsuggested adding a CRC check, but this is already more change than\\r\\n	what we can put in at this point.\\r\\n\\r\\n	I think there should be some deep change to apply to the builder, but \\r\\nthis is post-june.\\r\\n\\r\\n	It should really compile the changed sources, producing some new \\r\\nbinaries, and add the externally changed binaries in the update/indictment loop.\\r\\n	Note: there should not be any need to remember the structure of \\r\\nbinaries in memory, since it would only compute a binary delta upon replacing \\r\\nthe existing class\\r\\n	file.\\r\\n\\r\\n	Those binary deltas would be the only things remembered in memory for \\r\\nthe duration of an incremental build.

Summary: Cross-project builder efficiency issues
Description: In response to another PR (3137), I have been investigating builder performance \\nfor the following scenario:\\n\\n- user has a large workspace, many projects with many interdependencies\\n- user makes a small, localized change\\n- user waits a long time for the build to happen.\\n\\nThe core side was largely guilty for this, as it was naively recomputing deltas \\nas demanded by each builder.  For example, with 70 projects, each project \\ndependent on about 5 other projects, 350 deltas were being generated.  I have \\nmade a number of improvements in core, and the time spent in core code for this \\ncase has dropped from the 30-50% range to under 2%.\\n\\nHowever, I think there are probably similar improvents that can be made on the \\njavabuilder side.  Consider the following case:\\n\\n- A workspace with most of eclipse platform source and tests (65 projects).\\n- Edit a comment in any file in org.eclipse.core.runtime\\n    (which many projects depend on)\\n- Build takes about 2 seconds on a very fast machine.\\n\\nCases like these are very common (if you're on the core team ;), and I'm sure \\nthere is room for improvement.  Much of the time is spent in the following \\nmethods (these numbers are after my core optimizations):\\n\\nJavaBuilder#classpathChanged() (22%)\\nIncrementalImageBuilder#computeAllPackages (23%)\\nIncrementalImageBuilder#computeNamespaceChanges (21%)\\n\\nSum of all time in JavaBuilder (excluding delta comp): 95%

Summary: Duplicate type collisions
Description: Currently when 2 types collide, the collision error is only reported when their \\n2 files are compiled together.\\n\\nThere are several cases with auto-build on when no error is reported.\\n\\nCase #1:\\n- create a file A.java with a public type A and secondary type B, then\\n- create a file B.java with a public type B -> a collision error should be \\nreported\\n\\nCase #1b:\\n- rebuild the entire project from the above testcase so the error exists, then\\n- remove the secondary type B from A.java -> the collision error should be \\nremoved\\n\\nCase #2:\\n- create a file A.java with a public type A, then\\n- create a file B.java with a public type B, then\\n- add a secondary type B to the file A.java -> a collision error should be \\nreported\\n\\nCase #3:\\n- perform all the above testcases with A.java defining only a public type A, \\nand B.java defining a public type B and secondary type A,\\n- the order in which the files are defined can affect which file is tagged with \\nthe collision error\\n\\nThis PR was added to merge several similar cases into one PR.

It will attempt to copy both foo.txt files, one from \\neach source, to the destination folder.\\n\\nThere are two bugs:\\n\\nBug #1: The problem/marker description isn't very helpful. Summary: Build collisions should be non-fatal?
Description: build 20011219\\nSee also http://dev.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=7324\\n\\nThe case is the same, ie:\\n\\n1. Create a java project with two source folders, say src1 and src2\\n2. Add the same file (eg. foo.txt) to each source folder so that you have\\n  MyProject\\n    /bin\\n    /src1\\n      foo.txt\\n    /src2\\n      foo.txt\\n\\n3. Build the project.  It will attempt to copy both foo.txt files, one from \\neach source, to the destination folder.\\n\\nThis results in a fatal build problem(the project doesn't get build).\\n\\nThis is a problem given the builder's overly helpful habit of copying \\neverything from the source folders to the build output folder.  In our specific \\ncase, our new CVS support will create the 'correct' CVS client folder and meta \\nfiles for each directory.  As a result, for projects with multiple source \\nfolders, we will get a case similar to the foo.txt one above, where foo.txt is \\nthe CVS meta files.\\n\\nI assume there will exist cases other than CVS where some client tool that the \\nuser is attempting to apply against the workspace data is creating additional \\nfiles that may collide when copied to the build output folder.\\n\\nWould it be possible to make this a non-fatal error?  A warning would be even \\nbetter.  Since the builder copies files which are not required for the \\nexecution of the program being built, I don't believe we can assume that a \\ncollision disqualifies the build.

Summary: Output folder scrubbing
Description: When scrubbing the output folder, you should only scrub java class files. In a \\nweb application, it is common to put properties files, xml files, etc. in \\nthe /WEB-INF/classes directory for a Tomcat application. \\n\\nWhen you do this, you generally have the classes directory set as the output \\ndirectory, so that Tomcat can pick up and dynamically load changed classes on \\nthe fly.\\n\\nWhen the output directory is set to /WEB-INF/classes directory, the scrubbing \\ndeletes property files, and xml files as well as the java class files.\\n\\nIf you must scrub more than just java .class files, then at least can you make \\nit configurable to be able to exclude file extensions from being scrubbed.\\n\\nGeorge L. Smith\\nPinnacle Corporation

Summary: Scalability problem in compiling classes with default access level
Description: When a project contains classes with a default access level and these classes \\nare contained in files with different names than the class names, the \\ncorrectness of the compilation depends on the number of such classes.\\n\\nI created a test case for it. In order to run it, you need to create two \\nprojects under the same workspace. The first project will contain file \\nGenerator that I used to generate test files for the problem. The name of the \\nproject is not important. Put Generator class (below) into the project and \\ncompile it.\\nThe second project I called package-test. It is the place where generated test \\nfiles will be stored.\\nGenerator class takes one parameter: number of files to create. When you run it \\nwith parameter 10, you will see 10 files created in the project. Compile them \\nand you will not see any compilation error.\\nWhen I ran Generator with parameter 2000 (the default value) and compiled the \\nresult, I got lots of compilation errors that class names cannot be resolved. \\nWhen I repeated the compilation without cleaning, all errors were gone. \\nEven more funny thing happened when I ran Generator with parameter 1000. In \\nthat case, the compiler did not report any error, but the editor for the test \\nfiles did.\\n\\nI don't exclude that the limit for the compiler for such case depends on the \\nmachine configuration. So, you may need to increase the parameter of Generator.\\nI hope my test case will help.\\nIs there any way around the problem?\\n\\n\\n-- file Generator.java --\\nimport java.io.*;\\n\\n\\n/**\\n * \\n * Generates test for package wide classes compilation\\n */\\npublic class Generator\\n{\\n    /**\\n     * \\n     * @param args first argument (optional) is number of files to generate\\n     *             second argument (optional) defines the shift expressed in \\npercents.\\n     */\\n    public static void main(String[] args)\\n    {\\n        int count = 2000;   // Number of classes to generate\\n        int perc= 26;\\n  \\n        String currentDirectory = System.getProperty(\\"user.dir\\");\\n        File generatorDir = new File(currentDirectory);\\n        String directory = generatorDir.getParent() + \\"/package-test/test\\";\\n    \\n        \\n        if(args != null && args.length > 0)\\n        {\\n            count = Integer.parseInt(args[0]);\\n        }\\n        if(args != null && args.length > 1)\\n        {\\n            perc = Integer.parseInt(args[1]);\\n        }\\n        \\n        int shift = perc * count / 100;\\n        try\\n        {\\n            File dir = new File(directory);\\n            if(!dir.exists())\\n            {\\n                dir.mkdirs();\\n            }\\n            \\n            // delete old files\\n            File[] list = dir.listFiles();\\n            for(int i = 0; i<list.length; i++)\\n            {\\n                list[i].delete();\\n            }\\n    \\n            FileReader rd = new FileReader(\\"template.txt\\");\\n            char[] tmp = new char[10000];\\n            int size = rd.read(tmp);\\n            String template = new String(tmp,0,size);\\n            \\n        \\n            \\n            for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)\\n            {\\n                String firstClassName = \\"First_\\" + i;\\n                String secondClassName = \\"Second_\\" + i;\\n                String calledClassName = \\"First_\\" + (i+shift)%count;\\n                String anotherClassName = \\"First_\\" + (i+2*shift/3)%count;\\n                String someClassName =\\"Second_\\" +((i*i)>>10)%count;\\n        \\n                String res = template.replaceAll(\\"FirstClass\\", firstClassName)\\n                    .replaceAll(\\"SecondClass\\",secondClassName)\\n                    .replaceAll(\\"CalledClass\\",calledClassName)\\n                    .replaceAll(\\"AnotherClass\\",anotherClassName)\\n                    .replaceAll(\\"SomeClass\\",someClassName);\\n                \\n                \\n                File file = new File(directory, \\"Test_\\" + i + \\".java\\");\\n                if(file.exists())\\n                {\\n                    file.delete();\\n                }\\n                \\n                file.createNewFile();\\n                FileWriter writer = new FileWriter(file);\\n                writer.write(res);\\n                writer.close();\\n                \\n            }\\n        }\\n        catch (IOException ex)\\n        {\\n            System.out.println(ex);\\n        }\\n\\n    }\\n}

Summary: [builder] Enabling other builders to create a state.dat which the JavaBuilder understands
Description: I would like to be able to create a state.dat within my own builder which the \\njava builder understands.\\n\\nThe reasons/explanation behind this is:\\n\\nMy particular situation is that I'm working on the development of AJDT and\\nwant to allow users to have two projects, A and B, where A depends on B,\\nproject B is an AspectJ project (so contains aspects as well as java\\nclasses) and project A is a normal java project which has a project\\ndependency on project B (via Project > properties > project references).\\n\\nWhat I would like the JavaBuilder to do when it builds project A is\\nunderstand project B. Unfortunately, because project B has an AspectJ\\nbuilder and not a Java one it doesn't have the build state which the java\\nbuilder is looking for. Consequently, java project A doesn't build and has\\nthe \\"please rebuild prerequisite project A first\\" type message. Rebuilding\\nproject B does nothing to help the situation because it doesn't create a\\nvalid state file. (this is all buried in the call to isWorthBuilding() in the \\nJavaBuilder)\\n\\nWe have got around this by forcing a java build first on creation of new\\nAspectJ projects which creates the state file and keeps the java builder\\nhappy. However, there is the one remaining case on a clean checkout of an\\nAJ project from CVS when the creation of the AJ project doesn't go through\\nthis route. An obvious answer is to force it to do this, however, a nicer\\nanswer would be for either the javabuilder to understand that our project\\nis an AJ project and that it can still build, or for us in our AspectJ\\nbuilder to be able to create a state which the javabuilder understands.\\n\\nWe have tried switching the dependencies to be class folder ones, and in this \\ncase everything builds. Unfortunately, not only are there a lot of special \\ncases with class folder dependencies (which are dealt with automatically with \\nproject depenendencies i.e. to do with exporting jars), but also features like \\nfinding references in the workspace don't work. Therefore, keeping the project \\ndependencies (or the dependencies how the user defines them) is the nicest \\n(and cleanest) solution (switching the dependency was advised in bug 56703)\\n\\nIt would be really nice if in the builder within AJDT, we can create a \\nmeaningful state.dat which the java builder understands. That way we could \\ntake advantage of the other nice things the state keeps track of (and not just \\nuse it to keep the java builder happy with project dependencies).\\n\\nThanks, Helen

Summary: Java Project builder doing unnecessary full builds
Description: I am working on a Java project with more than 20000 Java files. Not \\nsurprisingly,\\nit takes a LONG time to build this project from scratch. \\n\\nWe do integration builds weekly and the class files and other artifacts\\nproduced are installed by individual developers. Each individual developer\\ntypically modifies only a few files. Often these files depend on many classes\\nin the larger codebase but the larger codebase does not depend on these\\nchanges.\\n\\nSo, setting up an Eclipse workspace/project(s) for this application is quite\\ntime-consuming because of the initial, complete build. This would perhaps be\\ntolerable except for the fact that, for no apparent reason, during development\\nEclipse appears to repeat the full project/workspace build. As far as I can\\ntell, this is not triggered by large numbers of java files being newer than\\ntheir class files or by large numbers of class files being dependent on a\\nmodified Java file.\\n\\nWhat's needed is a mechanism to insure that builds include *only* the\\nstrictly necessary Java files. It would be very desirable if a mechanism\\ncould be found to speed up initial creation of very large projects like\\nthese. Failing that, however, Eclipse needs to treat the information gleaned\\nfrom the initial build as a \\"precious\\" resource.

Summary: JDT output folder isn't marked "Derived"
Description: The output folder of a java project doesn't have the \\"Derived\\" property.\\n\\nCreate a java project, and set its \\"default output folder\\" to a subdirectory \\nlike \\"bin\\".\\n\\nAdd a java class to the project.\\n\\nSwitch to the Resource Perspective, and you will see that the build created \\na \\"bin\\" directory. If you have a\\nabstract generic class with an inner class and a method that returns an instance\\nof the inner type, such as: \\npublic abstract class Foo<T>\\n{\\n	protected class SomeObject\\n	{\\n\\n	}\\n	abstract SomeObject getSomeObject();\\n}\\nAnd then you override it normally, implementing the abstract method:\\npublic class Bar extends Foo<Baz>\\n{\\n	@Override\\n	SomeObject getSomeObject()\\n	{\\n		// TODO Auto-generated method stub\\n		return null;\\n	}\\n}\\nWhat you get is a compilation error that states that the return type of\\ngetSomeObject is incompatible with the superclass method. Earlier versions (at\\nleast up to M4) would report the error in the editor but run the code. Another\\nthing to note is that when the method is autogenerated in a subclass, an import\\nto SomeObject is created that automatically renders a compilation warning that\\nstates that SomeObject is never used even if it is. \\nTo solve the compilation error, you can qualify the return type of the method in\\nthe subclasses, so this: \\n	@Override\\n	Foo.SomeObject getSomeObject()\\n	{\\n		// TODO Auto-generated method stub\\n		return null;\\n	}\\nwould yield warnings but no errors. \\nSo it seems that there is a problem with qualification of the inner class. I\\nmight be wrong, but I think such a construct should be legal and it does run\\nunder a version 5 JRE. \\nMy apologies if a repeated a report, I searched and couldn't find anything\\nsimmilar. Cheers.

ERROR in d:\\tests_sources\\p\\X.java\\n (at line 8)\\n	int getValue() { return t.value; }\\n	                        ^^^^^^^\\nThe field A.value is not visible\\n----------\\n1 problem (1 error)\\n\\nBut if you keep A inside the same package, but as a public class:\\n\\np/A.java:\\npackage p;\\n\\npublic class A {\\n	int value;\\n}\\n\\nGoing back to the previous declaration of X.\\nThen Eclipse doesn't complain. But technically it is possible that T is a class outside of the package p for which the field value would not be visible.\\nThis test case clearly shows some inconsistencies in the way javac handle this case, but it also shows that the visibility check in Eclipse should be done on the class and the field.\\nI thought it was worth reporting it.

Summary: Compiler fails on valid multiple secondary classes in a java file
Description: This is a tough bug to describe, so my apologies in advance.\\n\\nThe Java language spec allows multiple top-level classes to be written in a single .java file as long as only the main one is public.  For example:\\n\\n--- begin Bob.java ---\\npublic class Bob { }\\nclass BobSecondClass { }\\n--- end bob.java ---\\n\\nIn this example, BobSecondClass is package-private, so it may legally be accessed from other .java files in the same package.\\n\\nI'm currently working with a closed repository that makes use of referencing such secondary package-private classes defined in other .java files.  It compiles without incident with javac, but the Eclipse compiler marks all references to secondary package-private classes with errors (class def not found) after a clean build.  All references are marked with an error - including references to that class in other classes within the same .java file.\\n\\nHowever, it *does* know where the definitions are, because I am able to ctrl-click navigate to the definition.  If I then change the class name and change it back (e.g. adding and deleting a space in the middle of the secondary class name) and then save, the file is compiled correctly and all references elsewhere in the package work as expected.\\n\\nA clean build causes the errors to return, and necessitates a repeat of the workaround.\\n\\nThis bug occurs with Eclipse 3.2M4, as well as 3.1, with all versions of Sun's JDK 1.5 that I've tried (including 1.5.0_05).\\n\\nI have been unable to reproduce the error condition in a new project, but it is a significant headache preventing Eclipse adoption among developers working on our existing code base.\\n\\nPlease don't hesistate to contact me for clarification as necessary.

Summary: Incorrect accessibility check for field reference
Description: The following source should compile:\\n\\nabstract class Base {\\n	private int i;\\n	static void foo() {\\n		Child c = new Child();\\n		c.i = 0; // complains - not accessible\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nclass Child extends Base {}\\n\\njavac accepts this. The JDT rejects the assignment to the field \\"i\\".\\n\\nI don't see anywhere in the spec that the type of the receiver is relevant. JLS3 section 6.6.1 simply says \\"if the member is private, then access is permitted if and only if it occurs within the body of the top level class that encloses the declaration of the member or constructor.\\"\\n\\nThat seems to be the case here. Note that it compiles fine if one just assigns c to another variable say \\"b\\" of type Base. ie:\\n\\nBase b = c;\\nb.i = 1;   //ok\\nc.i = 1;   //not ok

Summary: .class file time-stamps out of sync with .java files
Description: After compiling a .java file, the incremental java builder checks if the new \\nbytecodes are identical to those in the corresponding .class file (it actually \\ndoes a byte-by-byte comparison), and if they are identical, it does not update \\nthe class file.\\n\\nThis leaves the .class file with a time-stamp that is older than the \\ncorresponding .java file, which can confuse external tools like RMIC that rely \\non comparing time-stamps to detect if a file is out-of-date.\\n\\nThe builder should at least update the timestamp on the .class file in this \\ncase.

Summary: Java compiler misses dependency on 'static final' class variables.
Description: The Java compiler is failing to notice a dependency on static final class\\nvariables. When the value of the variable is modified, classes that reference\\nthat value are not recompiled...and are using a stale value of the variable.\\n\\nSynopsis:\\nClass2 defines a 'public static final long' class variable.\\nClass1 uses that statically defined value.\\nIf Class1 is already compiled, and Class2 is modified, then the compiler\\ndoes not notice the dependency, and fails to refresh Class1's compilation.\\nExample:\\n--------------Class1.java----------------------\\npublic class Class1\\n{\\n	static public void main(String[] args)\\n	{\\n		System.out.println(\\"Class1 thinks it is: \\" + \\nClass2.A_MISSED_DEPENDENCY);\\n		new Class2().showMe();\\n	}\\n}\\n--------------------Class2.java------------------\\npublic class Class2\\n{\\n	public static final long A_MISSED_DEPENDENCY = 200;\\n	\\n	public void showMe()\\n	{\\n		System.out.println(\\"Class2 thinks it is: \\" + \\nA_MISSED_DEPENDENCY);\\n	}\\n\\n}\\n-----------------------\\nCompile and execute Class1.main. The following results are shown:\\n-----------------------\\nClass1 thinks it is: 100\\nClass2 thinks it is: 100\\n-----------------------\\nNow, modify the value of Class2.A_MISSED_DEPENDENCY to something else.\\n(I changed it to 200.)\\nNow save and compile Class2 (File | Save) and re-run the program.\\nThe following results will be shown:\\n------------------------\\nClass1 thinks it is: 100\\nClass2 thinks it is: 200\\n------------------------\\nThe compiler failed to detect the dependency that Class1 has on Class2, and\\ndid not recompile Class1. Class1 incorrectly used a stale\\nvalue for Class2.A_MISSED_DEPENDENCY.\\n\\nAdditional Info:\\njava version \\"1.4.1_02\\"\\nJava(TM) 2 Runtime Environment, Standard Edition (build 1.4.1_02-b06)\\nJava HotSpot(TM) Client VM (build 1.4.1_02-b06, mixed mode)

Summary: Performance issues with builder
Description: We are using eclipse 2.1.1 on windows 2000. All our projects reside on a main \\nsamba server including multiple jars, some of them large (e.g. weblogic.jar).\\n\\nBuilding a project (even in increamental build caused by a save operation) is \\nvery time consuming. \\nWe already moved our output directory locally (using linked resource).\\nWe found out that a large portion of the compilation time is spent \\nin \\"ClasspathJar.isPackage\\". In that method all the entries of the jar are read \\nto find what packages are available in the jar to optimize class search later. \\nThe result is cached for further use. The problem is that this cache is local \\nto the compiling project and is cleared after the end of each build!\\nThus for every project built (even if multiple projects are built at once), \\nthis operation is performed, and takes a long long time.\\n\\nAttached is a patch to org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.builder.ClasspathJar that \\ncaches the available packages per jar and reloads only if the modification time \\nhas changed.\\n\\nIn our environment is cause a significat performance improvment.\\n\\n-- Tal Lev-Ami

Summary: Should revisit reference recording
Description: Build 20040506\\n\\nAfter addressing bug 61882, we forced to fault-in type hierarchies of all \\ntypes for which members are further accessed. \\n\\nThus we match javac behavior, and our expectation when doing reference \\nrecording for incremental builds.\\n\\nQuestion: why does the reference recording need to trigger resolution at all ? \\nIt should only collect information about the types which already got resolved \\nduring name resolution. It would be up to the name resolution to trigger the \\nproper initializations. \\n\\nI suspect the faulting-in during reference recording is unnecessary and simply \\nadd unnecessarily to the build state.\\n\\nFix for bug 61882 addresses short term behavior, and compliance to other \\ntools, but we should clarify whether:\\n1- accesses to members should really force to fault-in hierarchies (suspecting \\nthis is just an artifact from javac implementation, and not mandated by the \\nspec).\\n2- we really need the extra information about unresolved supertypes amongst \\ndependencies (providing we disable the faulting-in behavior of (1)).

Description: While trying to fix bug 511676, I came across this difference in behavior between eclipse and javac\\n\\nThe following code is rejected by eclipse but compiles and runs fine using javac\\n\\nimport java.util.function.Consumer;\\n@SuppressWarnings(\\"all\\")\\npublic class X {\\n  private final String text = \\"Bug?\\";\\n  public static void main(String[] args) {\\n    new X().doIt();\\n  }\\n  \\n  private void doIt() {\\n    new Sub();\\n  }\\n  private class Super<T> {\\n	  public Super(String s) {}\\n    public Super(Consumer<T> consumer) {\\n    }\\n  }\\n  private class Sub extends Super<String> {\\n    public Sub() {\\n      super(s -> System.out.println(text));  \\n    }\\n    \\n  }\\n}\\n\\nThis is the same case as reported in bug 446317 comment 0.\\nThere we concluded that because lambda requires access to enclosing instance which is not available in a constructor call, it is illegal to accept this code.\\nHowever, javac captures the argument in the constructor for enclosing instance as outer local in the lambda and thus allows this code to pass, which is nice.\\nNote that the field itself can be accessed directly in the constructor call, via the static synthetic accessor method generated for the field. This tells me that\\nit should be ok to allow this in a lambda as well.\\nI do not know (yet) if there's something in the spec that leads to this behavior or if it's just something javac does. This needs to be investigated and fixed

Summary: Optional compiler warning on use of newer Java API
Description: It would be nice if the Java compiler had an option to generate a warning on the use of an API from a newer Java version. But for one project I have the JDK Compiler compliance level set to 1.4. Summary: [1.8][compiler][lambda] Change ECJ grammar to support JSR 335
Description: The grammar changes to support JSR 335 come under three heads\\nrelative to the JLS7 grammar.\\n\\n(1) Lambda expressions:\\n-----------------------\\n\\nPrimaryNoNewArray:  \\n  LambdaExpression\\n\\nLambdaExpression:\\n  LambdaParameters '->' LambdaBody\\n\\nLambdaParameters:\\n  Identifier\\n  '(' FormalParameterListopt ')'\\n  '(' InferredFormalParameterList ')'\\n\\nInferredFormalParameterList:\\n  Identifier\\n  InferredFormalParameterList ',' Identifier\\n\\nLambdaBody:\\n  Expression\\n  Block\\n\\n(2) Method and constructor reference expressions:\\n------------------------------------------------\\n\\nPrimaryNoNewArray:\\n  MethodReference\\n  ConstructorReference\\n\\nMethodReference:\\n ExpressionName '::' NonWildTypeArgumentsopt Identifier\\n Primary '::' NonWildTypeArgumentsopt Identifier\\n ReferenceType '::' NonWildTypeArgumentsopt Identifier\\n\\nConstructorReference:\\n ClassType '::' NonWildTypeArgumentsopt 'new'\\n\\n\\n(3) Default methods aka Virtual extension methods aka Defender methods\\n \\n(a) Change JLS7 production\\n\\nInterfaceMemberDeclaration:  AbstractMethodDeclaration  ';'\\n\\ninto \\n\\nInterfaceMemberDeclaration:  InterfaceMethodDeclaration';'\\n\\nwhere\\n\\n(b) \\nInterfaceMethodDeclaration:\\n  InterfaceMethodModifiersopt TypeParametersopt Result\\n                      MethodDeclarator Throwsopt InterfaceMethodBody\\n\\nInterfaceMethodModifiers:\\n  InterfaceMethodModifier\\n  InterfaceMethodModifiers InterfaceMethodModifier\\n\\nInterfaceMethodModifier:\\n  Annotation 'public' 'abstract' 'strictfp' 'synchronized'\\n\\nInterfaceMethodBody: 'default' Block';'\\n\\n\\n(c) Change JLS7 production\\nMethodInvocation:\\n  ClassName '.' 'super' '.'\\n          NonWildTypeArgumentsopt Identifier '(' ArgumentListopt ')'\\n\\ninto \\n\\nMethodInvocation:\\n  TypeName '.' 'super' '.'\\n          NonWildTypeArgumentsopt Identifier '(' ArgumentListopt ')'\\n\\n\\n(d) Change JLS7 production\\n\\nAnnotationTypeElementDeclaration:\\n  AbstractMethodModifiersopt \\n            Type Identifier '(' ')' Dimsopt DefaultValueopt ';'\\n\\ninto \\n\\nAnnotationTypeElementDeclaration:\\n  InterfaceMethodModifiersopt\\n            Type Identifier '(' ')' Dimsopt DefaultValueopt ';'\\n\\n\\nI'll shortly post the massage version that uses jikespg notation\\nas well as altered grammar symbols as we use in ECJ grammar so\\nit could be copy + pasted and experimented with.

Summary: [1.8] Compiler should gracefully reject JSR 335 constructs at source levels 1.7-
Description: BETA_JAVA8 top of branch.\\n\\n(1) The following program does not elicit an error message at the\\nmoment, when compiled as a 1.7- project. It should be rejected with\\na message that reads \\"Default methods are available only at source \\nlevel 1.8 or above\\"\\n\\n// -----\\ninterface I {\\n  public void foo() default { System.out.println(\\"Place holder\\"); }\\n}\\n// -----\\n\\n(2) The following program while compiled as a 1.7- project triggers\\nthree error messages:\\n\\n// ---\\nclass X {\\n  X x = () -> 10;\\n}\\n// ----\\n\\n    - Syntax error on token \\")\\", invalid TypeElidedFormalParameter\\n    - Syntax error, insert \\"ElidedSemicolonAndRightBrace\\" to complete \\n      LambdaBody\\n    - Syntax error, insert \\")\\" to complete Expression.\\n\\nIt should emit a single error message saying \\"Lambda expressions are\\navailable only at source level 1.8 or above\\"\\n\\n(3) The following program should be rejected at 1.7-, but is not at \\nthe moment:\\n// ---\\nclass X {\\n  X x = System::exit;\\n}\\n// ----\\n\\n(4) The following program generates the message \\"Syntax error on token\\n COLON_COLON, delete this token\\", it should instead complain that\\n\\"Reference expressions are available only at source level 1.8 or above\\"\\n\\n(2) & (4) are a bit tricky in that, at source levels 1.7-, for performance\\nreasons we don't look ahead in the token stream to disambiguate between \\nthe different uses of the tokens '(' and '<'. That means that we don't build\\na parse subtree for these constructs at 1.7- levels. So the parser will\\nsee a badly mangled program and that could result in a slew of errors as\\nin case (2) above.\\n\\nOne strategy is to recognize the operators '::' and '->' which are\\nreturned as tokens at any source level and issue the \\"available at\\nsource level 1.8+\\" messages upon encountering these tokens. Summary: [1.8][compiler] Running alternate parser/scanner in reconnaissance mode could add rigor.
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nAs discussed in bug 380194, JSR335 introduces a number of complexities\\nand challenges in parsing the new constructs. The grammar could very well\\nbe intrinsically non-LALR(1) (not ascertained as of now). \\n\\nThe current solution depends upon tight collaboration between the \\nparser & scanner - in particular the scanner is responsible for \\ndisambiguating on demand (normal parser) or always (Diagnose parser) \\nthe usages of certain overloaded tokens.\\n\\nThis disambiguation is achieved by looking ahead in the input stream as \\nmany tokens as necessary to discern the presence/absence of certain \\nsignature tokens like \\"->\\" and \\"::\\" and heralding these tokens well \\nahead of time to the parser by injecting certain synthetic tokens.\\n\\nThis look ahead is implemented at the moment all in the scanner by\\nleveraging the pre-existing and well tested jumpOverMethodBody() method.\\nWhile it works well for the lambda parameter list case, it is a bit\\nclunky when used to determine if we are at the head of a reference\\nexpression.\\n\\nThe current bug is to develop a completely new look ahead mechanism\\ndriven by a new abstractions called VanguardParser and VanguardScanner\\nthat will eliminate all traces of kludginess from the current solution\\nand provide an alternate mechanism with full rigor.\\n\\nThe idea is that when the scanner sees a '(' and would like to\\ndisambiguate this usage of '(' to determine if it is starting a\\nlambda parameter list, it would a launch a new parser and scanner\\npair at the current cursor position with the parser's explicit\\ngoal state set to the nonterminal ParenthesizedLambdaParameterList.\\nThe new Parser/Scanner operate in a parallel universe i.e they don't\\nshare any state with the original parser/scanner. If the new parser\\nenters ACCEPT_STATE when given the explicit goal of reducing \\nParenthesizedLambdaParameterList, we surely know we are at the head\\nof a lambda parameter list - it can't get better than that !\\n\\nPros:\\n\\n    - Very structured, maximally rigorous solution.\\n    - Much smaller implementation that the prior one.\\n    - Much more maintainable solution.\\n    - Will fail early when it should - it is guaranteed that the\\n      LALR(1) automaton will signal error at the first erroneous\\n      token. Prior implementation suffered from the drawback that\\n      it could look ahead several tokens well after the point of\\n      first error to fail.\\n    - Current work does not handle annotations in some places.\\n      JSR 308 introduces annotations all over the place. So a\\n      reference expression could look like:\\n      X<@Blah String>. @BlahBlah Y<@Foo Integer> @DimAnnot []::goo;\\n      By using a scouting parser driven by the exact same grammar \\n      rules as the normal parser ensures we handle all cases seamlessly.\\n\\nPatch will follow shortly.

Description: BETA_JAVA8: \\n\\nThe following compiles alright with Lambda JDK8b56, but fails\\nto compile on Eclipse top of beta8 branch. I believe the right\\nbehavior is to compile this fine. As Map's method replaces MapStream's\\nasIterable(), at X, only the more immediate method should be seen\\nthus eliminating any chance of a clash.\\n\\nHowever, the current code leaves in MapStream's method also\\nperhaps under the influence of https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=302358: Essentially we should not skip the inherited method if any \\noverriding version in a subclass may have a different erasure.\\n\\nIn the present case since Map and MapStream are isomorphic with pass-through\\nparameterization, it is kosher to eliminate MapStream's method.\\n\\n// ----\\npublic interface X extends Map {\\n}\\n\\ninterface Map<K,V> extends MapStream<K, V>  {\\n	Iterable<BiValue<K, V>> asIterable() default {\\n		return null;\\n	}\\n}\\ninterface MapStream<K, V> {\\n	Iterable<BiValue<K, V>> asIterable();\\n}\\n\\ninterface BiValue<T, U> {\\n    T getKey();\\n    U getValue();\\n}

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Redesign ECJ grammar for type annotations support - JSR 308
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nWhile working on adding support for type annotations on nested qualified \\ntype names (bug 383596), it has become clear that the existing grammar\\nchanges done for 308 support are too complicated to work with and problem\\nprone. This bug will be used to document/track a brand new design that has\\nbeen prototyped that is very clean, elegant and orders of magnitude \\nsimpler. \\n\\nBasically, type annotations are recognized as type annotations in some \\nplaces in the present grammar and as modifiers in other places to satisfy\\nthe parser generator's requirement on the LALR(1)'ness of the input grammar. \\n\\nAs a result,\\n\\n    -  If we stack type annotations purely in the expression stack as we\\ndo for Java SE5 annotations, they get interspersed with other expressions \\nand some of the code is not prepared to handle such interleaving and will \\nlook ugly if changed. Maintaining type annotations in a separate stack\\naltogether was not possible with the present design since they are \\nrecognized as modifiers in certain parts of the grammar - So type \\nannotations end  up in the expression stack at times and in type \\nannotation stack at others. This greatly complicates the decoration of\\nAST nodes in a clean and consistent fashion - leading to a lot of \\ncode clutter.\\n\\n    - Signalling the absence of type annotations becomes very difficult in\\nsome places in the grammar: We need a non-terminal that reduces to epsilon\\nso we can attach a semantic action method to the production to push zero\\non the type annotation length stack, but empty productions can and do trigger\\nvarious conflicts when placed in the \\"right\\" location. This forces us to\\nplace them on occasions well after where they should be - sometimes well \\nafter other annotations are encountered. This causes us to violate the \\nstack protocol by having to push at locations other than the top of stack: \\nbasically unstack various items, push and restack - not a happy situation.\\n\\n    - In those locations where type annotations are recognized as modifiers,\\nthe language accepted by the parser is no longer conformant and call for\\nconstraining downstream by pruning the illegal programs (see bug 385293).\\nThis problem is not a blocker in itself and is also integral to the \\nalternate solution that has been prototyped, but is present only in a \\nvery non-virulent form in the new design (modifiers are not stacked, \\nneed to be retrieved before they evaporate  - see https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=385293#c4).\\n\\nThe new design starts with simple modifications to allow type annotations \\n*at the grammar level* before *any* type production in the grammar. Starting\\nfrom the observation that any type reference in Java must start\\nwith either a primitive type or a simple name, we can now proceed by \\ntweaking the relevant productions (shown somewhat simplistically, but \\nmaterially truthfully):\\n\\nPrimitiveType ::= TypeAnnotationsopt PrimitiveType\\nName ::= TypeAnnotationsopt SimpleName\\nName -> TypeAnnotationsopt QualifiedName\\nQualifiedName ::= Name '.' TypeAnnotationsopt SimpleName\\n\\nSince *all* other productions that describe various flavors of type\\n(ClassType, InterfaceType, ClassOrInterfaceType, ClassOrInterface,\\nGenericType, ArrayType ...) are composed of PrimiveTypes and Names\\nthese simple rules automatically ensure that *every use of a type* \\ncan be annotated with JSR308 style annotations without wholesale \\nchanges all over the place. \\n\\nTwo details need mention:\\n\\n(1) The specifications forbids type annotations in some places - in those \\nplaces the grammar would be seen to be too permissive - these cases are\\nhandled straighforwardly by rejecting the annotations if present in the \\nAST construction phase.\\n\\n(2) Such a change would make JSR308 annotations permissible at places\\nwhere SE5 annotations are acceptable - In the design this is handled\\nby feedback from the parser to the scanner using the machinery put in\\nplace for JSR335 support (See bug 380194 and bug 385009) so that in\\nplaces where SE5 annotations are legal, the scanner is able to discriminate\\nand scan and hand out a SE5 annotation to the parser.\\n\\nPatch to follow shortly.

[1.8][spec] Can a lambda throw exceptions when the throws clause of descriptor mentions a type variable ?
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nThis bug is to record & track a clarification request to the 335 EG:\\n\\n// ---- 8< -------\\n\\nThe following lambda expression does not compile with 8b74, while the \\nimplementation of the method in a class does compile: \\n\\n// ------------ \\ninterface G1 { \\n  <E extends Exception> Object m(E p) throws E; \\n} \\ninterface G2 { \\n  <F extends Exception> String m(F q) throws Exception; \\n} \\ninterface G extends G1, G2 {} \\n\\n// G has descriptor <F extends Exception> ()->String throws F \\n\\npublic class X { \\n        \\n        G g = (x) -> { // Elided type is inferred from descriptor to be F \\n            throw x;    // ~== throw new F() \\n        }; \\n} \\n\\nclass Y implements G { \\n        public <T extends Exception> String m(T t) throws T { \\n                throw t; \\n        } \\n} \\n// ----------------------- \\n\\nIs this a bug in the implementation or the specification ? \\nSince the lambda cannot refer to the type variables of the \\ndescriptor by name nor declare its own, if 8b74 behavior is \\ncorrect, that would mean that, no checked exceptions could \\nbe thrown from a lambda if the descriptor of the target \\ninterface method mentions a type variable in throws clause. \\n\\nMy analysis is that the lambda should be accepted as it does \\nnot manufacture any fresh exceptions and simply throws an \\nexception that is known to have satisfied the constraints at \\nthe invocation site, i.e no additional/unexpected surprises \\nare there due the lambda throwing the object it was handed.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] @FunctionalInterface annotation should only be allowed on functional interfaces

Summary: [1.8][spec] Broken example in 9.8, discussion box - bullet 2 ?
Description: 0.6.1 - 9.8, Discussion & motivation box, second bullet says:\\n\\n// --------8< -----------------\\n\\n\\nUnder the current definition, a functional interface may be parameterized in a way that produces distinct abstract methods—that is, multiple methods that cannot be legally overridden with a single declaration. For example: \\ninterface I { Object m(); }\\ninterface J<S> { S m(); }\\ninterface K<T> { T m(); }\\ninterface Functional<S,T> extends I, J<S>, K<T> {}\\nInterface Functional is functional—I.m is return-type-substitutable for the other two—but Functional<String,Integer> clearly cannot be implemented with a single method. This situation is acceptable, however: when functional interfaces are implicitly implemented, the overriding effectively occurs generically; instantiation of type parameters only occurs at the use site. In other words, if a lambda expression represents a Functional<String,Integer>, its treatment is similar to that of the following: \\nclass FunctionalImpl<S,T> implements Functional<S,T> { ... }\\nFunctional<String,Integer> f = new FunctionalImpl<String,Integer>();\\n\\n// --------8< -----------------\\n\\nI think this part needs a careful relook - Both javac 8b74 and eclipse refuse to compile this snippet *precisely* for the reason that certain parameterization could run into unrelated  return types.\\nErgo, `Functional' is not even a legal interface - let alone a functional interface.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Visibility checks are missing for lambda/reference expressions.
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nThe following program compiles silently with HEAD:\\n\\n// ---- X.java\\nimport p.I;\\n\\npublic class X {\\n	I i = (p) -> { return null; };\\n}\\n// ---- I.java\\npackage p;\\npublic interface I {\\n	ReturnType doit(ParameterType p) throws ExceptionType;\\n}\\n\\nclass ReturnType {\\n}\\n\\nclass ParameterType {\\n}\\n\\nclass ExceptionType extends Exception {\\n}\\n// ----------------------\\n\\nIt should report three errors, one each about ReturnType, ParameterType\\nand Exception type as they are not visible at the lambda definition site.\\n\\nInterestingly javac 8b74 complains:\\n\\nX.java:6: error: ParameterType is not public in p; cannot be accessed from outsi\\nde package\\nX.java:4: error: ParameterType is not public in p; cannot be accessed from outsi\\nde package\\n        I i = (p) -> { return null; };\\n              ^\\n2 errors\\n\\n// ----\\n\\nHere is the relevant wording:\\n\\n For each checked exception that can result from execution of the body of the lambda expression, a compile-time error occurs unless that exception type or a supertype of that exception type is mentioned in the throws clause of the descriptor of T'.\\n\\n It is a compile-time error if any class or interface mentioned by either T' or the descriptor of T' is not accessible from the class in which the lambda expression appears.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Overhaul overload resolution to reconcile with JLS8 15.12.2

Summary: [1.8][spec] Clarification required on how raw types interact with interface descriptor computation.
Description:
0.6.1 9.8 is silent about descriptor computation in the presence of raw types.\\nIs this specified somewhere else ? Discouraged though this scenario may be, \\nwe can expect to run into this sooner or later, intentionally coded or otherwise.\\n\\nThe reference compiler at 8b74 seems to erase the descriptor as seen by the\\nfollowing program: This seems reasonable from one pov. From another, this is\\nsomewhat at odds with the ban on lambdas implementing generic methods in that,\\nin both cases we have (or are likely to have) unadaptable type variable usage in\\nvarious constituents of the descriptor. And the target type is raw in one case\\nand the lambda is \\"raw\\" in the other case (by virtue of there being no grammar\\nsupport for type parameter encoding)\\n\\nI am happy erasing the descriptor, but (a) should this stay unspecified if it indeed\\nis and (b) does the inconsistency in treatment with generic lambdas OK ?\\n\\n// ---\\nimport java.util.List;\\ninterface I {\\n void foo(List f);\\n}\\n\\nclass Y {\\n void goo(I f) {\\n }\\n}\\n\\nclass Z {\\n void zoo(I f) {\\n }\\n}\\npublic class X {\\n public static void main(String [] args) {\\n new Y().goo((List ls) -> {}); // Compiles OK with 8b74\\n new Z().zoo((List ls) -> {}); // OK\\n }\\n}\\n\\n--------------------\\n\\nTo see the correlation between generic lambdas and raw types in target type\\nstudy this program in which 8b74 is inadvertently allowing a generic lambda\\nsince it does not see the descriptor as being generic due to erasure:\\n\\n// -----\\nimport java.util.List;\\ninterface I {\\n

P foo(List f);\\n}\\n\\nclass Y {\\n void goo(I f) {\\n }\\n}\\n\\nclass Z {\\n void zoo(I f) {\\n }\\n}\\npublic class X {\\n public static void main(String [] args) {\\n new Y().goo((List ls) -> { return null; }); // Fails: descriptor is generic \\n new Z().zoo((List ls) -> { return null; }); // compiles fine, we are overriding a generic method with another that has no type variables!!\\n }\\n}

Summary: [1.8][spec] Are arrays allowed in intersection casts ?
Description: A while ago, in the context of the method/constructor reference expression\\ngrammar changes, it was pointed out that JLS7 has two definitions of \\nReferenceType in different chapters: one that includes arrays and one \\nthat doesn't. We said that the one that includes arrays is the right one to \\nuse for parsers.\\n\\nIt appears that this split-personality could be influencing 8b74's behavior in\\nrejecting the snippet below:\\n\\n// ----\\nimport java.io.serializeable;\\npublic class X {\\n    X [] x = (X[] & Serializable & Cloneable) new X[0];  // error: unexpected type, required class, found X[]\\n}\\n\\nI cannot think of a non-pedantic case where this should matter, calling it \\nout and tracking it just the same in case I missed some subtleties.

Summary: [1.8][spec] Various issues in specification of method/constructor references.
Description: (1) 0.6.1, 15.28 says: \\n\\n\\"It is a compile-time error if the ClassType of a constructor reference denotes a class that is an enum type or that is abstract. \\" \\n\\nWhile JLS7 15.9 in addition says: \\n\\n\\"It is a compile-time error if any of the type arguments used in a class instance \\ncreation expression are wildcard type arguments (§4.5.1).\\" \\n\\nSo is the less restrictive version with constructor references intentional ? I don't see anything in \\nthe design/motivation section regarding this to determine if it is. \\n\\nI would like to use one definition of what can be instantiated unless the relaxation is deliberate. \\n\\nSo, should the following program compile ? \\n\\n// --- \\ninterface I { \\n  X<?> zoo(int x, String p); \\n} \\npublic class X<T> { \\n        X(int x, String p) {} \\n        I i = X<? extends String>::new; // will compile \\n      X<?> x = new X<? extends String>(); // will not compile. \\n} \\n\\nI don't see a type safety issue here since the parameterization would have pass bounds check, only a consistency issue. \\n\\n(2) And since the production for ClassType (despite the name) cannot prune type variables and \\nannotation types, should these also be called out as error scenarios ? \\n\\n(3) Should the (obvious) point about primary evaluating to base type being a forbidden scenario \\nbe mentioned ? \\n\\n(4) \\"The immediately enclosing instance of an inner class instance (15.9.2) must be provided for a constructor reference by a lexically enclosing instance of this (8.1.3). \\" \\nIs this restrictive ? Can this be supplied at method invocation time or even via a primary from ? Implementable != useful and \\nI don't have an assessment as to how useful practically it would be though. Again this is a consistency issue: the call to \\nnew Inner() can occur outside of the enclosing class in an entirely unrelated class as long as there an enclosing instance is \\navailable and the types are visible.

Summary: [1.8][spec] Clarification required on computation of compile time declaration for a method reference
Description: (1) 0.6.1, 15.28.1 reads: \\n\\n----------------------- \\nGiven a function descriptor with parameter types P1..Pn, the compile-time declaration for a method reference is determined as follows. \\n\\nIf the method reference is qualified by a ReferenceType, two searches for a most-specific applicable method are performed, following the process outlined in 15.12.2. Each search may produce a method or, in the case of an error as specified in 15.12.2, no result. \\nFirst, the reference is treated as if it were an invocation of a method named by Identifier with argument expressions of types P1..Pn; the type to search is the ReferenceType; the type arguments, if any, are given by the method reference. \\n\\nSecond, if P1..Pn is not empty and P1 is a subtype of ReferenceType, the reference is treated as if it were an invocation of a method named by Identifier with argument expressions of types P2..Pn. If the ReferenceType is a raw type, and there exists a parameterization of this type, G, that is a supertype of P1, the type to search is G; otherwise, the type to search is the ReferenceType. Again, the type arguments, if any, are given by the method reference. \\n\\nIf both of these searches match a method, the reference is considered ambiguous. \\n\\nOtherwise, if the first search matches an instance method or the second search matches a static method, no method is chosen. \\n\\nOtherwise, if one of the searches matches a method, that is the compile-time declaration. \\n---------------------------- \\n\\nThe first mention of static occurs in the penultimate sentence of the quoted text: Does that mean the following program \\nshould be declared ambiguous ? (8b74 compiles this fine, but at run time there is an NPE) - There is no real ambiguity here. \\n\\n// ---- \\ninterface I { \\n  void zoo(Y y, String s); \\n} \\n\\nclass Y { \\n        void zoo(String s) { \\n                System.out.println(\\"Y.zoo(String)\\"); \\n        } \\n        void zoo(Y y, String s) { \\n                System.out.println(\\"Y.zoo(Y, String)\\"); \\n        } \\n} \\n\\n\\npublic class X  { \\n    public static void main(String[] args) { \\n            I i = Y::zoo; \\n            i.zoo(null,  null); \\n        } \\n} \\n// ----------- \\n\\nI think this calls for a reordering of clauses and perhaps some rewording ? \\nThe sentence \\"Otherwise, if the first search matches an instance method or \\nthe second search matches a static method, no method is chosen.\\" is a bit \\nvague ? i.e does this mean \\"No method is chosen as the compile declaration \\nof the method reference\\" or that \\"these matches are eliminated from further \\nreckoning ?\\" \\n\\nAlso the sentence \\"If both of these searches match a method, the reference \\nis considered ambiguous.\\" preceding the first utterance of 'static' would \\nrender the program above illegal. \\n\\nOr reword the passage \\"First, the reference is treated as if it were an \\ninvocation of a method\\" to \\"First, the reference is treated as if it were an \\ninvocation of a _static_ method\\" and likewise massage the second part too ? \\n\\n(2) Should the passage \\"Also note that static method invocations have the form TypeName.method(), \\nwhile here we're using the more general ReferenceType; an error occurs if the reference ends up being a \\nstatic method reference and the qualifier is a parameterized type.\\" be relegated to the motivation box ?

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Allow lambda expressions in non-overloaded method invocation contexts
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n-----------\\n\\nWhile the broader issue of overload resolution is the subject matter\\nof bug 400871, we can already enable lambda/reference expressions in\\nnon-overloaded scenarios : i.e where we have just a single candidate\\nmethod that is both potentially applicable and applicable under one\\nof strict, loose or variable arity invocation. This would enable us\\nto compile the following program which fails to compile as of now:\\n\\n// ---\\ninterface I {\\n    void foo();\\n}\\npublic class X {\\n\\n  void foo(I i) {\\n    System.out.println(\\"foo\\");\\n  }\\n	\\n  public static void main(String[] args) {\\n    new X().foo(()->{}); // incorrect complaint about non-functional interface.\\n  }\\n}\\n// -----\\n\\nThis solution would also outline how the concern raised in\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=382701 could be\\nreadily addressed and can serve as a sketch for how the overall\\noverload resolution problem is planned to be tackled.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Explore solutions with better performance characteristics than LambdaExpression#copy()
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nAs outlined in https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=400874#c12,\\nin order to determine whether a lambda is compatible with a type T from\\nits context, we need to compute the set of all \\"results expressions\\". These\\nare the types of the expressions in return statements of the lambda body\\nin all possible paths of execution.\\n\\nComputing this set requires us to traverse the lambda more than once,\\none time each for possible target types from an overloaded call context.\\n\\nThe present solution adopted is from https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=400874#c18. While this is a super clean solution, it is not also super\\nefficient. The method LambdaExpression#isComptaibleWith is coded to\\nminimize the copies - for example if the lambda is not even potentially\\napplicable, we will not traverse it multiple times. Another opportunity\\nis for isComptaibleWith to always return true, IFF we are in a INVOCATION_CONTEXT\\nbut not in an overload resolution scenario (i.e singleton potentially\\napplicable method) - this could allow resolution to succeed where it should\\nnot, but the error will surface itself during resolve.\\n\\nEven better solutions could exist - This bug is to explore them.

Summary: [1.8][compiler][infrastructure] Implement Expression.tIsMoreSpecific(TypeBinding t, TypeBinding s)
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nThe most specific applicable overloaded method resolution in Java8 differs from \\nJava 7 in that it is not just a pair wise comparison of methods as in the case\\nof Java 7. Summary: [1.8][spec] JSR308 should restrict position of TYPE_USE annotations in BodyDeclaration modifiers
Description: JSR308 should restrict the position of TYPE_USE annotations in BodyDeclaration modifiers, so that all TYPE_USE annotations must be placed at the end of the modifiers list.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\npackage jsr308.bug;\\n\\nimport java.lang.annotation.ElementType;\\nimport java.lang.annotation.Target;\\n\\n@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)\\n@interface NonNull { }\\n\\npublic class Bug {\\n	@Deprecated @NonNull String s  = new @NonNull String();\\n	@NonNull @Deprecated String s2 = new @NonNull String();\\n}\\n\\nA declaration like \\"@NonNull @Deprecated String\\" is hard to understand for Java programmers. It doesn't make sense to allow the TYPE_USE annotation to occur anywhere in the modifiers list. Unlike e.g. an ElementType.FIELD annotation, a TYPE_USE annotation is not a general modifier of the body declaration. A TYPE_USE annotation always belongs to the following type, so it should also be right in front of the type in the source.

Summary: [1.8][dom ast] Move TYPE_USE annotations from the modifiers list to the type
Description: Spawned from bug 403816. This bug is about the DOM AST representation of TYPE_USE annotations.\\n\\nNote that this proposal can only be implemented if bug 403816 is fixed as requested. Otherwise, picking annotations from the middle of the modifiers list is a no-go, since that would violate the parent-child containment rules of the AST nodes.\\n\\n(In reply to bug 403816 comment #3)\\n> Where a type annotation occurs in a SE7 annotation location, unless binding\\n> resolution is requested, the compiler cannot discriminate between a type\\n> annotation and a declaration (i.e SE 7) annotation.\\n> \\n> During resolve, the compiler can hypothetically transfer the type annotation\\n> to\\n> the type reference - but this goes back to the question we earlier discussed\\n> about it whether clients can cope with parse trees that could look different \\n> based on whether bindings are being resolved or not. (See\\n> https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c33)\\n\\nWithout a classpath, it's indeed impossible to know which annotations belong to the method/field/localVariable declaration and which annotations belong to the type. This is reflected by the ambiguities in the Java grammar, where the same annotation can either come from a 'Modifier' or 'VariableModifier' production, or it can be part of a 'Type' production that follows the modifiers.\\n\\nIn bug 391847, the annotations on Name nodes would have had a huge impact on clients of the AST API. Here, the impact is much smaller. I don't think we should try to guess the classpath and try to do partial resolution in ASTs without bindings.\\n\\nI would just go with these simple rules:\\n- By default, all annotations go into the modifiers list.\\n- If bindings are requested, then TYPE_USE annotations at the tail of the modifiers list are transferred to the declaration's type.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Misattribution of annotations with C style array declarations
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nWe just ran into this testing APT changes for JSR308.\\n\\nGiven:\\n\\n// ---\\nimport org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.NonNull;\\nimport org.eclipse.jdt.annotation.Nullable;\\n\\n\\npublic class X {\\n	int @Nullable [] f @NonNull [] = null; \\n}\\n// ----\\n\\n\\non the compiler side, when incorrectly fold the extra dimensions into total \\ndimensions and end up with \\n\\nint @Nullable [] @NonNull [] f;\\n\\nIt should be \\n\\nint @NonNull [] @Nullable[] f;\\n\\nSince in a C style array declaration, the extra dimension should bind\\nmore readily with the field than any type components preceding it.\\n\\nWhile the compiler side story is easy to fix, it will break DOM/AST encoding\\nunless care it taken: some original dimensions could start showing up as\\nextra dimensions and vice versa !\\n\\nI think it is not hard to fix cleanly end to end. I'll see what can be done.

Summary: [1.8][APT] Element.getAnnotation and Element.getAnnotationsByType are ignoring inherited annotations
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nElement.getAnnotation() should return the annotations present on an element.\\n\\nAn annotation A is present on a construct C if either:\\n◆ A is directly present on C; or\\n◆ No annotation of A's type is directly present on C, and C is a class, \\nand A's type is inheritable (§9.6.3.3), and A is present on the superclass of C.\\n\\nElement.getAnnotationsByType() should return all annotations associated with\\nan element:\\n\\nAn annotation A is associated with a construct C if either:\\n◆ A is directly or indirectly present on C; or\\n◆ No annotation of A's type is directly or indirectly present on C, and \\nC is a class, and A's type is inheritable (§9.6.3.3), and A is associated \\nwith the superclass of C.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Delayed assignment of declaring scope for arguments creates a race condition.
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nStaring at LocalVariableBinding.getAnnotations(), I see that there is a potential\\nrace condition there: The setting of declaringScope happens far away from the\\ncreation of LVB and if there are calls in between to getAnnotations(), we can't\\nretrieve it from the annotation holder since this requires a handle to enclosing\\nsource type which is obtainable only from a scope. \\n\\nTo circumvent this, there is a block of code in this method that manufactures\\nan array of annotation bindings and returns it without going to the holder.\\nHowever, this is problematic since with Java 8 some of the annotations could\\nactually be type annotations which should be detached from the parameters.\\n\\nThis block of code itself cannot filter the type annotations because there are\\nclients that need to see all the annotations to transfer the type annotations \\nto type.\\n\\nI think the solution is to set the declaring scope eagerly. At least for arguments,\\nI don't know what side effects ensue for doing this for all locals.\\n\\nPatch will follow shortly.

Description: BETA_JAVA8\\n----------\\n\\nAn earlier draft of JSR 335 required the compiler to eliminate overloaded\\nmethod candidates based on whether the choice of that method would trigger\\nerrors in lambda body.\\n\\nThe latest draft has eliminated this requirement. Summary: [1.8][compiler] Implement shape analysis as a preliminary pass.
Description: BETA_JAVA8: \\n\\nEarlier drafts of JSR335 required the lambda body to be type checked and analysed\\nover and over for every potentially applicable method. The latest draft has done\\naway with this requirement, but we still need some information about the lambda\\neven in the absence of target type in invocation contexts.\\n\\n    - Is a lambda value-compatible or void compatible or both ?\\n    - Is a lambda explicitly typed or not ? If the former, what are its\\n      parameter types ?\\n    - What are the return expressions of the lambda ? Is one or more of them\\n      pertinent to applicability ?\\n\\nFor reference expressions,\\n\\n    - Is a reference expression an exact one or an inexact one.\\n\\nThis ER is to implement a preprocess step in INVOCATION_CONTEXT's to\\ngather this information.\\n\\nAs part of this, we should be able to reenable the two tests that were\\ndisabled namely:\\n\\nNegativeLambdaExpressionsTest._test401610h\\nNegativeLambdaExpressionsTest._test401610i
