Summary: [1.8][assist] Code assist issues with type elided lambda parameters
Description: BETA_JAVA8:\\n\\nAt present, there are a set of problems in the way type elided lambda parameters\\nare handled by SelectionEngine/SelectionParser. Similar but different issues \\nexist with CompletionEngine/CompletionParser too.\\n\\nGiven:\\n\\n// --\\ninterface I {\\n	String foo(String x, Integer y);\\n}\\npublic class X {\\n	static void foo(I i) {}\\n	public static void main(String[] args) {\\n		foo((x, y) -> x + y);\\n	}\\n} \\n\\n(1) if you hover on either of x or y in x + y, we claim those are of type\\nObject - this is blatantly wrong, but happens because the selection parser\\nbuilds minimal parse trees in which a good bit of the pertinent contextual\\ninformation is lost.\\n\\nThe flattened parse tree for the method looks like:\\n\\npublic static void main(String[] args) {\\n    (<no type> x, <no type> y) -> <SelectOnName:y>;\\n}\\n\\nSee that the fact about lambda being a method parameter is completely\\nlost.\\n\\nI see this as requiring good amount of work to get correctly. Because\\nlambda's can occur is deeply nested subexpressions, involving numerous\\nnode types, this is not going to be easy solution to \\"enhance\\" the\\nselection/completion parser\\n\\n(2) If you hover on the parameter declaration, you get nothing. This is\\nproblematic as users will identify this as a classic situation where the\\nIDE should help clarify things for them.\\n\\n(3) The hover on the use actually claims:\\n\\n Object y - X.main(String[])\\n\\nThis could perhaps be due to bug 416559 ? \\n\\n// --\\n\\nDiscussions welcome on how to go about solving this or alternate strategies.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Build heuristics based shape discovery capability as fall back.
Description: In the normal compiler workflow, data/control flow analysis is not undertaken \\nif resolution phase has errors. For lambda expressions, we need information from \\nflow analysis right during resolution stage. \\n\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=422801 and https://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=422489\\n\\nexposed problems in our analyzeCode infrastructure's ability to deal with\\nhandling bad data handed to them. I suspect the problem is pervasive and these\\nbugs are just a few instances of the systemtic problem.\\n\\nAt the moment, I have disabled shape discovery if there are resolution errors\\neither in the lambda or its enclosing scopes. This is perfectly OK and will not\\nhave any material effect - other than some spurious *secondary* errors that may\\nshow up during compilation: We may claim a certain method call is ambiguous while\\nit is not, or that no applicable method is found when such is not the case.\\n\\nThis ER is to build a fall back mechanism using ASTVisitor to discover shape.\\nWhile the general problem is not amenable to being solved using ASTVisitor, several\\ncommon cases can be solved leaving only pathological cases unanalyzed.\\n\\nThis problem is only for lambdas with block bodies. We already to use heuristics\\nto some extent: for example if we have seen a return statement without an\\nexpression (during resolve) then we can declare the lambda as being NOT value\\ncompatible - without control flow analysis.\\n\\nLikewise, if we don't see any loops, any throws etc, we can draw some \\nconclusions that could suffice for the vast majority of the cases.\\n\\nThis is not a correctness issue, but could lead to better programmer experience.

Summary: [1.8][compiler] Problems running ECJ
Description: Mea culpa !\\n\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.parser.Parser.consumeNestedLambda()\\n\\nhas this line of code: \\n\\nLambdaExpression lambda = new LambdaExpression(this.compilationUnit.compilationResult, this instanceof AssistParser);\\n\\nthat breaks ECJ runs with a ClassDefNotFound error.\\n\\nFix is simple - to introduce a level of indirection using a virtual call.\\n\\n(A lambda needs to know if it was created by the assist parser so it can\\napply less strict rules for compatibility. Code is being written \\"just now\\",\\nif we apply strict rules, we would often reject overloaded calls that\\nwould be resolved correctly once the completion which was the raison d'etre\\nfor the lambda is done.)\\n\\n(There are also some interesting chicken and egg situations here. Summary: [1.8] poly conditional expression must not use lub
Description: Consider an example like this:\\n\\n  class A{/**/}\\n  class B extends A {/**/}\\n\\n  class G<T> {\\n    G<B> gb=null;\\n    G<? super A> gsa=null;\\n    G<? super B> l = (true)? gsa : gb;\\n  }\\n\\nThe conditional expression is a poly expression (appears in an assignment context) and hence should apply this rule from 15.25.3:\\n\\"The type of a poly reference conditional expression is the same as its target type.\\"\\n\\nECJ, however still seems to use lub computation based on which the assignment is rejected.\\n\\nAvoiding lub in situations like this is important because lub(capture1,capture2) doesn't produce good results, whereas the new rules are much more permissive.

Summary: [1.8] implement "potential compatible" check, applicable before type inference

Summary: [1.5][compiler] varargs overloading problem
Description: The following should compile:\\n\\nclass Test implements IClass{\\n\\n    Test(IClass c, Test t, IType... args) {}\\n    Test(IClass c, IType... args) {}\\n\\n    public static void main(String args[]) {\\n        IClass c = null;\\n        Test t = null;\\n\\n        Test t2 = new Test(c, t);\\n    }\\n\\n}\\n\\ninterface IType{}\\ninterface IClass extends IType{}\\n\\n\\nEclipse incorrectly calls the method constructor invocation as ambiguous. Both\\nconstructors are applicable. So is the first constructor more specific than the\\nsecond constructor? According to the rules of JLS3 in the middle of page 448:\\n\\nThe first constructor has n=3 parameters & the second constructor has k=2\\nparameters. This is the first set of rules for n >= k.\\n\\nFor all j from 1 to k - 1 (1): Tj <: Uj\\nThat gives: IClass <: IClass\\n\\nThen, For all j from k (2) to n, Tj <: Uk\\nThat gives: Test <: IType\\nand       : IType <: IType\\n\\nNote that the element types of the array (vararg) parameters are used\\nin the comparison, not the array type itself. \\n\\nNote also that javac has this same bug.\\nSee: http://bugs.sun.com/bugdatabase/view_bug.do?bug_id=5088429

Summary: [model] JavaCore.newLibraryEntry(.., IClasspathAttribute[], ..) should check for null
Description: I20070109-1805\\n\\nJavaCore.newLibraryEntry(.., IClasspathAttribute[], ..) should throw an exception if the given IClasspathAttribute[] is not null. Currently, null is silently accepted and leads to NPEs when the extra attributes are accessed later.\\n\\nAlthough unspecified, passing null for accessRules is currently accepted (and explicitly handled). Therefore, it's maybe better to continue allowing null for accessRules. Even jdt.core code currently relies on this behavior, see ClasspathEntry.decodeAccessRules(NodeList).\\n\\nI just fixed a broken invocation in our class BuildPathSupport, but such problems may be hard to find in general since creation and usage are quite separated.

So the text needs to change to \\"Illegal type of archive for library\\" or ignore the message when the ClassPathEntry is marked as optional.

Summary: Thread-unsafe manipulation of UserLibraryManager#listener within UserLibraryManager#internalSetUserLibrary
Description: Source based, R3_2_maintenance stream.\\n\\nThis is a fup on bug 154984. internalSetUserLibrary removes then re-adds a listener from the property changes listeners, potentially missing some changes in the interim. Except if another mechanism strikes that would tell the caller that the library needs to be refreshed, this is due to lead to wrong library contents in some cases. \\nA potential path for a solution would be to tell the listener to queue the change events for a while, then pick up any changes when the work that needs the listener not to interfere is done. (Caveats: change events may be destroyed in  the interim, hence the listener should copy the information it needs from them; multiple threads may ask the listener to suspend real changes, which introduces a contention - the ultimate solution may hence be quite different than what I suggest here).

Summary: Strange errors when mixing java 1.4 and 5.0 projects
Description: Eclipse reports strange errors when using Java 1.5+ project from Java 1.4 project. There are no errors in Problems tab but error is shown in editor. In the attached test case problem shows in Test14 project in file src/Test14.java in line:\\n\\ntest.add(new java.io.File(\\"foo\\"));\\n\\n'add' is marked as error: \\"The method add(File) is undefined for the type 'Test15'\\". I understand that Eclipse somehow compiles parts of Java 1.4 project which don't use Java 5.0 features and show only these parts but user isn't told about it.\\n\\nQuickFix suggests following solutions:\\n- create method 'add(File)' in type 'Test15'\\n- add cast to 'test'\\n- rename in file\\n\\nFirst suggestion is clearly wrong as this method already exists (albeit using Java 5.0 features). Second quick fix produces garbage code:\\n\\n((Object)test).add(new java.io.File(\\"foo\\"));\\n\\nWhat's interesting is that resulting project runs perfectly fine both from command line and from within Eclipse.\\n\\n\\nI must admit I have no clear suggestion about how this problem should be resolved, but current behavior is misleading (invalid error message), incorrect (invalid quick fix suggestions) and incoherent (errors are shown, but project compiles and runs fine). It's obvious that user should either be told exactly what is wrong or, preferably, no errors should be reported at all (after all, resulting code runs fine!).

Summary: [compiler] Deprecation problem on inherited return type
Description: N20080911-2000\\n\\nScenario:\\nClient implements interface ISomething. It needs to implement all methods.\\nNow the developer of ISomething decides to deprecate a method on the interface with it's corresponding return type (eg. public void DeprecatedReturnType doSomething(); ).\\nOption \\"Signal overriding or implementing deprecated method\\" is off.\\nThe problem here is that the warning for the implemented (and deprecated) method is not flagged but the return type.\\nAs the client need to implement the interface we force to produce a warning.\\nCurrent workaround: Add the @deprecated tag to the implementing method.\\n\\nSee the following snippet:\\n---- E.java ----\\n\\npackage test1;\\n\\npublic class E implements I{\\n	public I2 foo() {\\n		return null;\\n	}\\n}\\n\\ninterface I {\\n	/**\\n	 * @deprecated\\n	 */\\n	public I2 foo();\\n}\\n\\n---- I2.java\\npackage test1;\\n\\n/**\\n * @deprecated\\n */\\npublic interface I2 {\\n}\\n\\nWhile there is no warning on interface I for I2 because foo() is deprecated, there is still a warning on E#foo as the deprecated flag of the interface method is not concerned.\\n\\njavac produces two warnings in this scenario which looks like the following:\\nE.java:4: warning: [deprecation] test1.I2 in test1 has been deprecated\\n		public I2 foo() {\\n		       ^\\nE.java:4: warning: [deprecation] foo() in test1.I has been deprecated\\n		public I2 foo() {\\n		          ^\\n2 warnings\\n\\nIn my eyes the deprecated return type should not be flagged if the interface method declaration is already deprecated.

Summary: [compiler] Fup of bug 115814, comparing doubles should not be flagged
Description: When comparing a double with itself, we should not report a comparison with the same expression since comparing a double with itself is the only way to detect that this is not Double.NaN.\\nIndeed Double.NaN == Double.NaN returns false.\\n\\nThat code pattern exists in the databinding bundle. Description: Created attachment 149624\\nProposed patch\\n\\nHEAD\\n\\nHere is a fragment of the java grammar from java.g on HEAD\\n\\n      CastExpression ::= PushLPAREN Name PushRPAREN InsideCastExpressionLL1\\nUnaryExpressionNotPlusMinus\\n\\n      InsideCastExpressionLL1 ::= $empty\\n      /.$putCase consumeInsideCastExpressionLL1(); $break ./\\n\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.parser.Parser.consumeInsideCastExpressionLL1()\\nlooks like:\\n\\nprotected void consumeInsideCastExpressionLL1() {\\n      // InsideCastExpressionLL1 ::= $empty\\n      pushOnExpressionStack(getUnspecifiedReferenceOptimized());\\n} and\\n\\nwhere getUnspecifiedReferenceOptimized() constructs a SingleNameReference\\nor QualifiedNameReference as the case demands.\\n\\nIntuitively as well per spec the Name here is guaranteed to be a \\nTypename  (JLS3.0, page 128, 6.5.1) and so we should be constructing\\na TypeReference.\\n\\nThe 4 other productions for CastExpression use TypeReference and the\\nproduction above is the only one that constructs a NameReference.\\n\\nTo give some context as to why this matters - JSR308 adds type annotations\\nto java and so TypeReferences must now be enhanced to capture annotations.\\nName here is really a TypeReference, but if it was coded to be a\\nNameReference for some unalterable reason, we would need to add annotations\\nfields to these types also.

Summary: Wrong warning: The assignment to variable has no effect
Description: Build Identifier: M20100211-1343\\n\\nIf as variable is assigned to itself, the compiler issues a warning, as in the following:\\n\\n  int x = 2;\\n  x = x;\\n\\nThis warning is usually a sign of a programming problem, so for itself it is a good thing to have it, yet in the case that the variable is volatile, the warning is incorrect.\\n\\n  int y = 0;\\n  volatile int x = 2;\\n  y = 3;\\n  x = x;\\n\\nThe java memory model enforces that every thread reading x and y in that order is guaranteed to see the value 3 for y. This is because assigning to x in one thread and reading x in the other establishes a happens-before-ordering.\\n\\nYet eclipse also warns, if this assignment is done with a volatile variable. I think that it should not warn for volatiles or have an option to disable warnings in that special case.\\n\\nAt least the warning is incorrect: The assignment has no effect to the value of the variable but it does have a huge effect for concurrency.\\n\\nNote that in the example above the warning can be suppressed by using\\n  \\n  x = x + 0;\\n\\nYet there is no such hack for references. One case that hit me was when trying to sync the content of a int[]. One thread reads a member:  \\n\\n  myarray[3] \\n\\nand another thread writes the member: \\n\\n  myarray[3] = 2;\\n\\nBecause array members themselfes cannot be volatile, I made myarray volatile and added the following to the writing thread:\\n\\n  myarrray = myarray;\\n\\n(Effecively enforcing a happens-before-order between this write and the member reads in the other thread.) Yet eclipse gave me the warning...\\n\\nReproducible: Always

Description: I20100810-0800\\n\\nWhile generifying the JDT plug-ins, I found some places where I couldn't get rid of warnings because the used API was still on 1.4 (e.g. in TestRunnerViewPart in org.eclipse.jdt.junit).\\n\\nI would like to have a new compiler option to ignore unavoidable type safety problems due to raw APIs. These warnings are not interesting until the API is generified, but they should not be completely suppressed, since they are only applicable as long as the used API stays raw. @SuppressWarnings(..) should only be used to hide \\"real\\" problems.\\n\\nThe new option should modify the existing two options that generate problems for raw types and unchecked operations (e.g. COMPILER_PB_UNAVOIDABLE_GENERIC_TYPE_PROBLEMS, enabled by default).\\n\\nBelow is an example that shows various kinds of type safety problems that should be ignorable. Note that I don't make a difference on whether 'Top' is declared in a 1.4 or in a 1.5 project (although the former will be the common use case).\\n\\n\\npackage problems;\\n\\nimport java.util.List;\\n\\nclass Top {\\n    public void set(List arg) { } // OK to warn in 1.5 code\\n    public List get() { return null; } // OK to warn in 1.5 code\\n}\\n\\nclass Sub extends Top {\\n    @Override\\n    public void set(List arg) { // should not warn (overrides)\\n        super.set(arg);\\n        arg.set(0, \\"A\\"); // should not warn ('arg' is forced raw)\\n    }\\n    \\n    @Override\\n    public List get() { // should not warn (overrides)\\n        return super.get();\\n    }\\n}\\n\\npublic class GenericWarnings {\\n    void run() {\\n        new Top().get().add(\\"arg\\"); // should not warn (uses raw API)\\n        \\n        List raw= new Top().get(); // OK to warn ('raw' declared here)\\n        raw.add(\\"arg\\"); // OK to warn ('raw' declared here)\\n        \\n        \\n        // When Top#get() is generified, both of the following will fail\\n        // with a compile error if type arguments don't match:\\n        \\n        List<String> unchecked= new Top().get(); // should not warn (forced)\\n        unchecked.add(\\"x\\");\\n        \\n        // Should not warn about unchecked cast, but should warn about\\n        // unnecessary cast:\\n        List<String> cast= (List<String>) new Top().get();\\n        cast.add(\\"x\\");\\n    }\\n}

Summary: Surround With... should use positions to track the document
Description: I20050215\\n\\nSee a similar scenario to the one from bug 127692:\\n\\n- have this code\\npublic class A {\\n    public static void main(String[] args) {\\n        System.out.println(\\"ouch\\");\\n    }\\n    \\n    \\n    void foo() {\\n        String s= \\"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\\";\\n        String s1= \\"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\\";\\n        String s2= \\"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\\";\\n        String s3= \\"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz\\";\\n    }\\n}\\n\\n- select the entire three lines of the main method\\n- press Ctrl+1\\n- type 'f' to filter the proposals (this also replaces the main method with f\\n- press <return> to apply the for-template\\n\\n> too much of the document gets replaced.\\n\\nThe problem here is that QuickTemplateProcessor::collectSurroundTemplates uses the (int, int) version of CompilationUnitContextType::createContext. This produces a template context that cannot properly track changes in the underlying document. When passing a tracked Position to the createContext() factory method, this problem would be fixed as the document modification would update the position properly.\\n\\nThe hard part in using a position is that you have to remove the position again after the quick assist session is over - even if your proposal never got executed. One could do this by listening for completion sessions (see ICompletionListener).

Summary: [build path] Default Java project layout should create separate source and output folders
Description: Eclipse 3.2\\nCurrently, when a user creates a new Java project, the default project layout is set to use the project's folder as the root for source and output class files. This creates a very cluttered directory structure for the user, should there ever be a need to examine the project's folder in the \\"Navigator\\" view or in some file manager. Most developers creates a separate build folder when compiling with Ant, so having this similar \\"feature\\" activated from the get-go as the default will teach new (Java) programmers how to properly organize their files in the event that they are not using an IDE.

Summary: [quick assist] Hint to user why some quick fixes/assist can't be executed/are not available
Description: I20060810-1230\\n\\nFor some quick fixes/assists it is very hard for the user to understand why they are not available in some situations. Such quick assists are i.e. 'Convert to enhanced for loop' (Bug 148419), 'Change block to statement' (Bug 149990), 'Remove this qualifier' (Bug 150481), and maybe others (Add serial version id).\\n\\nThe strategy at the moment is not to show this fixes/assists when they can't be applied and leave the user clueless. I can think of several better approaches:\\n\\n1. Show the fix and when applied do not change the code but show an error with description in the status line.\\n2. Show the fix in the proposal but with a diffrend color (red/gray/whatever) and a description in the content assist preview.\\n3. Show the fix and when applied show a warning dialog with explanation what may go wrong.\\n\\n1 may be too strict, we should allow the user to apply the fix although it may change the semantic of the code.\\n2 may require new infrastructure, and I'm not sure if we want to go this path\\n3 is a bit too intrusive\\n\\nAny opinions?

Summary: [breadcrumb] project breadcrumbs for the Java editor
Description: Intellij IDEA has a dockable bar that shows breadcrumbs for the project path for whichever file is currently selected. This is the single biggest feature that I miss when I go back and forth between IDEA and Eclipse. (I use IDEA at work and Eclipse at home.)\\n\\nIn Eclipse, I can right click in a java file and click \\"Show In | Package\\nExplorer\\". But, that only works for java files and it's inconvenient when I want to jump to some higher node in the tree.\\n\\nFor example, if I open the file\\n    $PROJECT/foo/bar/blip/hello.txt\\nthe breadcrumbs \\"$PROJECT << foo << bar << blip\\" would appear in a breadcrumb bar. Each of those nodes would be clickable and open the appropriate node in the package explorer when clicked.\\n\\nI often have files deep in package trees and it's annoying to have to open\\nup the tree manually for all files that aren't java files. Breadcrumbs\\nsolve that.\\n\\nDue to the depth of some of my trees, I've gone so far as to create fake java files in certain locations so that I can open them up and then use \\"Show In\\" to jump to the correct point in the package explorer tree. Breadcrumbs would allow me to just open up whatever files are actually in there and then use the breadcrumbs to navigate there.\\n\\nAnother use case is when I want to open a particular package. I sometimes use ctrl-shift-r to open up a java file and then use \\"Show In\\" to jump to the package explorer and then close nodes until I get up to the location I want to be. Having breadcrumbs would remove the last part of the process because I could just open a file and then click on the appropriate breadcrumb.

Unfortunately the mac launcher completely hides -XstartOnFirstThread from users. Since it does not show up in the launch configuration, the wizard currently does not even show a warning.

Summary: suboptimal solution computed by type constraints (refactoring)
Description: For the following example program:\\n\\npublic class Foo {\\n	public void bar(){\\n		java.util.Dictionary dd = new java.util.Hashtable();\\n		dd.put(new Object(), new Object());\\n		\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nthe computed type constraints include:\\n         [dd] <= Decl(Dictionary:put(Object, Object))\\nwhich leads us to believe that the type of variable dd must be a subtype\\nof Dictionary.\\n\\nHowever, what could have been computed is the less restrictive:\\n          [dd] <= Decl(Dictionary:put(Object, Object)) OR\\n          [dd] <= Decl(Map:put(Object, Object))\\n\\nThis would allow greater flexibility in the \\"Generalize Type\\" refactoring\\nthat I'm currently implementing. Specifically, we could have inferred that\\ntype java.util.Map is also allowed for variable dd in this case.\\n\\n  -Frank

Summary: Refactor should obey formatting rules
Description: Refactoring operations should:\\n a) attempt to preserve the original formatting as much as possible\\n b) when new code is being generated, obey the formatting rules set in the \\npreferences page.\\n\\nI have a specific example of Refactor disobeying the rules.  There may be more:\\n\\n#1) ensure that your formatting rules are all set to default values.  In \\nparticular, 'Compact assignment' should be turned off\\n#2) enter the following class:\\npackage foo;\\n\\npublic class Bar {\\n	int getX() {\\n		return 0;\\n	}\\n\\n	void foo() {\\n		int y = 0;\\n		System.out.println(getX());\\n		System.out.println(getX());\\n		System.out.println(getX());\\n	}\\n}\\n\\n#3) format the class to verify that nothing changes\\n#4) select one of the calls to \\"getX()\\" and choose 'Refactor'->'Extract local \\nvariable'\\n#5) call the variable x (couldn't refactor have guessed this name?) and \\nhit \\"Finish\\"\\n#6) the resulting class looks like:\\npackage foo;\\n\\npublic class Bar {\\n	int getX() {\\n		return 0;\\n	}\\n\\n	void foo() {\\n		int y = 0;\\n		int x=getX();\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nNote that the \\"int x=getX();\\" statement is compacted, even though we turned \\nthis option off.\\n\\n#7) Reformat the class again:\\npackage foo;\\n\\npublic class Bar {\\n	int getX() {\\n		return 0;\\n	}\\n\\n	void foo() {\\n		int y = 0;\\n		int x = getX();\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n		System.out.println(x);\\n	}\\n}\\n\\n#8) IMHO, After a Format and Refactor, an additional Format should have no \\neffect.\\n\\n(20020215 build)

Summary: PullUp of variable disrupts Javadoc [refactoring]
Description: Refactoring problem.\\n\\nWhen a member variable is selected for PullUp, then it is moved to the parent \\nclass, and the specifier 'protected' is added to its declaration. This is great.\\n\\nIf the member variable had Javadoc comments with it, then these are moved up to \\nthe parent class when the refactoring takes place. This is also great.\\n\\nHowever, the 'protected' keyword is added /in front/ of the Javadoc comments, \\nnot between the comments and the variable declaration. This is not so good, and \\nwill probably exclude the comments from being processed correctly by the \\nJavadoc compiler - and just looks wrong etc...\\n\\nFor example, the end result of such a refactoring may well look like this:\\n\\n    protected /**\\n     * The filename of the current image\\n     */\\n    String filename = null;\\n\\nBasically a fairly minor problem, but quite a nuisance as it then requires \\nmanual intervention to correct the code...

Summary: Type Hierarchy shows wrong drop cursor
Description: If you drag and drop a Java Element onto the Type Hierarchy, there are several\\ndifferent reactions depending on the drop target you point at:\\n1. Point at a binary type -> NO DROP cursor: no drop possible\\n2. Point at source type -> COPY cursor: copies the drag source into the target\\n3. Point at the TreeViewer, but NOT at an element\\n  (i.e. besides or below of the tree's items)\\n  -> COPY cursor: doesn't copy, but sets hierarchy's focus to the drag source.\\n\\nCase 3 is confusing. We shouldn't show a copy cursor if we are not going to copy\\nanything. The right cursor for this 'setFocus' action is the LINK cursor.\\n\\nThe current behaviour is even more confusing because placing the mouse besides a\\ntype label highlights the label (even though that label has nothing to do with\\nthe 'setFocus' action that is triggered on mouseup).\\nUsing the link cursor would allow a visual discrimination between these two\\nhighly differing actions.

Summary: Drag member to another Type performs copy instead of move[dnd] [ccp]
Description: DND should be a shortcut to refactoring. But by default most drag operations \\namong JDT views perform a copy. This is counter-intuitive and is bad coding \\npractice.\\n\\nFirst, it doesn't make sense to copy methods, fields, or inner classes. Move \\n(which is a refactor) is a more common operation. If I am using the same member \\nin two places, I should refactor it to a location where I can access it from \\nboth locations. Copying means I have to maintain the same code twice.\\n\\nSecond, holding Control to indicate copy is more widespread than holding Shift \\nto indicate don't copy.\\n\\nThird, if the user assumed a move occurred, but it was actually copy, it is \\nunlikely to cause a compile error, and the user might not realize a copy \\nhappened. But, if the user assumed a copy occured when a move actually \\noccurred, this will often introduce a compile error, alerting the user.\\n\\nIn my opinion, a default of Copy was chosen because limited refactoring support \\nat the time meant that Copy would be enabled more often than Move.  For \\nexample, moving a nested Type into the package as a top-level Type. I think 2.1 \\nsupports more Moves.\\n\\nIf nothing else, allow the default operation to be changed via preference.

Summary: smart * performance
Description: There is swirl around the performance impact of the smart features.  We need to \\ndo some real benchmarks to understand the cost of these. Summary: [1.8][dom ast] Incorrect conversion of JSR308 TYPE_USE annotations on qualified name
Description: Example:\\n\\npackage jsr308.bug;\\nimport java.lang.annotation.*;\\npublic class AnnotatedQualifiedType {\\n	@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)\\n	@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)\\n	@Documented\\n	static @interface NonNull { }\\n\\n	java.io.@NonNull IOException foo(\\n			java.io.@NonNull FileNotFoundException arg)\\n			throws java.io.@NonNull EOFException {\\n		try {\\n		} catch (java.io.@NonNull IOError e) {\\n		}\\n		return null;\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nThe \\"java.io.@NonNull XyException\\" are all represented like this in the AST:\\n\\nSimpleType                         \\"java.io.@NonNull XyException\\"\\n+ annotations: MarkerAnnotation            \\"@NonNull\\"\\n+ name: QualifiedName              \\"java.io.@NonNull XyException\\"\\n        + qualifier: QualifiedName \\"java.io\\"\\n        + name: SimpleName                          \\"XyException\\"\\n\\nThis is incorrect. The first QualifiedName's source range cannot contain the \\"@NonNull\\". In the current API, the legal representation would be:\\n\\nQualifiedType                       \\"java.io.@NonNull XyException\\"\\n+ qualifier: SimpleType             \\"java.io\\"\\n             + annotations: <empty>\\n             + name: QualifiedName  \\"java.io\\"\\n+ annotations: MarkerAnnotation             \\"@NonNull\\"\\n+ name: SimpleName                                   \\"XyException\\"\\n\\nAlternatively, the first qualifier could also be a QualifiedType containing a SimpleType and a SimpleName. Both of these representations have the problem that the \\"qualifier\\" property of a QualifiedType is a Type, but \\"java.io\\" is not a type.\\n\\nI don't have a good solution right now.

Summary: [14] JEP 359 : Records (Preview)
Description: JEP 359 at : https://openjdk.java.net/jeps/359\\n\\nSnippet from above:\\n\\nRecords are a new kind of type declaration in the Java language. Like an enum, a record is a restricted form of class. It declares its representation, and commits to an API that matches that representation. Records give up a freedom that classes usually enjoy: the ability to decouple API from representation. In return, records gain a significant degree of concision.\\n\\nA record has a name and a state description. The state description declares the components of the record. Optionally, a record has a body. For example:\\n\\nrecord Point(int x, int y) { }\\nBecause records make the semantic claim of being simple, transparent holders for their data, a record acquires many standard members automatically:\\n\\nA private final field for each component of the state description;\\nA public read accessor method for each component of the state description, with the same name and type as the component;\\nA public constructor, whose signature is the same as the state description, which initializes each field from the corresponding argument;\\nImplementations of equals and hashCode that say two records are equal if they are of the same type and contain the same state; and\\nAn implementation of toString that includes the string representation of all the record components, with their names.\\nIn other words, the representation of a record is derived mechanically and completely from the state description, as are the protocols for construction, deconstruction (accessors initially, and deconstruction patterns when we have pattern matching), equality, and display.

Summary: [1.8][dom ast] AST for annotated multi-dimensional array type is not well-formed
Description: The AST for a multi-dimensional array type with annotations on the array dimensions is not well-formed. The problem is that for ArrayType nodes, the linearization of the AST (i.e. the source order of AST nodes) doesn't correspond to the language model. This is a new problem, not bug 403834 or bug 391894 comment 4.\\n\\nExample:\\n\\nimport java.lang.annotation.*;\\n\\n@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)\\n@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)\\n@Documented\\n@interface A {\\n	int value() default 0;\\n}\\n\\npublic class TestArrayAnnotations {\\n	@A(3) String @A(1)[] @A(2)[] arr =\\n			new @A(3) String @A(1)[11] @A(2)[12];\\n}\\n\\nThe AST node for the type of field 'arr' is:\\n\\nASTNode type/property  Source range\\n---------------------  ---------------------------------\\nArrayType              String @A(1)[] @A(2)[]\\n+annotations                          @A(2)\\n+componentType         String @A(1)[]\\n +annotations                 @A(1)\\n +componentType        String\\n  +name                String\\n\\nThe problem is that this componentType is just a parsing artifact, but it doesn't make sense from a semantic point of view. As http://types.cs.washington.edu/jsr308/specification/java-annotation-design.html#array-syntax explains, the type nesting in the language model is actually going like this:\\n\\nArrayType        @A(3) String @A(1)[] @A(2)[]\\n+annotations                  @A(1)\\n+componentType   @A(3) String         @A(2)[]\\n +annotations                         @A(2)\\n +componentType  @A(3) String\\n  +annotations   @A(3)\\n  +name                String\\n\\nAs long as nobody could actually distinguish the different array brackets, we could live with that. I.e. it usually doesn't matter whether the component type of String[][] is String[] with the first or with the second set of brackets.\\n\\nBut as soon as we add annotations, the picture changes. With the current AST node structure, it's e.g. impossible to implement bug 409586 correctly, because the top-level ArrayType's annotation is \\"@A(2)\\", but the binding of the top-level ArrayType must have annotation \\"@A(1)\\", because that's the annotation on the outermost array brackets.\\n\\nThe type \\"String @A(1)[]\\" doesn't exist from a language point of view, because the annotation \\"@A(1)\\" annotates the type String[][], not a String[].\\n\\nThe only way I see how we could reconcile AST nodes and bindings would be to replace the nestable ArrayType by a FlatArrayType node with these properties:\\n+componentType: Type (cannot be another FlatArrayType)\\n+dimensions: List<ExtraDimension>\\n\\nThen, the binding of the FlatArrayType would be identical to the binding of the leftmost dimension.

Summary: [1.8][formatter] Add option: "Insert new line after type annotation"
Description: The formatter should have an option \\"Insert new line after type annotation\\", which should be disabled by default.\\n\\nE.g. for the following source, the formatter should only insert a new line after \\"@Deprecated\\", but not after any occurrence of @Annot (even if all other \\"Insert new line after annotations on ...\\" options are enabled):\\n\\npackage xy;\\n\\nimport java.lang.annotation.*;\\nimport java.util.List;\\n\\npublic class Try extends@Annot Object {\\n    @Deprecated public @Annot int b;\\n    public@Annot()int foo(@Annot  List<@Annot()Object> a) {\\n        return 0;\\n    }\\n}\\n\\n@Documented\\n@Target(ElementType.TYPE_USE)\\n@interface Annot {\\n}\\n\\n\\nBug 401848 / bug 403816 have already discussed the problem that type annotations cannot be distinguished from declaration annotations in all cases, e.g.:\\n\\n    @Deprecated @Annot boolean hardToDecide() {\\n        return true;\\n    }\\n\\nI don't think the formatter should resolve types, so the next best solution is to rely on a heuristic:\\n\\n    In ambiguous cases, consider annotations as type annotations\\n    iff they appear after the last keyword in a modifier list.\\n\\nThis heuristic fails for the hardToDecide() example, but that's acceptable (and still way better than the current state, where the formatter produces bad results in many more cases).

[1.8][DOM/AST] Withdraw annotations property from Name nodes.
Description: As part of the fix for bug 391890, ANNOTATIONS_PROPERTY was added to Name nodes.\\nThese need to be removed since the specification has changed to disallow\\nconstructs of the form:\\n\\n    @Marker java.util.List\\n\\nThe proper way to annotate these is to say:\\n\\n    java.util. @Marker List\\n\\nThus the presence of annotations before a certain segment of a qualified type\\nsignals that what follows is a type and cannot be a name. Very similar to how\\nthe presence of type parameters signals a type.\\n\\nSee also:\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c4\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c7\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c33\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c34\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c37\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c39\\nhttps://bugs.eclipse.org/bugs/show_bug.cgi?id=391847#c46\\n\\n\\nWhen we converty a QualifiedTypeReference or its subtypes, we should\\nconvert everything before the first type annotation seen as a SimpleType of\\nQualifiedName/SimpleName and convert everything further as types.\\n\\nCompare how type parameters are handled in conversion of PQTR.

[1.8][dom ast] Bad source ranges for non-marker annotations with nontrivial arguments
Description: The ASTParser has various problems where it generates wrong source ranges with nontrivial annotations. While investigating these problems I found the problem with the wrong nesting of ArrayType nodes (bug 413569).\\n\\nThe problem is that various ASTConverter#retrieve*(..) methods make wrong assumptions about the possible form of annotations. E.g. retrieveExtraDimension(..) and retrieveEndOfElementTypeNamePosition(..) assume they can just skip \\"@AnnotationName\\", but that strategy fails as soon as the annotation has arguments. retrieveProperRightBracketPosition(..) and its callers also use a similarly doomed strategy in trying to find the brackets of an array type starting from the beginning of the array type.\\n\\nThe loops in the retrieve*(..) methods should only skip over TokenNameCOMMENT_* tokens, and otherwise give up when they encounter an unknown token id.\\n\\nThe strategy should not be to scan over annotations, but to use the annotation nodes' source ranges to update the start position and then only scan for the brackets after the annotation node.\\n\\n\\nTest case with all kinds of problems (but syntactically correct):\\n\\npublic class ArrayTypeAnnotations extends @NonNull(int[].class) Object {\\n    Object field = new ArrayList< @NonEmpty(Bla) int @NonNull(Bla) [] @NonEmpty(Blu) [ ]>() ;\\n    \\n    int[][] xxx;\\n    ArrayList<int[]> [][] yyy; // source ranges already broken in AST.JLS4\\n    ArrayList<int[][]> [][][][] zzz;\\n    ArrayList<Float> [][][] zzz2;\\n    Object a = new ArrayList< @TakeType(int[].class) int @TakeType(float.class) [] @TakeType(double.class) []>() ;\\n    Object b = new @NonNull(Math.PI) ArrayList< >() ;\\n    Object c = new ArrayList<@NonNull(Math.PI) Object[]>() ;\\n\\n    void foo(int i) {\\n        for (String tab@TakeType(int[].class) [] = null;; ++i) { break; }\\n        for (@Deprecated String tab@TakeType(int[].class) [][]  = null;; ++i) {}\\n    }\\n}

Summary: [1.8][dom] ParameterizedType's 'type' property could be AnnotatableType instead of Type
Description: In an example like this:\\n\\n@NonNull List<@NonNull List<@Nullable String>>\\n\\neven though the 'type' property can only be an AnnotatableType, the clients need to cast it into AnnotatableType in order to access the annotations. Ideally, clients shouldn't have to use Type@isAnnotatable() or type cast.\\n\\nThe same can argued for the ParameterizedType#typeArguments. However, in this case, converting 'typeArguments' to AnnotatableType.class node has a little problem:\\n\\nCurrently ParameterizedType is not an AnnotatableType and hence we will have to make the former a subclass of latter (to cover the scenario where the type argument itself will be a ParameterizedType)\\n\\nSimilar code can be found in many places such as WildcardType and other nodes too. To make it consistent, we should make all such cases (where annotations are supported) to use AnnotatableType.\\n\\nInterestingly, in the current model, the only node to specify AnnotatableType is MethodDeclaration#receiverType.

Summary: [9] DOM AST for (restricted) keywords in ModuleDeclaration
Description: [Spec: http://cr.openjdk.java.net/~mr/jigsaw/spec/lang-vm.html from 2017/2/23]\\n\\nThe DOM AST somehow needs to model the (restricted) keywords in ModuleDeclaration that look like modifiers.\\n\\nThe keywords are very different from regular Java language keywords:\\n- not applicable in OrdinaryCompilationUnits\\n- not \\"mixable\\" with annotations:\\n  - ModuleDeclaration: {Annotation} [open] module ...\\n     => annotation always go first (that would also have been smarter in Java) \\n  - \\"requires\\" statement doesn't even allow annotations\\n=> we don't need things like IExtendedModifier\\n- unlike for Java keywords, the values of the proposed VM flags ...\\n  - contain conflicts: 0x0020 (ACC_OPEN), 0x0020 (ACC_TRANSITIVE)\\n  - use a different value for keyword \\"static\\": 0x0040 (ACC_STATIC_PHASE), 0x0008 (ACC_STATIC)\\n\\nUnfortunately, we have no clue how the module-info language will evolve, and we also don't know whether there will eventually be more keywords besides the \\"open\\" in the ModuleDeclaration.\\n\\nI see two good ways forward, and I currently don't have a strong preference:\\n\\na) Assume that more keywords will be added in the module-info language; plan for full flexibility.\\n=> Add class ModuleModifier extends ASTNode { ... keywords OPEN, TRANSITIVE, STATIC like in class Modifier ... }\\n\\nb) Assume we don't know the future; don't over-engineer the solution:\\n=> Model the \\"open\\" keyword as a simple boolean value (cf. ImportDeclaration#STATIC_PROPERTY)\\n=>  Add class RequiresModifier extends ASTNode { ... keywords TRANSITIVE & STATIC like in class Modifier ... }\\n\\nMaybe the best solution is a mix of both, i.e. use (b), but call the class ModuleModifier (in anticipation of more modifiers in other places).

(Finality can be considered a strong form of sealing, where subtyping is prohibited completely.)\\n\\nSealing serves two distinct purposes. The first is that it restricts which classes may be a subclass of a sealed class. The second is that it potentially enables exhaustiveness analysis at the use site, such as when switching over type patterns for an instance of a sealed type.\\n\\nWe specify that a class is sealed by applying the sealed modifier to a class or interface, with an optional permits clause:\\n\\nsealed interface Node\\n    permits A, B, C { ... }\\nWith an explicit permits clause, Node may be extended only by the types enumerated by the clause, which further must be members of the same module, or, if in the unnamed module, the same package.\\n...

Summary: Endless loop in AbstractCommentParser caused by JavadocParser
Description: Created attachment 227060\\nProject to reproduce the bug\\n\\nOVERVIEW\\nSelecting code fragments or using \\"Open Declaration\\" on a selected part of code causes an endless loop in AbstractCommentParser:177 and eclipse generates 100% cpu  load on one core. If main thread gets in the loop eclipse is not responding and can only be terminated by task manager with losing all unsaved code.\\n\\nREPRODUCTION\\nImport the attached project in a clean workspace. Open the class \\"Bug\\" and scroll to the \\"TODO\\" task tag. Double click on \\"componentShown\\" in the next line and press F3.\\n\\nRESULT\\nEclipse is hanging in an endless lopp with 100% cpu load on one core.\\n\\nEXPECTED\\nEclipse should jump to the marked method.\\n\\nADDITIONAL INFORMATION\\nThe problem is caused by the JavadocParse. The parser tries to parse the package-info.java of a referenced package. After that the actual source is parsed, but the scanner used by the parser has still the source of the package-info.java. This leads to parsing the same source range over and over again.\\n\\nWORKAROUND\\nDisable javadoc comment processing in compiler options.\\n\\nPOSSIBLE FIX\\nInitialising the source of the Scanner in org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.parser.JavadocParser:94\\n\\nCURRENT CODE\\npublic boolean checkDeprecation(int commentPtr) {\\n  [...]\\n  // Parse\\n  try {\\n    this.source = this.sourceParser.scanner.source;\\n    [...]\\n  } finally {\\n    this.source = null; // release source as soon as finished\\n  }\\n  return this.deprecated;\\n}\\n\\nCODE FIXING THE PROBLEM\\npublic boolean checkDeprecation(int commentPtr) {\\n  [...]\\n  // Parse\\n  try {\\n    this.source = this.sourceParser.scanner.source;\\n    this.scanner.setSource(this.source); //updating source in scanner\\n    [...]\\n  } finally {\\n    this.source = null; // release source as soon as finished\\n    this.scanner.setSource((char[]) null); //release source in scanner\\n  }\\n  return this.deprecated;\\n}

Both classes are on one file with source code and second class is not in classpath and you have not got binaries. You do not want build it. You just want create AST then this aproach where you are searching for binary .class file names are completely fails. This will back you class not found and compile error when everything is fine.\\n\\nQuick fix could be looks something like that:\\n\\n    @Override\\n    public NameEnvironmentAnswer findType(final char[] aTypeName, final char[][] aaPackageName)\\n    {\\n        NameEnvironmentAnswer findType = super.findType(aTypeName, aaPackageName); // invoked actual version of findType()\\n        if ((findType == null) && (_packagePrivateClasses != null) && CharOperation.equals(aaPackageName, _sOriginalPackage)) {\\n            // if we could not find this type it means that could be package private type declared in another .java file. We should inspect all .java files in this\\n            // package to discover it\\n            final String string = getContainingJavaFileForType(CharOperation.charToString(aTypeName));\\n            if (UString.isNonEmptyString(string)) {\\n                findType = super.findType(string.toCharArray(), aaPackageName);\\n            }\\n\\n        }\\n        return findType;\\n    }\\n\\nIf you need more details to reproduce this bug on for ideas how to fix it please do not hesitate to contact me :)

Summary: [1.8][dom] MethodReference#resolveMethodBinding() API should return null for CreationReference of an ArrayType
Description: import java.util.function.*;\\n\\npublic class Snippet {\\n	Function<Integer, int[]> m1 = int[]::new;\\n}\\n\\nIn the above example, CreationReference#resolveMethodBinding() returns a synthetic method binding for the constructor of int[] i.e.  \\n> method binding: Snippet.lambda$0(int)\\n\\nThe binding is \\"private static\\" and has \\"IS CONSTRUCTOR: false\\", hence it cannot be used to identify if the method is a constructor.\\n\\nThe DOM APIs should not create a fake constructor binding for array types in CreationReference as it cannot tell anything interesting to the API clients.\\n\\nInstead, CreationReference#resolveMethodBinding() should return null if the type is an array type.

Summary: -d none option generates package-info.class files
Description: At the Apache Lucene project, we use the eclipse compiler (invoked via ant) as a linter for javadocs. We set -d none so that it does not generate any class files, since we are using it to find malformed javadocs and fail the build.\\n\\nBut if the source code contains package-info.java files, it will still generate unwanted package-info.class files. Practically this means, to avoid littering our source code tree with unwanted 0-byte class files, we can't use -d none and have to create a temp throwaway directory instead, which makes the check much slower.

Summary: ASTParser.createASTs() performance slowdown in 4.5.2
Description: Created attachment 261480\\nSample project showcasing a performance regression in createASTs\\n\\nSince Eclipse Mars 4.5.2 we see a performance regression when calling ASTParser.createASTs().\\n\\nI used a k9mail as a sample app which has 264 compilation units (android application compiled with java 7).\\n\\nIf I use the JDT released with Eclipse Luna 4.4.2 createASTs() runs in 2 seconds. With the JDT released with Eclipse Mars 4.5.2 the same code runs in 100 seconds.\\n\\nAll that the project does is to build the AST compilation units, nothing else.\\n\\nThe sample project that I have does something odd it provides the compiled classes for the source files to the AST parser. This is due to the nature of android projects configured through gradle where some classes are generated by the android toolchain and by laziness I opted for including the classes in to the classpath. This means that the project has both the sources and compiled code for the compilation units.\\n\\nWhile building a small sample project that demonstrates the bug I noticed that if the compiled classes (the ones that match the sources) are stored in a jar vs a folder. There's no longer a regression in performance.\\n\\nCan it be that loading classes from a folder is somehow way slower than loading from a jar?

Summary: [DOM] Via "Double-Checked Locking" idiom lazy initialized fields have to be "volatile"
Description: In \\"org.eclipse.jdt.core.dom\\", the \\"Double-Checked Locking\\" idiom is used multiple times, but without the corresponding lazy initialized fields being \\"volatile\\".\\n\\nA field that is lazy initialized via the \\"Double-Checked Locking\\" idiom has to be \\"volatile\\" to be multithreaded-safe. Otherwise, another thread may get a partial initialized field since the initialization of a non-volatile non-primitiv field is not guaranteed to be atomic.\\n\\nThe double-check idiom wasn't guaranteed to work until Java 1.5. Since Java 1.5 the \\"volatile\\" keyword ensures that multiple threads handle the singleton instance correctly. In \\"org.eclipse.jdt.core.dom\\", at least some of the via the double-check idiom lazy initialized fields have been introduced before Java 1.5.\\n\\nSee:\\n- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-checked_locking#Usage_in_Java\\n- http://www.cs.umd.edu/~pugh/java/memoryModel/DoubleCheckedLocking.html\\n\\nFor example, org.eclipse.jdt.core.dom.ForStatement:\\n\\npublic class ForStatement extends Statement {\\n	// ...\\n	private Statement body = null;\\n	// ...\\n	public Statement getBody() {\\n		if (this.body == null) {\\n			// lazy init must be thread-safe for readers\\n			synchronized (this) {\\n				if (this.body == null) {\\n					preLazyInit();\\n					this.body = new Block(this.ast);\\n					postLazyInit(this.body, BODY_PROPERTY);\\n				}\\n			}\\n		}\\n		return this.body;\\n	}\\n	// ...\\n}\\n\\n... has to be (with \\"volatile\\" and with \\"localRef\\" to access the \\"volatile\\" field only once for better performance):\\n\\npublic class ForStatement extends Statement {\\n	// ...\\n	private volatile Statement body = null;\\n	// ...\\n	public Statement getBody() {\\n		Statement localRef = this.body;\\n		if (localRef == null) {\\n			// lazy init must be thread-safe for readers\\n			synchronized (this) {\\n				localRef = this.body;\\n				if (localRef == null) {\\n					preLazyInit();\\n					this.body = localRef = new Block(this.ast);\\n					postLazyInit(this.body, BODY_PROPERTY);\\n				}\\n			}\\n		}\\n		return localRef;\\n	}\\n	// ...\\n}\\n\\nOr do I miss something?

Summary: [launch] Deprecation of of getClasspath and instead getClasspathAndModulepath to be used in LaunchDelegate
Description: After Bug 525948 and Bug 522333, Launching needs to come up with a wiki/guideline for adopters to follow the rules to support their launch configuration for Java 9.\\n\\nNow thinking about generalizing, currently launcher is calling getClasspath() to get classpath and getClasspathAndModulepath to get the modulepath which is totally unnecessary as getClasspathAndModulepath gives both. I think we can have a constant to define if getClasspathAndModulepath can be used for both. \\nThis is beacuse of the various ways of combination of inheritance. Like Junit has it's own launch delegate and getClasspath but it was calling super.getClasspath where as m2e uses JavaLaunchDelegate but has a totally overridden getClasspath and PDE again has a different combination. Because of m2e failures we had to continue using getClasspath Bug 522333.\\nSo for a launch Configuration, suppose IJavaLaunchConfigurationConstants.ATTR_USE_CLASSPATH_AND_MODULEPATH is set to true, Java launcher can use getClasspathAndModule path only. if false it can use getClasspath.

Summary: java.library.path contains pointers to JVM used to launch the IDE
Description: If you launch an application the java.library.path not only contains the directory of the JVM you are running with but many other directories as well.\\n\\nSome of those directories are from the JVM your Eclipse IDE is running in which causes problems eg to JavaFX-11 because it loads DLLs from an Old JVM (eg Java-8).\\n\\nFor example this is a java.library.path I get when launching a simple Java-Application on JDK-11 from within the IDE.\\n\\nC:\\Dev\\Tools\\openjdk-11_windows-x64_bin\\jdk-11\\bin;\\nC:\\WINDOWS\\Sun\\Java\\bin;C:\\WINDOWS\\system32;\\nC:\\WINDOWS;C:/Program Files/Java/jre1.8.0_172/bin/server;\\nC:/Program Files/Java/jre1.8.0_172/bin;\\nC:/Program Files/Java/jre1.8.0_172/lib/amd64;\\nC:\\Program Files (x86)\\Common Files\\Oracle\\Java\\javapath;\\nC:\\WINDOWS\\system32;C:\\WINDOWS;C:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\Wbem;\\nC:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\WindowsPowerShell\\v1.0\\;\\nC:\\Program Files\\Git\\cmd;C:\\WINDOWS\\System32\\OpenSSH\\;\\nC:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\;C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft SQL Server\\130\\Tools\\Binn\\;\\nC:\\Users\\Tom Schindl\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\WindowsApps;;\\nC:\\Program Files\\Microsoft VS Code\\bin;\\nC:\\Dev\\Tools\\eclipse-SDK-4.9-win32-x86_64\\eclipse;;.\\n\\nThe problem is that JavaFX-Dlls are not part of the jdk-11 install anymore hence they the JavaFX loads the one from JRE-1.8.0_172. Summary: IVMInstallType api and AbstractVMInstallType impl are not thread safe
Description: The IVMInstallType.createVMInstall(<id>) method call immediately makes the vm install visible to everyone. I hit a race condition that looked like this:\\n\\nThread 1\\n========\\n\\nIVMInstall vm = type.createVMInstall(vmId);\\nvm.setInstallLocation( vmLocation );\\nvm.setName(vmName);\\n\\nThread 2\\n========\\n\\njava.lang.NullPointerException\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.launching.AbstractVMInstallType.findVMInstallByName(AbstractVMInstallType.java:146)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.JREContainerInitializer.resolveVM(JREContainerInitializer.java:82)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.JREContainerInitializer.initialize(JREContainerInitializer.java:52)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.LaunchingPlugin$VMChanges.rebind(LaunchingPlugin.java:279)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.LaunchingPlugin$VMChanges.access$0(LaunchingPlugin.java:244)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.LaunchingPlugin$1.run(LaunchingPlugin.java:232)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.BatchOperation.executeOperation(BatchOperation.java:39)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.core.JavaModelOperation.run(JavaModelOperation.java:720)\\nat org.eclipse.core.internal.resources.Workspace.run(Workspace.java:1737)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.core.JavaCore.run(JavaCore.java:4024)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.LaunchingPlugin$VMChanges.doit(LaunchingPlugin.java:236)\\nat org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.LaunchingPlugin$JREUpdateJob.run(LaunchingPlugin.java:316)\\nat org.eclipse.core.internal.jobs.Worker.run(Worker.java:58)\\n\\n	public IVMInstall findVMInstallByName(String name) {\\n		for (int i= 0; i < fVMs.size(); i++) {\\n			IVMInstall vm= (IVMInstall)fVMs.get(i);\\n			if (vm.getName().equals(name)) {   <-- NPE right here\\n				return vm;\\n			}\\n		}\\n		return null;\\n	}\\n\\nThere are two thread safety problems here:\\n\\n1. IVMInstallType api causes new runtimes to be made available to everyone before they can be fully initialized.\\n\\n2. AbstractVMInstallType internally does not use synchronization. Most specifically, access to fVMs list member variable is not synchronized.\\n\\nPotential fix:\\n\\nCan't change existing IVMInstallType api, but the AbstractVMInstallType implementation can be changed to synchronize on the vm type object for all getter and setter methods that deal with vm instances. That directly addresses #2 and allows #1 to be worked around by adding a synchronized block around code in Thread 1 above...\\n\\nsynchronized( type )\\n{\\n    IVMInstall vm = type.createVMInstall(vmId);\\n    vm.setInstallLocation( vmLocation );\\n    vm.setName(vmName);\\n}

Summary: Need additional property for Virtual Machine XML support for execution environment descriptions
Description: We are using Execution Environment Descriptions http://wiki.eclipse.org/Execution_Environment_Descriptions to contribute custom Java VM installations to eclipse. VM has ee.language.level=1.4 and eclipse IDE decides that it has support for JAXP for some reason. This is needed to evaluating VM system properties by executing special class org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.support.SystemProperties used for retrieving system information for the VM itself. This class uses JAXP which is NOT mandatory functionality for jdk 1.4. As result all features of eclipse which use these system properties doesn't work. New property should be added to the execution environment descriptions which informs eclipse to use the legacy org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.support.LegacySystemProperties instead of detecting XML support by language level.

Summary: JavaClassPrepareBreakpoint does not handle wildcards
Description: JDI supports class prepare requests not only with fully qualified class names, but also with a pattern starting or ending with an asterisk as wildcard [1].\\n\\nIn contrast, JDIDebugModel.createClassPrepareBreakpoint() only supports exact class names.\\n\\nMore precisely, when using a wildcard name to create a breakpoint, the underlying VM does fire a ClassPrepareEvent, but this event gets swallowed in JavaClassPrepareBreakpoint.handleClassPrepareEvent() since the pattern and the actual class name get compared using equals().\\n\\n[1] https://docs.oracle.com/javase/6/docs/jdk/api/jpda/jdi/com/sun/jdi/request/ClassPrepareRequest.html#addClassFilter%28java.lang.String%29

Summary: Gracefully handle partial absence of line information
Description: Classes generated at run-time or processed by byte code manipulators may contain source line information for some but not all methods.\\n\\nFor this reason, ReferenceType.allLineLocations() should return all available line locations from all methods that do provide line locations, rather than throwing an AbsentInformationException for the first method without line locations.\\n\\nThe exception should only be thrown when no method of the given class provides any line locations. This is the behaviour observed with the JDI implementation of the Oracle JDK.

Summary: [9] Cannot launch JUnit Plugin test with Java 9 instead of Java 8
Description: DESCRIPTION:\\nUsing a nested eclipse running the JAVA_BETA9 branch on a workspace with another copy of the JAVA_BETA9 branch,\\nlaunch org.eclipse.jdt.core.tests.model.Java9ElementTests als JUnit Plugin test.\\n\\nNo test will be executed, because the projects JRE is Java 8 and this Test needs a java 9 JRE.\\n\\nSwitch the JRE in the the launch configuration's \\"Main\\"-Tab  to \\"Java SE 9 [9]\\" and launch it.\\n\\nThe launch fails:\\n\\"-Xbootclasspath is no longer a supported option.\\nError: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.\\nError: A fatal exception has occurred. Program will exit.\\"\\n\\nANALYSIS:\\nIn org.eclipse.jdt.launching.StandardClasspathProvider.computeUnresolvedClasspath(ILaunchConfiguration), org.eclipse.jdt.launching.JavaRuntime.computeUnresolvedRuntimeDependencies(IJavaProject) is used for the entries, but\\norg.eclipse.jdt.launching.JavaRuntime.computeJREEntry(IJavaProject) to get the JRE.\\n\\nBecause of this the \\"entry.equals(projEntry)\\" never matches, because the projEntry has IRuntimeClasspathEntry.STANDARD_CLASSES, but the\\nentry for the JRE has IRuntimeClasspathEntry.CLASS_PATH\\n\\nPATCH:\\nUse org.eclipse.jdt.launching.JavaRuntime.computeModularJREEntry(IJavaProject) to get the project's JRE

Summary: Breakpoints are not hit if there is an alternate stratum
Description: When a Java class has more than just the Java stratum (e.g it was generated by Xtend, so it also has an Xtend stratum), breakpoints in the Java file are not hit.\\n\\nTo reproduce:\\n- download Eclipse for Java and DSL developers\\n- new -> Examples -> Xtend Introductory Examples\\n- Open xtend-gen/example1/HelloWorld.java\\n- set a breakpoint in the main method\\n- debug as Java application, the breakpoint is not hit\\n\\nThe reason lies in JavaLineBreakpoint#determineLocations, which calls ReferenceTypeImpl#locationsOfLine(int). This one-argument version tries to look up the Java line number in the default stratum, which in our case is Xtend. This leads to either no or wrong locations.\\n\\nPlain JavaLineBreakpoints should always use the Java stratum by calling ReferenceTypeImpl#locationsOfLine(String, String, int).

Summary: Missing Java project context in stratum breakpoints
Description: Before the fix for Bug 368212 there was this fallback code in JavaLineBreakpoint#getJavaProject\\n\\nif (sourceElement instanceof IJavaElement) {\\n  return ((IJavaElement) sourceElement).getJavaProject();\\n} else if (sourceElement instanceof IResource) {\\n  IJavaProject project = JavaCore.create(((IResource) sourceElement).getProject());\\n  if (project.exists()) {\\n    return project;\\n  }\\n}\\n\\nThis fallback code was deleted, even though the bug only required deleting a block further up in that method.\\n\\nThis is critical because for stratum line breakpoints (e.g. Xtend) the source will generally be some IFile and not an IJavaElement. This blocks conditional breakpoints in Xtend in Eclipse 4.3+

Summary: Many debug features break with alternate strata
Description: Many debug features rely on finding the Java source element for the current debug element.\\n\\nThese include:\\n\\n- Change Variable\\n- Logical Structure\\n- Content Assist in Display View\\n- Evaluate Expression\\n\\nand probably some more I'm missing.\\n\\nCurrently all these eventually call JavaDebugUtils#getSourceName(Object). This uses the default stratum of the current StackFrame. But the callers listed above always need Java, no matter what other Strata are available. \\n\\nAs a result, all these features are broken in Xtend and other Xbase languages, which add additional Strata.\\n\\nInstead, this function should really be getSourceName(Object o, String stratum) and be called with the \\"Java\\" argument by all clients that need Java source elements.

Summary: Allow Overriding the JDIThread step handlers
Description: Created attachment 254444\\npatch file for the proposed changes\\n\\nIn the context of the Ceylon Eclipse plugin (https://github.com/ceylon/ceylon-ide-eclipse/tree/master/plugins/com.redhat.ceylon.eclipse.ui), we override the JDIThread class to customize several aspects of the debugging when encountering stack frames written in Ceylon code.\\n\\nIn order to customize step filtering, we have the need to override the step handlers inner classes instanciated by the JDIThread class, but we are limited by the fact that :\\n\\nJDIThread.StepOverHandler\\nJDIThread.StepIntoHandler\\nJDIThread.StepReturnHandler\\n\\nare package-private, and thus not visible from our code.\\n\\nMaking them `protected` would greatly help and avoid us the use of the following fragment whose only purpose is to make them visible and let use override them :\\n\\nhttps://github.com/ceylon/ceylon-ide-eclipse/tree/master/plugins/com.redhat.ceylon.eclipse.ui.jdt.debug.fragment\\n\\n\\nThis change would be sufficient to remove the fragment project.\\n\\nHowever, extracting the instanciation of those step handlers into methods called `newStepXXXHandler()` would also help : we would only have to   \\noverride the newStepXXXHandler() methods to create an overriden version of each StepHandler.\\n\\nYou will find attach a patch file with proposed changed to the JDIThread.java file.

Summary: [1.9] Latest Jigsaw JRE is no longer recognized
Description: The problem is two fold:\\n\\n1. The boot.class.path environment variable has been removed. This results in JREContainer not being created at all. Apparently a container can not be created with zero library entries.\\n\\n2. JDT Core also assumes that the bootmodules.jimage will be the path representing the JDK. This needs to change too.\\n\\nWhile we work on a longer term solution, I propose this short term fix:\\n\\nWhile trying to look up the VM install, let's look for jrt-fs.jar in java.home and add that to the container. And in JDT Core, accommodate the new reality that presence of a jrt-fs.jar means we are dealing with a Jigsaw.\\n\\nJDT Core anyway relies on jrt-fs to get to the modules. So, this is not an additional restriction.

Summary: Add collapse all to Debug View
Description: I work on eclipse.org/osee and we develop a client server architecture.  Because of this, we run/debug a server, a client and sometimes a test suite. For an example instance\\nwhere this can occur, please see bndtools issue 1639: \\"Launch configurations not created with an expected project name\\" (https://github.com/bndtools/bndtools/issues/1639).\\n\\nSince this occurs after a connection is established, and `IllegalArgumentException` is not caught, the `org.eclipse.jdt.internal.launching.SocketAttachConnector.abort(String, Throwable, int)` method is also not called. Summary: Classpath entry jars in run/debug configuration are not used with Java 9 JRE
Description: Version: Oxygen.1a (4.7.1a)\\nBuild id: U20170928-1310\\n\\nCreate a Java 1.8 compliant project p1 containing a single class:\\n\\npackage rde.p1;\\n\\npublic class Main {\\n\\n  public static void main(String ... args) throws Exception {\\n    System.out.println(Class.forName(\\"rde.p2.X\\"));\\n  }\\n}\\n\\nCreate a second Java 1.8 project p2 containing just:\\n\\npackage rde.p2;\\n\\npublic class X {\\n}\\n\\nManually create p2.jar in p2 containing rde/p2/X.class.  Create a run configuration for p1 with the Main class set to rde.p1.Main.  Set the JRE for the run configuration to a Java 9 (GA) installation.  In the dependencies tab, add p2.jar from p2 to the Classpath entries.\\n\\nRun the configuration.  If fails with:\\n\\nException in thread \\"main\\" java.lang.ClassNotFoundException: rde.p2.X\\n\\nNow edit the run configuration to change the JRE to 1.8 and re-run.  The Dependencies tab changes to Classpath, and the run succeeds.\\n\\nIf p2.jar is added to the build path for p1 then the Java 9 run succeeds.  Inspection of the runtime classpath with Jconsole shows that only the jars in the build path are used at runtime with Java 9.  Additional Classpath entry jars on the dependencies tab are not used.\\n\\nThis is a trivial example of something found in a much larger project.  We do not want to all all jars to the build path of the project, just those needed for building.  However the application then fails to run from Eclipse using Java 9, even though all the additional jars have been added to the Classpath entries on the Dependencies tab.

In this example,\\nwe cannot change the signature of E.foo(A), so we can also not change\\nthe signature of J.foo(A). \\n\\nI think the solution will be to generate additional type constraints\\nthat enforce equality of parameter types and return types for such\\nmethods, similar to the way overridden methods are currently handled.\\n\\n  -Frank\\n\\n\\npackage typeConstraintBug;\\n\\npublic class TypeConstraintBug {\\n	public static void main(String[] args){\\n		J j = new C();\\n		j.foo(new A());\\n		System.out.println(\\"done\\");\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nclass A {\\n	public void zip(){ }\\n	public void zap(){ }\\n}\\n\\ninterface J {\\n	public void foo(A a1);\\n}\\nclass B implements J {\\n	public void foo(A a3){\\n		a3.zip();\\n	}\\n}\\nclass E {\\n	public void foo(A a4){\\n		a4.zap();\\n	}\\n}\\nclass C extends E implements J  {\\n	/* no foo() here */\\n}

Summary: [Performance] PasteAction is making selection slow
Description: The method PasteAction.canOperateOn is invoked on every selection change.  \\nThis is not required and is extremely slow on many platforms.\\n\\nThe PasteAction is checking that there is something on the clipboard that can \\nbe pasted on every single selection change event.  This is an expensive \\noperation and is entirely unneccessary.  The check should be done when the \\nuser invokes Ctrl+V or when the user opens the context menu.  \\n\\nIn addition to being slow, it is not correct.  Another application could \\nchange the contents of the clipboard invalidating the check performed on \\nselection change.  I am not quite sure why the selection has anything to do \\nwith pasting other than the fact that on paste, the selection will be \\nreplaced.  At one time when there was a Paste toolitem in the toolbar, back \\nthen it was neccessary to poll the clipboard to toggle the enabling of the \\ntoolitem but I do not understand why that was tied to selection.  I can change \\nthe contents of the clipboard to not contain any valid data using another \\napplication and the Paste menu item is still enabled in the context menu of \\nthe java editor.

Summary: [refactoring] modifying a serializable inner class breaks (de)serialization
Description: I stumbled over a very peculiar bug:\\n\\nI had refactored a static local class out into a file of its own. In the process eclipse obviously also modified the visibility of the two methods\\n\\n	private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream out) { ... } \\n	private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) { ... }\\n\\nto package visibility, i.e.:\\n\\n	void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream out) { ... } \\n	void readObject(ObjectInputStream in) { ... }\\n\\nBut these two methods are used for (de)serialization and obviously, for proper (de)serialization, the *private* visibility of these methods is important! If the methods are not private, they will not be called at all. I thus ran into the strange problem that fields of a class were null, even though they had NOT been null before serializing them. And the (de-)serialization (at first) did not appear to be the culprit, since it had always worked perfectly before the refactoring.\\n\\nI recall that eclipse popped up a list of possible problems, among them that it was going to change the visibility of the \\"constructors\\" writeObject() & readObject() to default, but those warnings were obviously not enough to make me aware of the consequence, that these methods were going to be turned into useless, dead code...\\n\\nSummarizing: the refactoring MUST ABSOLUTELY NOT modify the visibility of these two very special methods!\\n\\nMichael

Summary: Efficiency of TextFileChange#isValid
Description: Build: I20060110\\n\\nI am investigating bug 121571.  Part of the problem is that the EFS method to get local timestamp and read-only state is more expensive than before.  This is largely because an IFileInfo object is created, where previously no objects were created.\\n\\nHowever, from looking at the profiler output of TextFileChange#isValid, I see that it causes four separate file system accesses.  It checks if the file is read-only twice, and it checks if the file is in sync twice.  This can theoretically be done now with one file system call (IFileStore#fetchInfo), but I would be happy if it could be optimized to one IResource.isSynchronized and one IResource.isReadOnly.  That would cut file system access in half.  I don't know the code well enough to suggest a fix, but I will attach the profiler stack trace.

Summary: [hashcode/equals] running twice produces incorrect call to super
Description: The equals() and hashCode() generator in JDT generates different code when run twice on the same class.\\n\\nThe equals() Generator in JDT Source produces the following code when it\\nis run the first time. The following code is an example class.\\n\\npublic class Test {\\n	int a;\\n}\\n\\nGenerating equals() and hashCode() the first time:\\n\\npublic class Test {\\n	int a;\\n\\n	public int hashCode() {\\n		final int PRIME = 31;\\n		int result = 1;\\n		result = PRIME * result + a;\\n		return result;\\n	}\\n\\n	public boolean equals(Object obj) {\\n		if (this == obj)\\n			return true;\\n		if (obj == null)\\n			return false;\\n		if (getClass() != obj.getClass())\\n			return false;\\n		final Test other = (Test) obj;\\n		if (a != other.a)\\n			return false;\\n		return true;\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nGenerating equals() and hashCode() the second time produces slightly different code:\\n\\npublic class Test {\\n	int a;\\n\\n	public int hashCode() {\\n		final int PRIME = 31;\\n		int result = super.hashCode();\\n		result = PRIME * result + a;\\n		return result;\\n	}\\n\\n	public boolean equals(Object obj) {\\n		if (this == obj)\\n			return true;\\n		if (!super.equals(obj))\\n			return false;\\n		if (getClass() != obj.getClass())\\n			return false;\\n		final Test other = (Test) obj;\\n		if (a != other.a)\\n			return false;\\n		return true;\\n	}\\n}\\n\\nNote the additional call to super.equals() and super.hashCode();\\n\\nIf it is run the second time (where it asks the user to overwrite the\\nalready existing equals() and hashCode() methods), it generates different\\ncode. The second variation is wrong, as it additionally calls\\nsuper.equals(). \\n\\nThe JavaDoc of ... states: \\"To deal with reference types of fields and\\nwith supertypes, the implementation calls hashCode() and equals() on\\nreference types of fields and on the superclass (except if the superclass\\nis Object)\\". It does call super.equals(), although the exmple class\\ndirectly subclasses java.lang.Object. The problem is that the operation searches\\nthe hierarchy of types until it finds a superclass implementing equals() and hashCode().\\nIt seems that if the target class already contains equals()/hashCode(), the algorithm finds itself.\\n\\nThe problem seems to be in this code in\\norg.eclipse.jdt.internal.corext.codemanipulation.GenerateHashCodeEqualsOperation:\\n\\n	private boolean needsNoSuperCall(ITypeBinding typeBinding, String name,\\nITypeBinding[] parameters) {\\n		Assert.isNotNull(typeBinding);\\n		IMethodBinding binding= findMethodInHierarchy(typeBinding, name,\\nparameters);\\n		if (binding != null)\\n			return\\nbinding.getDeclaringClass().getQualifiedName().equals(JAVA_LANG_OBJECT);\\n		return true;\\n	}\\n\\n\\"binding.getDeclaringClass().getQualifiedName()\\" returns \\"Test\\",\\nand therefor the method returns false. The refactoring thinks that \\"Test\\"\\nis a superclass and so we also need a call to super.equals().\\n\\nUsing Eclipse 3.2.0, Build ID M20060629-1905 on Win32\\nCVS-HEAD 3.3 as of 2006/08/19 is also affected.\\n\\nTestcase GenerateHashCodeEqualsTest does not check generation of super() calls at all.
